"The Crime That Killed Humanity," it was called. When they discovered the Fountain of Youth. Sure, Ponce de Leon found it first. But we didn't know that until a crazy billionaire that was convinced that the Fountain existed staged a silly expedition into the middle of nowhere in Florida. There, he found the bones. What we used to know is that Ponce de Leon gave up the search and decided to keep on gallivanting around the world. What we now know is that there were a few men he left behind to guard his discovery. Turns out that when the discovery of the century was made, he was told off for searching for something that wasn't gold or of benefit to the Spanish Crown. So off he went, leaving a few men to guard the Fountain. There, they kept their promise, drinking the water. And when we found what was left of them, then we didn't believe them. Even though we encountered something that was life-restoring, but we didn't believe anything they wrote on whatever they could write on - rocks, trees, their armor and clothing. All in Spanish. Curses in Spanish, pleading of God to end their suffering. We didn't know why they wrote it. Only that they showed remorse for having indulged in living. We ignored the warnings, and we paid the price. The Fountain of Youth was opened a few years later. The crazy billionaire flaunted it, drinking it in public, saying that the Fountain was going to make America great again. He wasn't wrong. Those who drank the stuff had their wounds healed, their vision restored. Muscle dystrophy was treated, cancer was done in, the blind regained their vision, the deaf their hearing, it was a miracle - the water healed everything that wasn't right. The religious were chanting how the Fountain was their gift from God (as was he, chugging bottles of it and then cutting himself just to show how the water healed him), atheists were baffled, scientific experiments were conducted to find out why the water healed. That's where science decided to keep quiet. I'm not sure why, only that it did. The Fountain of Youth was never empty. In fact, it was very badly overcrowded. Each time an expansion was commissioned, the Fountain never underscored in attendance. The hardest part of expansion was how fiercely the local wildlife protected it - almost zealously, without giving up. But as soon as the expansion was made, up to a certain point, the wildlife gave up. Whatever animals were captured fought against their captors, baring teeth, claws, rabid. But after a few days they stopped. They reverted to their average behavior. The parrots, instead of shrieking and flying everywhere, resumed their calm melodies and mocking tones of the zookeepers. The crocodiles were crocodiles. Everything was fine with them after a week of drinking non-youth water. The water was akin to a drug in how the body handled the it. First it released a huge amount of dopamine. Then adrenaline. Then it healed any wounds or afflictions. And then it went straight to the bladder within five minutes. That was the concentrated mix, derived straight from the fountain and had flavors added. The consumer version was diluted twentyfold, but was half as effective as the concentrate. But it was tastier, considering how many flavors could be added to it. Health-Juice was monopolized world-wide. And hence why only one company was ever blamed for the genocide. Not like the company exists now to keep taking the blame like a champ. They say, by the time seven years have passed, that all cells from seven years ago are gone and have been replaced with newer versions within your body. The water that was left within your body after you drank it left some minor healing effects, that much was apparent. Then the Fountain ran dry, five years later. By that time, five hundred billion consumer bottles have been sold. Considering that the consumer version was diluted twentyfold. The company was rich, the billionaire was rich, most investors were rich. And everyone was chugging the stuff. Those that didn't chug right away set up stockpiles. When the Fountain ran dry, there was a rapid spike in prices - each bottle, instead of costing ten bucks, cost two hundred. Assuming that the bottles weren't tampered with and then diluted even further until the water's healing effects were on par with the body's own regeneration. The well ran dry not because of overconsumption, but because the water's effects were adjusted by the body. After six months of drinking one bottle a day to heal a bone that was being broken continuously, five bottles were needed to do the same job per day. After another six months, two tonnes of the stuff was needed to heal anything per day. The madness and the quest for eternal youth never stopped. By 2027, humanity was dead. Because of the body's adjusted healing effects, the water became unnecessary. One could make do like Deadpool and heal any injury. Five years after drinking the last drop (for the average human), the healing effects stopped for most people. In fact, due to the immune system's new state of being obsolete, the body rejected it. The water's adding effects did the job better. And then the healing ran out. Wounds that could heal within seconds festered. Bones didn't heal. Those who regained vision and hearing kept their senses, but weren't so different from the rest of humanity when everyone shared a festering gangrene papercut. Whoever didn't stop healing within five years stopped within six. Those who stockpiled their shares were often robbed for it. Vaccines, by virtue of not being needed, killed whoever was injected with them. Humanity couldn't do anything, not even the weakest of injections. Because even the tiniest virus could undo everything. Viruses never go away. Even in the body, they remain dormant while waiting for the right conditions to start the incubation period. And then they strike. That's what happened. The common rhinovirus, a common little cold, something everybody shared..... killed humanity. Few people survived, and only because they were careful to watch their steps. I watched mine. I knew where we were heading. Accelerated healing and youth have a terrible price. A price I never cared to pay. I watched most people I know die, but I didn't care because of how delusional they were, thinking there was no catch to endless healing, tasty water, and eternal youth. I only had a few bottles in my entire life - one to get me up on my legs from the wheelchair that plagued me for twenty years, one to heal my poor eyes, and another for alcohol poisoning. All within four years. Not like I care. I can do what I like, now that no one's here. Now that I think about it, I know why we never weaned off the water. We liked health too much to think about giving up a little bit of living just to experience invulnerability from the common cold.

Negotiations over who will run the PS200m Metrobus network have stalled as bus companies are reluctant to run the service on a completely commercial basis. Metrobus admits public subsidies might be needed to provide a service in the south of the city. The Department for Transport insisted the Busway "is not a public service." A Department for Transport spokesman said the service was open to both bus operators and other users. It said a public subsidy would only be paid if a "commercially-viable service" was not provided. The city's new mayoral cabinet met on Friday to discuss the future of the busway, which has been operating without a dedicated operator since January. It is understood that the cabinet has approved a bus operator submitting an outline business plan for a service, however the Tories have called for a full council meeting to discuss the future of the busway. The DfT said the council could still apply to be the service's operator, or "run the service through a service provider." It said the service would only be eligible for a subsidy if "commercial operators were not able to provide a service which is economically viable." "The cost of operating a service on the Busway is very high, but there are a number of different ways the council can subsidise it," the DfT said. "Therefore, if a council does decide to provide a service, it will be able to consider a number of different funding options." The council's cabinet will meet again on Monday. The Busway, which was part-funded by the former Conservative-led council, opened in January but only two operators - Stagecoach and First - are currently running services on it. An agreement between the two companies saw them share the workload of running the service. However, the cabinet agreed to pay Stagecoach 100,000 a month to run 12 services, with the money coming from the city's budget and public subsidies. The council also agreed to pay the operating costs of 10 buses, which would have run empty between the existing Stagecoach services. The council's cabinet also decided to withhold payments from Stagecoach until they had signed a contract to provide a "commercially viable" service. The DfT has said it will decide whether to provide a subsidy for the busway in early July. It said it would be up to the council to run the service if it was determined there was no commercial operator. Councillor Keith Wakefield, the council's deputy leader, said the council would keep "all options on the table." "The busway has been in operation now since January 2011 and we have had discussions with the operator and also with other operators and we are now at the point where we are going to have to look at whether there is any other option," he said. "The council has never said it is going to run the busway service itself. "We have been very clear about that from the start and it is now time to take a decision about what we are going to do. "The council has to make a decision in the next few weeks about what it is going to do." Both Stagecoach and First have declined to run the service independently because of the high costs involved. Mr Wakefield said he was not in a position to reveal the number of council employees working on the busway, but it was "very few." "We are not talking about thousands of council employees running the busway," he said. "We are talking about a very small number of people and also a small amount of money. "The funding for the busway is not coming from the council's general fund. "It is coming from the Government grant that the council receives for the busway." "This is not about providing a service to people for free. This is about providing a service that is viable for the operator." The Cabinet agreed to pay Stagecoach 100,000 a month to run services on the busway, but the company has not signed a contract. Stagecoach previously said it would not take on any more services until a financial deal was reached. The company's UK chief executive Richard Watson said: "We are in discussions with the council and the Department for Transport and are continuing to work with them to reach a commercial agreement for the provision of services on the Busway. "Until we do, we are unable to comment further." A spokesman for First said it was "still in negotiations" with the council and the DfT.

Proposed is an algorithm for compressive sensing, utilizing image geometry for generating high-quality reconstructions using minimal measurements. This approach can effectively incorporate non-local operators and graph structures to enhance recovery of intricate texture details. Empirical studies indicate significant enhancement in image quality and robustness against noise, diverse image types, and diminished measurements compared to contemporary approaches.

We introduce a general and simple structural design called "Multiplicative Integration" (MI) to improve recurrent neural networks (RNNs). MI changes the way in which information from difference sources flows and is integrated into activation functions, allowing RNNs to perform more powerful learning tasks. We show how this approach can be applied across different models of signal processing for voice conversation enhancement with near-perfect results using Transformer Least Squares (TLS), Kernel Least Squares (KLSS), or Random Forests. We also present several applications that demonstrate its use as an optimization tool on linear regression problems such as those used in image classification.

Scientists have developed a new gene-editing tool that is more accurate than CRISPR-Cas9. Prime editing can mend about 89 percent of the 75,000 or so harmful mutations in the human genome - even correcting for glitches at very specific places where DNA breaks occur, known as "hot spots" on chromosomes near genes in our body cells and tissues, such as the brain. The scientists behind this discovery consider it proof of concept: It works better with bigger genomes (humans currently make up 20 percent to 25 percent of the Earth), but they believe that their work could be adapted to other organisms by simply changing one simple parameter. The team will report its findings online today in Nature Communications. CRISPR was invented two decades ago to quickly tweak single strands of DNA using an enzyme called Cas9, which has been engineered from bacteria, and then snipped out to create a piece just like itself. Scientists use CRISPR to alter all sorts of traits in plants, animals, and microbes; for example, they used it last year to edit eggs inside mice, making them produce healthy embryos when fertilized by sperm containing diseased genetic material. But many biologists dislike CRISPR because it requires complex biological machinery designed specifically to target specific sections of DNA within each cell. Moreover, it tends to cause unintended edits elsewhere along the genome. Instead of targeting precise segments, researchers have tried different ways to cut off stretches of DNA in fish or fruit flies without affecting nearby regions. One group made proteins called zinc fingers that bind tightly to DNA and disable genes above certain levels. In some cases, these methods worked far better than conventional CRISPR, allowing researchers to fix only a small fraction (a few hundred) of allele defects. Another approach uses chemical enzymes called nuclease proteins whose activity depends partly on how much oxygen is present around them. A third method involves chemically modifying the structure of DNA before altering it. This technique allows researchers to insert fragments into specific points of existing genomic sequences rather than systematically cutting away entire chunks. According to the research team, this method eliminated hot spots in Drosophila fly embryos after seven tries. They also confirmed that they were able to correct both disease-causing genes and benign changes associated with aging. To test whether their method would actually do a good job on larger genomes, the Harvard team created three-dimensional structures of yeast cells showing exactly what hot spots remain intact if you turn off most of the cellular machinery required for protein synthesis. The scientists found that PrimeEdit targeted 90 percent to 95 percent of those hotspots, depending on which version the engineers had created. And while PrimeEdit did still result in errors across the genome during normal development, it appeared more stable once the organism reached adulthood. It seems likely, says geneticist Michael Deem, who studies evolution alongside Deem's collaborator, Emmanuelle Charpentier, professor of evolutionary biology, that genetic engineering may soon become standard practice among biologists. She predicts that any alterations caused by prime editing will eventually disappear over time by themselves. That means people might someday be able to get rid of cancer-causing variants - though there are big ethical questions surrounding splicing disease-fighting genes into babies, she notes.

Historical interpretations of John have been subject to considerable change over the years. Medieval chroniclers provided the first contemporary, or near contemporary, histories of John's reign. One group of chroniclers wrote early in John's life, or around the time of his accession, including Richard of Devizes, William of Newburgh, Roger of Hoveden and Ralph de Diceto. These historians were generally unsympathetic to John's behaviour under Richard's rule, but slightly more positive towards the very earliest years of John's reign. Reliable accounts of the middle and later parts of John's reign are more limited, with Gervase of Canterbury and Ralph of Coggeshall writing the main accounts; neither of them were positive about John's performance as king. Much of John's later, negative reputation was established by two chroniclers writing after the king's death, Roger of Wendover and Matthew Paris, the latter claiming that John attempted conversion to Islam in exchange for military aid from the Almohad ruler Muhammad al-Nasir - a story which is considered to be untrue by modern historians.

NASA will test drive a robot underneath Antarctica's sea ice in preparation for a mission in the subsurface oceans of Jupiter's moon, Europa. Buoyant Rover for Under-Ice Exploration, or BRUIE, will spend three weeks in Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys, an ice-free region, as part of the 2019 field season for the McMurdo Long Term Ecological Research (MCM LTER) project. The researchers will test BRUIE's endurance, durability, navigation, power systems, and communications. "We've found that life often lives at the interface, both the sea ice and the water beneath it," said MCM LTER Project Manager Jack DiTullio. "If there's an environment on Europa where there's an ocean that might be similar to Antarctica, this would be a good way to start to understand what kind of life could possibly survive there." Understanding the biogeochemical and geophysical interactions between ice and water in the Antarctic Dry Valleys, which is similar to conditions on Mars and the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn, is a primary focus of the MCM LTER. Ice-covered moons in the outer solar system, such as Europa, are of interest to astrobiologists because they may contain liquid oceans. A NASA mission to Europa, tentatively scheduled for the 2020s, would attempt to look for evidence of extraterrestrial life in the moon's subsurface oceans. The BRUIE has a buoyant cylindrical body that is 3.3 feet (1 meter) long and has a diameter of 1.7 feet (0.5 meters). The buoyancy allows the rover to roam under sea ice for extended periods without having to manage the power necessary for surfacing and submerging. BRUIE is equipped with two thrusters that propel the vehicle forward or backward. It also has a camera, lights, a communications system, a water sampler, and a sediment corer. The BRUIE will not carry instruments to detect life, because scientists do not want to contaminate the environment they are trying to study. "We don't have life detection instruments, because this is a platform for us to go investigate the area under the ice," said MCM LTER Scientist Kirsty Tinto. "It's about going back to the same place over multiple years, which is how you start to understand what type of life is there, how it's surviving, and how it's adapting to its environment." Tinto is the principal investigator of the Benthic Rover project and has been working on it for several years. She recently joined the MCM LTER team as the field season support scientist. Tinto and her colleagues in the Benthic Rover team at JPL will spend two weeks in Antarctica testing BRUIE. They plan to deploy the rover under the sea ice in McMurdo Sound, where the average ice thickness is 6 feet (2 meters). They will guide the rover back and forth as it autonomously samples and records data. BRUIE will be the first instrument to carry out a science mission under sea ice in Antarctica. The rover is designed to stay under the ice for weeks at a time. It will carry a communications system and an electric heater to prevent the electronics from freezing. "We hope to get it to go under the ice, maybe 10 to 20 meters, stay there for a little while, and then come up and resurface through the ice," said Tinto. The BRUIE will be equipped with a radio antenna, GPS unit, and a Wi-Fi modem for communications. It will also be equipped with a pair of sonars to provide real-time data about the ice and water conditions around the rover. The BRUIE team plans to test its navigation system, as well as the camera and lights. The navigation system is based on an algorithm developed at JPL called the Anywhere-on-Ice algorithm. The algorithm works with information from the GPS and the sonar to determine the rover's position in the ice. "We're not going to have a rover that can go anywhere, but we are going to have a rover that can go anywhere under the ice," said Tinto. In the initial stages of vinyl record production, sounds were recorded directly onto the "master disc" during studio sessions. However, starting around 1950 (with earlier adoption by some larger labels and later by smaller ones), recordings were initially captured on audio tape. This tape allowed for processing, editing, and subsequent transfer to the master disc. The master disc was then etched with grooves using a record cutter. Early master discs consisted of soft wax, while hard lacquer was adopted in later iterations. The mastering procedure, initially considered an artistic endeavor, required the operator to adjust for sound variations that determined the appropriate width of the groove on each rotation.

Previously, an instrument's tuning influenced which chords sounded harmonious or discordant. Today, most instruments employ "equal temperament," resulting in a consistent sound for all keys on a piano, organ, or comparable instruments. In the past, many classical compositions lacked official titles, with scholars assigning them posthumously for ease of identification. Modern classical music pieces often include the key as part of their title when they follow typical names, such as a C major sonata or a B minor fugue. However, when a composition bears a unique name, like "Turkish March," "Eine Kleine Nachtmusik," "Clair de Lune," or "Don Giovanni," specifying the key is unnecessary since only one exists for that particular piece.

In many parts of Europe, the natural water fluoride levels are sufficient to derive the advantages of fluoridation. Contrastingly, only around two-thirds of the American population accesses fluoridated water, either naturally or artificially. Approximately half of Canadians have fluoridated water, but availability varies significantly between provinces. However, it's important to acknowledge the existence of natural fluoridation in Europe as well. In England, Spain, and Ireland, over 13 million people consume fluoridated water. Several European countries operate fluoridated milk programs, and fluoridated table salt is available in nine European nations, benefiting over 80 million individuals in Germany, Switzerland, France, and elsewhere. Most European countries finance initiatives supplying fluoride varnishes or rinses to schoolchildren. The absence of a national water fluoridation policy in Italy can be attributed to the presence of natural fluoride in numerous Italian water sources at optimal levels. Salt fluoridation, endorsed by the World Health Organization, is implemented in regions where water fluoridation isn't feasible due to technical, financial, or socio-cultural factors. Notably, Germany and Switzerland, with their low rates of tooth decay, boast the highest percentages of residents reached by fluoridated salt. Nevertheless, individuals on salt-limited diets will not gain its benefits.

By'regular' Mathematics you are probably referring to'pure' Mathematics, which basically boils down to trying to understand numbers, concepts and theories in Mathematics. 'Applied' Mathematics is concerned with those theories and concepts which can be'applied' to other topics and real world situations; think engineering or Physics. TL;DR'Regular' (Pure) is Maths for the sake of understanding Maths;'Applied' is using Maths to understand real situations.,Pure mathematics is done for its own sake, essentially asking "if we assume these things to be true, what can we prove?," and maybe moving on to "how little do we have to assume to still be able to prove those things?" Applied mathematics is concerned with solving real-world problems like mechanics and statistics - as the name suggests, it has applications in the real world. The distinction has become a bit more fuzzy since it turned out even apparently very pure mathematics which was originally done for its own sake can have real applications, particularly number theory being used in encryption. Sometimes this is referred to as "applicable" mathematics.

Electricity stems from a property of matter called charge. Electric charges exert forces on other electric charges through what is known as an electric field. There are positive and negative charging points, those located near the electrical connection between electrodes. If these charged volumes are disturbed by disturbance in electricity flowing around them, the voltage drop will cause the electricity to flow away from the battery pack into the battery pack which causes it to lose its electric potential difference for a short period of time until the battery cells can be replaced with fresh cells. The energy loss from this phenomenon occurs when electric currents flow across the electrical connections between different types of batteries. This process creates heat that causes currents among various levels of charge which will eventually heat up three or four times more than normal wireless conductors such as copper wire strands used today. Although there are many possible solutions available they tend to be difficult to accomplish since most techniques involve attaching multiple layers of metal wires together so that each layer must be separate to allow easy removal within the battery packs using a separate power supply or power distribution system without creating additional cost constraints (such as installation costs). However, these methods have been efficacious enough even if the lithium ion batteries use the same materials as today's batteries because of their relatively small size thus making them ideal candidates for use alongside standard batteries due to their low weighting requirements while providing long life cycles compared to current lead acid batteries. The drawbacks of using wire-connected battery chargers include: the lack of control over voltages applied to devices; the need for additional protection circuitry; the inability to store large quantities of data; and the possibility of defects affecting design values due to corrosion caused by elevated temperatures during discharge processes due to temperature variations outside the confines of typical consumer electronics. These problems may reduce efficiency significantly because battery charger designs typically incorporate a single source of voltage regulation instead of two alternating current sources. Furthermore, battery chargers designed for use alone provide insufficient advantages at higher wattage ranges where one device can generally produce much greater output than another but still achieve similar performance results relative to one unit equipped separately. Accordingly, it would be desirable to develop improved lithium ion rechargeable batteries having improvements relative to existing chargers wherein both harnesses were operated independently rather than relying solely upon individual systems operating simultaneously against a common supply.

Over the last few years, and especially now with the popularity of Bernie Sanders, a heavily debated subject is the raising of the minimum wage to 15hour. While many would expect this to strengthen the lower class and only decreasing the wealth of the upper class, I feel as if it would end up hurting those it is meant to help. These company's would now have to spend much more of their budget on paying employees, and it's not as if they're going to magically have more money. I understand that the increase of wealth in the lower class would eventually circulate back to the business's, but I highly doubt it would be enough to make up for the increased wages of their employees, and it definitely wouldn't happen right away. Since I highly doubt the CEO or other upper management would take cuts from their pay to make up for this, that leaves two possible solutions that I can see: The first would be to decrease the amount of employees. If approximately an equal percentage of employees are let go to the increase in pay the company will be able to function without upper management having to take a pay cut. While those who are able to keep there jobs would be greatly helped by this, for the most part it would just increase the unemployment rate; with these lay offs happening in a large portion of minimum wag paying company's there would be no demand for jobs while the supply would be sky rocketing. The other solution would be for the company to increase prices (for retailrestaurants). With increasing prices nobody would have to loose their job, however it would still end up hurting the lower class. Practically all people get there basic necessities and luxuries from retail and grocery stores- the lower and middle classes especially rely heavily on major stores such as Walmart or Target. Even if your paycheck is increasing you'd still end up paying more the things you already buy, taking a large chunk of your paycheck. While ideally an increased minimum wage seems perfect, it would in reality end up creating a combination of these two things. I'm sure I didn't hit on some points, so please try to change my view on this, I, as a minimum wage employee myself, would love to have a good reason to support raising it. EDIT: Okay, my views been changed. I still don't think something as drastic as upping it to 15hour right away would be a good idea, but I think a gradual increase could be really good. The biggest things that helped my view change were the historical instances of MW rising, the average proportion of price increase vs. wage increase, as well as the fact that businesses are already operating with the minimum number of employees and that jobs wouldn't just become expendable. Thousands of protesters took to the streets to call for Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi to resign. Mr Sisi has faced heavy criticism over his executive decision to give away the Red Sea islands, during a visit by Saudi Arabia's King Salman. The uninhabited islands have been under Egyptian control since 1950. The protesters in Cairo chanted "Sisi out" and "We own the land." Mohamed Hussein, an engineer, told Reuters: "I'm protesting because of the overall situation in the country, not just the islands." Some also chanted "The people want the downfall of the regime!" - a slogan from the 2011 Arab Spring uprising that toppled former leader Hosni Mubarak - as well as "Sisi - Mubarak." At least 80 people were arrested in Cairo and Alexandria, officials said. The White House said the US would watch the situation in Egypt, a key ally, carefully. Both secular and Islamist activists had called for people to demonstrate against the transfer of the uninhabited islands. Mr Sisi was forced to publicly defend his decision to give away the islands, Tiran and Sanafir, which are situated at the mouth of the Gulf of Aqaba. He said they had always belonged to the Saudis and Egypt had simply been asked to look after them. "We did not surrender our rights but we restored the rights of others," Mr Sisi said. "Egypt did not relinquish even a grain of sand. All the data and documents say nothing except that this particular right is theirs." Critics of the deal say Mr Sisi's decision to hand over the islands without parliamentary approval, and only announce the deal after it was done, was improper. Others have accused the president of giving the islands away in return for Saudi aid and investment. Some theories of civil disobedience hold that civil disobedience is only justified against governmental entities. Brownlee argues that disobedience in opposition to the decisions of non-governmental agencies such as trade unions can be justifiable. Brownlees concept of "the principle" refers specifically to trade unionism and its supposed monopoly on moral authority, but it also has implications for other social movements. For example, a group seeking to stop nuclear weapons production could use his idea when taking action against government decision making; an environmentalist movement might employ similar tactics if they felt local governments were impeding their efforts (which has happened). In The Principle: A Primer of Civil Disobedience (2006), Brownlee offers his framework for applying this approach. He identifies seven principles, or guidelines, which are defined by both positive and negative obligations. Positive obligations relate to specific actions that may need to take place within certain situations. Negative obligations concern the obligation not to act upon certain people or organizations, either because some individuals seek retribution after disobeying these rules, or due to a lack of fit between the organization itself and the way it operates. He then discusses how each individual circumstance will require an analysis based on these responsibilities. The philosophy addresses the nature of dissent and resistance from the perspective of modern society. It does so through the application of rights relating to freedom of speech, assembly, association and the right to property - all set out and protected by the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights. These human rights apply regardless of whether said society makes agreement with this list of rights. By using these rights, as well as those he believes should exist under any progressive society including the Four Freedoms (freedom from oppression, freedom of expression, freedom of press and freedom from fear) the author argues that anyone can choose to disobey laws without facing arrest or prosecution. There are several ways one can become involved in civil disobedience activities according to the philosophical theory formulated by Professor Howard P. Brownlee. Some methods include joining protest groups advocating particular issues, forming cooperatives that do not comply with existing economic policies or distributing information about a proposed illegal activity to potential participants. One main method suggests that citizens partake in a political demonstration outside Parliament House where there would be many elected officials present who support the law being attempted to be enforced. Thus as the demonstration progresses, signs that state "We Will Not Comply" move closer and closer to the officers until eventually police begin to surround the demonstration. At this point, supporters standing behind them shout at the crowd to disperse as quickly as possible. According to this model, someone participating in large scale demonstrations should refuse orders given by the police unless shehe feels there is no chance of herhis safety. In most cases however, before a person crosses this line into civil disobedience, shehe must first discuss herhis plans with herhis family members and friends and ensure they understand what they are doing will result in legal ramifications. Other possibilities include advising fellow demonstrators to refuse officer requests to break up protests and attempting to peacefully reason with opponents who have been arrested. Finally, the best course of action suggested by the author involves staging sit-ins inside companies' buildings while demanding compliance at meetings and rallies with senior management, stating that you intend to remain there indefinitely until your demands are met. Introduced in 1949, 1954, and 1956 respectively, the Weston Cadet (model 852), Direct Reading (model 853), and Master III (models 737 and S141.3) marked the initial shift of Weston's exposure meter series towards employing the then-standardized ASA scale. Previous models adhered to the original Weston scale until approximately 1955. Post-1955, Weston continued publishing film ratings, yet their suggested values deviated marginally from the ASA film speeds indicated on film packaging. To utilize these new Weston values with older Weston meters, a 13-exposure-stop adjustment was required according to Weston's advice. Conversely, "ancient" Weston film speed ratings could be adjusted to "contemporary" Westons and the ASA scale by applying an identical offset. For instance, a film speed rating of 100 Weston (prior to 1955) equated to 125 ASA, as per ASA PH2.5-1954 and earlier specifications. This conversion was no longer essential on Weston meters produced and Weston film ratings published post-1956 because they intrinsically adopted the ASA system; nonetheless, the revisions of ASA PH2.5-1960 may merit consideration when contrasting with current ASA or ISO figures.

Driven by the challenge of labeling maps, we explore a problem involving a set of n disks D 1 through D n in the plane, each expanding at varying rates. Upon collision, the disk with the smaller index is eliminated. First introduced in [IWOCA 2016] by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt, we present the initial sub-quadratic solution for determining the disappearance times and sequence. Our approach can be extended to handle other shapes, including rectangles, and remains effective in any consistent dimensionality. By implementing quadtrees, we propose an additional method operating close to linearly, though it carries a logarithmic dependency on either the contrasting speeds' ratio among disks or the gap in their center distances (maximum to minimum). Our findings outperform those of Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt [IWOCA 2016], Bahrdt et al. [ALENEX 2017], and Funke and Storandt [EWCG 2017]. Lastly, we establish a (n log n) lower bound on the issue, demonstrating that our quadtree strategies closely approximate this theoretical limit.

Captain Harris and his crew of eight had been on a routine space exploration mission in the outer galaxy for over three months. They had encountered all sorts of challenges on their journey, from malfunctioning equipment to dangerous asteroid fields. But none of these obstacles prepared them for the ghost that haunted their ship, the Hermes. The Hermes was an old spacecraft, passed down from generation to generation of space explorers. It was said that the ship had been cursed, with every crew that sailed it haunted by a malevolent ghost. Some believed the ghost was a former crew member who died in a catastrophic malfunction, while others theorized that it was a vengeful spirit of an extraterrestrial race they had angered centuries ago. Whatever the cause, the ghost was real. It first made its presence known one night, when the captain and his crew were enjoying their rare leisure time. They heard a spine-tingling moan, followed by whispers that echoed through the hull of Hermes. At first, they brushed it off, assuming that it was just their overloaded imagination playing tricks on them. But as time went by, the ghost became more and more active. Objects would move on their own, doors would open and slam, and crew members saw apparitions of a humanoid figure hovering in the corridors. The ghost did not discriminate between crew members, either. Everyone experienced the haunting in one way or another, and soon they all began to fear for their lives. One night, Captain Harris decided to investigate the ghostly presence, taking his trusty blaster gun and a bag of detection equipment. As he descended into the lower levels of the ship, he heard the ghost's wail, louder and more menacing than ever before. Harris's heart raced as he felt the icy breath of the ghost on his neck, but he managed to hold his ground and confront the spirit. To his relief, the ghost did not lash out violently, but instead communicated with him telepathically. It informed Harris that it was not a malevolent entity, but merely a projection of the ship's consciousness, a manifestation of the Hermes's long history and the ghosts of all the crew who had sailed it in the past. The ghost begged Harris for mercy, not wanting to cause any harm to the current crew. Moved by the plea, Harris agreed to spare the ghost's existence, and returned to his crew with newfound knowledge about the haunted ship. For the rest of their journey, the ghost remained a harmless presence, and the crew sailed the Hermes back to Earth with a newfound appreciation for the superstitions and lore of their trade.

The most important qualification is that one must be nominated by another elected or appointed official at least 21 days before nomination day. Failure to comply with this requirement can result in automatic disqualification from office unless certain exceptions apply such as: failure was due exclusively to circumstances beyond the direct control of the person concerned; failure involved no moral turpitude; and, if it occurred after nomination day, when members could have been notified of their intention to run but failed to do so within 14 days thereafter. Appeals against decisions regarding candidacy may only take place on grounds of apathy, undue influence or mental incapacity according to section 20 (2). The use of specialized tools for nail care goes back to ancient Greece at least, where nail care was done by the same fellow who cut your hair. The tradition was imported to Rome. Getting earlier than Egypt and Greece, we'd be looking at Mesopotamia. The problems with North American were severe enough in late 1965 to cause Manned Space Flight Administrator George Mueller to appoint program director Samuel Phillips to head a "tiger team" to investigate the problems and propose solutions. The team was also given the responsibility of preparing a plan for an expeditious return to flight. Phillips's 33-page report was presented on January 21, 1966. It proposed a 10-month schedule to return to flight, including the first test flight of the new Saturn V. The tiger team was clearly concerned about the deterioration in the Apollo program schedule; a new Saturn V would be needed, and the new launch vehicle would take an estimated 18 months to develop. But the tiger team also recommended that the Apollo 204 launch be pushed forward to December 1966, as if the problems with the Apollo 203 launch were already solved. This was possible because Apollo 204 had been cut from 577 pounds to 454 pounds of payload, and because only a single launch vehicle would be needed instead of two. The tiger team also recommended that the second launch of the new Saturn V be delayed from November 1968 to January 1969, to coincide with the first launch of the Skylab space station. Apollo 203 would be the last launch using the old Apollo launch vehicle. That vehicle was now 6 years old and had suffered several failures. But the problems with the Apollo 203 launch could not be blamed on aging. It was caused by design errors, and most of these were identified and corrected. The problems began at the Cape when the T-10 test rocket, which was scheduled to be launched on December 3, 1965, failed to ignite its second stage. The following day, the first stage of the T-10 rocket failed to ignite. The problem was traced to defective electrical wiring, but the electrical wiring in the spacecrafts also had to be checked. In December, the command and service modules were stacked at the Cape and a second test rocket, the T-20, was readied for launch. That rocket also failed to ignite, apparently because of a problem with the second stage. The launch of T-20 was postponed from January 13, 1966, to January 17 because of a minor technical problem with the T-20 rocket. The launch was again postponed from January 25 to January 27 because of a fuel leak in the second stage of the T-20 rocket. It was postponed from January 27 to February 4 because of a problem with the third stage of the T-20 rocket. The T-20 launch was postponed from February 4 to February 12 because of a problem with the third stage of the T-20 rocket. On February 10, 1966, the third stage of the T-20 rocket was tested, and it worked. At that point, the T-20 rocket was ready to fly, and the Apollo 203 launch had been postponed long enough. On February 12, the launch was rescheduled for February 21. On February 21, the T-20 rocket was launched from the Cape and successfully reached orbit. But just after separation of the second stage, a problem developed in the rocket's autopilot. The command to shut off the engine was never sent, and the rocket veered out of orbit. Object detection and recognition algorithms using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) tend to be computationally intensive to implement. This presents a particular challenge for embedded systems, such as mobile robots, where the computational resources tend to be far less than for workstations. As an alternative to standard, uniformly sampled images, we propose the use of foveated image sampling here to reduce the size of images, which are faster to process in a CNN due to the reduced number of convolution operations. We evaluate object detection and recognition on the Microsoft COCO database, using foveated image sampling at different image sizes, ranging from 416 416 to 96 96 pixels, on an embedded GPU - an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 with 256 CUDA cores. The results show that it is possible to achieve a 4 speed-up in frame rates, from 3.59 FPS to 15.24 FPS, using 416 416 and 128 128 pixel images respectively. For foveated sampling, this image size reduction led to just a small decrease in recall performance in the foveal region, to 92.0 of the baseline performance with full-sized images, compared to a significant decrease to 50.1 of baseline recall performance in uniformly sampled images, demonstrating the advantage of foveated sampling.

They spent New Year's in the deserted cafeteria, his tired eyes gazing at her. Still beautiful, after so many years, heading for the certainty of Nature's resolve. And him, defying that very Nature. Yet he stood silent about his plan. He visited her daily at the care home, where she was lying on a bed with white linens. There had been arguments about what had been happening to him, how he never seemed to age, and he became increasingly isolated, firing all his research staff to keep a low profile, the Disk project abandoned with the room and building sold to an anonymous patron. A tear rolled down his cheek as gazed at her grey hair and sad eyes, eyes that he so vividly remembered as being vibrant and full of energy. As if it was yesterday. More work to be done for the night, he felt that he was nearing the end of the search, he would be successful, although at a heavy price. The wheelchair was waiting to transport her, all was set, it wouldn't be long. The phone rang, but he ignored it, his mind delved in the simulation. A nurse, a thin, young woman, out of breath. She told him of her, how she had told the nurse to call, to summon him to her linen bed, by the flowers. That she had passed away peacefully in her sleep, calling out his name. He told the nurse, in a hoarse, breathless voice, that he wanted to be left alone for a few moments, and the woman exited the room. Because most of these cells do not have any demonstrated mechanism for communication (neurons communicate exclusively through diffusion), these density fluctuations make it difficult to discern their locations with 2D electron microscopy, even if they were available [1]. However, bioluminescence imaging cameras such as JEOL provide excellent visibility into these low-density areas, enabling detailed structural analysis by scanning an entire object section at once. Instruments such as JEOL are designed specifically to address this problem: They use multiple high resolution camera sensors to amplify the light reflected off an object and strike an image sensor array directly behind it. As capacity increases, so does the number of photos taken in this way. This allows several ROI measurements to be made during a given exposure, opening up opportunities for clustering ROIs in dense regions or identifying parts of larger objects that rapidly change in illumination. Physician-assisted suicide (PAS) enables such individuals to pass away with respect and free from agony, humiliation, or distress. Despite potential hazards, I argue these risks can be managed under stringent guidelines. To qualify for PAS, a person must initially be diagnosed as terminally ill and unresponsive to treatment. Second, they must willingly and rationally opt for ending their life. Third, they must personally administer the lethal medication. Lastly, if a physician objects to PAS, they must provide an alternate doctor open to complying with the patient's desires. If morally opposed to PAS, kindly articulate reasons. If skeptical due to legality issues, clarify how decriminalization fails to address them. Please confine discussion to PAS rather than euthanasia.

China blocked Wikipedia in April, using DNS injections to prevent its citizens from accessing the encyclopedia. There has been no official statement as to why the website was blocked. In May 2014, China unblocked all sites on a temporary basis to allow users to access them during important exam period at high schools and universities. In November 2012, netizens began to question whether or not major Chinese websites have actually become "part of [the] state" after it came out that many popular websites are owned by companies with government ties.[1415] On 13 January 2008, Sina reported that Google had temporarily suspended operations in mainland China because of unreliable bandwidth.[16] The following day, Google issued an apology for what they called unscheduled maintenance: We're] sorry about the inconvenience this may cause our users.17] Afterward, several domestic web portals claimed to be able to connect to Google again.[18] It is believed that when Google's servers were overloaded, their IP addresses changed; therefore, when people tried to type into their browsers before 13 January 2008 (UTC 0001), only 404 pages would appear instead.[1920] However, according to some sources, there might also have been legal issues behind Google being inaccessible in China. On 15 February 2010, Google announced that Google.cn is set to return sometime later in March 2011[21], citing increased demand among other reasons. Later reports indicated that problems remain between Internet service providers and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. Even though some ISPs say they can't see any reason for blocking, others claim there will always be censorship due to technical constraints. Some experts believe that the issue may be a political decision by Beijing. Most officials do not directly respond to questions concerning censorship,[22] but only repeat generic statements regarding the protection of online information security. Some journalists assert that the real reason for the ban on China remains unclear.[23]Other analysts suggest that since 2007, taking control over the flow of information inside China has gradually become one of the priorities of Western governments, which could explain why there has been recent tension between them and Beijing.[24] Some social media outlets such as Twitter are accessible via proxy servers outside of China, while others use VPNs to circumvent the firewall.[2526272829] In 2003, Censorship-Free Web Sites published a list of Internet resources freely available worldwide without restrictions.[30] A more current version titled Free Access To Knowledge Online contains content up through 2013. The data includes search engines, discussion forums, e-mail, digital libraries, community portals, educational courses, video sharing services, peer-to-peer file transfer programs, news aggregators and RSS feeds and so forth.[31]

Chapel Bay Fort and Museum at Angle will open on 3 April after years of restoration work. The coast artillery fort was completed in 1891 and is the earliest known fort in the world constructed in concrete. Twelve Victorian forts were built in the 19th Century to defend the Milford Haven Waterway. On display will be the biggest gun and shell in Wales; a 25-pounder gun howitzer, a 5.5 inch gun and a 10 inch, 18 ton rifled muzzle loading gun. There will also be displays on World War One, bomb disposal, artillery, small arms, the telephone exchange and the Royal Artillery forge and workshop.

In recent years, and with the rising influence of Bernie Sanders, the topic of increasing the minimum wage to $15 per hour has sparked intense debate. Although some believe this would solely benefit the working class at the expense of the wealthy elite, I contend that it could actually harm those intended to be assisted. Companies would then need to allocate a substantial portion of their budget towards higher employee wages, yet this additional expenditure does not come with an automatic influx of funds. It is unlikely that the accumulated wealth from a larger working class would swiftly return to businesses to cover the costs of these increased salaries. Since I find it unlikely that top executives or upper management would sacrifice their earnings to bridge this gap, only two feasible options emerge: First, companies may reduce their workforce. If an equivalent number of employees are let go due to the wage hike, the remaining staff will receive improved compensation while contributing to an escalating unemployment rate. This mass layoff would particularly impact minimum wage industries, leaving a dearth of employment opportunities amidst a surplus of applicants. Alternatively, companies might raise their prices. With price increases, no jobs would be lost, but the living expenses of the lower class would nevertheless be adversely affected. Most people obtain their essentials and non-essentials from retail and grocery establishments, with the lower and middle classes relying significantly on corporations like Walmart and Target. Despite an enhanced income, consumers would still pay more for goods and services, diminishing the overall purchasing power. While an enhanced minimum wage appears commendable in theory, the potential consequences warrant careful consideration.

We consider a wireless distributed computing system, in which multiple mobile users, connected wirelessly through an access point, collaborate to perform a computation task. In particular, users communicate with each other wirelessly in order to exchange the information required for their collaboration. For example, a distributed sorting task can be performed by mobile users following a shared protocol that involves local computations and data exchanges. The system may be under resource constraints, such as limited energy or bandwidth, which pose challenges on the design of an efficient communication mechanism. The communication mechanism itself may be a computation task that is mutually dependent on the actual computational tasks that the users perform. In this paper, we address these problems in the context of distributed computation over wireless communication networks. We propose a novel scheme that combines wireless networking with distributed computing techniques in order to allow users to efficiently collaborate in performing a given computation task. Our scheme is based on the use of coding theory to enable communication among users without the need for a central entity. The proposed scheme is scalable and may be used to perform a variety of computation tasks under different resource constraints. We assume a wireless distributed computing system consisting of n users, connected wirelessly through an access point. The users communicate with each other in order to exchange the information required for their collaboration. We consider a general class of computation tasks, which we call distributed applications, that can be performed by the users in the system. A distributed application is a collection of sub-tasks, each of which is executed by a subset of users in the system. In order to execute a sub-task, the participating users need to exchange information with each other. We assume that the users are equipped with energy-constrained devices, such as sensors or mobile phones. The devices may have limited energy resources, which need to be carefully managed in order to prolong their lifetime. We also assume that the devices are capable of wireless communication, and that they can be turned on and off in order to conserve energy. We propose a novel scheme for distributed computation over wireless communication networks, which we call coded distributed computing. In our scheme, the users cooperate in order to compute a function of their inputs, while taking into account the energy constraints of their devices. The scheme is based on the use of coding theory to enable communication among the users without the need for a central entity. The proposed scheme is scalable and may be used to perform a variety of computation tasks under different resource constraints. Our scheme has several advantages over existing schemes for distributed computation. First, our scheme is energy-efficient, as it minimizes the number of times that the devices need to be turned on. Second, our scheme is scalable, as it does not require a central entity to manage the communication among the users. Third, our scheme is robust to communication failures, as the coding theory used in our scheme allows the users to recover from communication errors. We illustrate the use of our scheme with two examples. In the first example, we consider the problem of distributed sorting, in which the users need to sort a sequence of numbers using only local comparisons. We show that our scheme can be used to solve this problem with a significantly smaller number of comparisons than the best known scheme for distributed sorting. Determining a star's mass becomes relatively simple when observable phenomena such as orbiting objects exist. Leveraging our comprehension of gravitational forces and celestial motion, we can calculate a star's mass by analyzing the orbit of an object, be it a planet or another star. The primary methods involve measuring the period of the orbit and the orbital velocity.

The orbital period refers to the duration it takes for the object to complete one full revolution around the star. In parallel, we evaluate the orbital velocity, which represents the speed at which the object moves along its elliptical path. To determine this velocity, we observe the Doppler shift of the starlight caused by the gravitational influence of the orbiting object. With both measurements in hand, we can apply Kepler's laws and related astronomical equations to deduce the size of the orbit and the mass of the central star.

As long as our observations remain precise, the calculated star mass can exhibit high accuracy, often within several percentage points. It's important to note that these principles stem from fundamental laws of physics that have been extensively verified on Earth. The mechanics of orbits play a crucial role in space technology, evident in every satellite launch. Knowing an object's composition, weight, and dimensions equates to knowing its total weight.

The general issue of "squatters' rights" was first brought to my attention by [this article posted here on reddit.] I was appalled that someone could just break into an empty home and claim it as their own and would be protected by the law. After a bit of reading and research I see that the problem was not squatter's rights (which does exist, as "adverse possession" and I still believe is wrong, but I'll leave that for another CMV.) but that the person who broke into the home claimed a verbal contract. Even though both the home owner and the person who was entrusted the care of the house denied it, this makes it a civil matter and the police can't intervene. I think that the law should be changed in favor of the homeowner in order to prevent destruction of the property and theft which the homeowner will never recover. It's true that the squatters were moved out, but in the process they trashed the house and even if the homeowner sued for property damage he isn't likely to get anything. Embeddinghub is a database built for machine learning embeddings. Embeddings are dense numerical representations of real-world objects and relationships. They are used to quantify how similar vectors are to each other in a way that supports learning and reasoning. Embeddings are particularly useful for unstructured and non-tabular data like text or images. Machine learning models like neural networks can use embeddings to understand the similarity between two words or the relation between two objects. In the past few years, researchers have created embeddings for all sorts of domains. They've created embeddings for words and phrases, countries and cities, movies and actors, and even genes and proteins. However, these embeddings are siloed away in academic papers and software repositories. It's very hard to find embeddings for a particular domain, even when they've been published. Embeddinghub aims to solve this problem by creating a database for embeddings, where people can easily search, browse and compare them. Anyone who wants to use embeddings for their research can use the search and compare features to find the embeddings most appropriate for their domain. Researchers who've created embeddings can add them to the database, which will increase the visibility of their work and help others discover it. Theorem of Cover's functional analysis is a significant achievement in artificial neural network theory. It offers a solution to the essential query regarding the number of binary representations (dichotomies) that can linearly represent p points in n-dimensional space. Sadly, its methodology has proven challenging to expand beyond basic issues like point classification. A pressing requirement now is to devise techniques for handling structured data and non-point-like designs, such as invariant recognition where identification of a stimulus remains consistent amidst irrelevant input modifications (e.g., rotations or perspective shifts in images). For these cases, an object is characterized by an expanded perceptual manifold, comprised of analogously categorized inputs. Herein, we create a function counting theory for structured data of this sort, expanding upon Cover's combinatorial strategy, and we establish analytical expressions for the typical number of dichotomies within correlated sets of patterns. As an illustration, we derive a closed formula for the capacity of a binary classifier designed to discern general polytopes of arbitrary dimension. These findings might advance our theoretical comprehension of neural networks' generalization, feature extraction, and invariant object recognition.

On Thursday, an investment manager and hairdresser will challenge the right of the government to start the process of withdrawing the UK from the EU without a vote in Parliament. Lawyers will question whether Prime Minister Theresa May is entitled to act unilaterally, using powers left over from the days of medieval monarchs. It could end up - in theory - with Parliament being given a means to stop Brexit. So as constitutional rows go, it is box office stuff. Or as professor of public law at Cambridge University, Mark Elliott, puts it: "I don't rule out the possibility of the government losing the case." Leading the fight against the government is Gina Miller, who runs an investment firm in London, SCM Private. She argues that only Parliament can make a decision that leads to the loss of her "rights" under EU law. She is confident she has a strong case and is undaunted by criticism. "I do not back away from a fight," she says. "I'm very vocal about things and I'm no stranger to making enemies." She is joined by London-based Spanish hairdresser Deir Dos Santos and the People's Challenge group, set up by Grahame Pigney and backed by a crowd-funding campaign. Also weighing into the case against the government is the group, Fair Deal for Expats. Around two million British citizens are believed to live and work in other EU countries. The Brexit terms have not been decided but expats - some of whom were barred from voting in the referendum - fear potential repatriation and are worried about the impact on their jobs and homes as well as the ramifications for healthcare, their children's schooling and pensions. Three London law firms - Mishcon de Reya, Edwin Coe and Bindmans - have agreed to take up the case. Croft Solicitors is representing the expats. Superstar of the bar" Lord Pannick QC - also an independent member of the House of Lords - will be arguing Gina Miller's case while the government is turning to an old favourite, James Eadie QC. Attorney General Jeremy Wright QC, the government's legal adviser, will also play a big role. He said: "There must be no attempts to remain inside the EU, no attempts to re-join it through the back door, and no second referendum. "We do not believe this case has legal merit. The result should be respected and the government intends to do just that." In political terms, the UK is on course for departure from the EU. But as far as the law goes, nothing has changed. The UK remains a fully paid-up member of the EU until it triggers Article 50 of the Treaty of Lisbon 2007. The question at the heart of the row is: who should activate Article 50? The prime minister or Parliament? During the referendum campaign, the then prime minister, David Cameron, said that in the event of a Leave vote he would activate Article 50 immediately. The government maintains that his successor Theresa May has the authority to do so, without a vote by MPs. That right - they say - is based on the Royal Prerogative - powers once held by kings and queens to do, essentially, what they wished. The use of prerogative powers in a modern parliamentary democracy is a curious corner of British law. Over centuries, power in the UK has been wrested away from dictatorial monarchs and handed to elected politicians. But government ministers have managed to cling on to a few of those regal powers, usually in international affairs. One such prerogative is the power to make and break treaties with other countries. The government's position is that triggering Article 50 is all about ending a treaty with other EU countries and so using prerogative powers in these circumstances is "entirely consistent with standard constitutional practice." Critics will argue in the High Court that it is a bit more complicated than that. They say that activating Article 50 effectively wipes out the European Communities Act 1972, passed by Parliament and allowing EU law to apply in the UK. Lawyers opposing the government argue that the 1972 Act introduced a big constitutional change and gave British people new rights. It would be unlawful, they conclude, for a prime minister to use the Royal Prerogative to take away rights bestowed by Parliament. Grahame Pigney, from the People's Challenge, says the "enforced removal" of citizenship rights from 65 million people would be "completely unprecedented" in a modern democracy. "I believe that, as Parliament has granted us these rights, it is for Parliament to decide when, how and under what circumstances they are taken away," he says. Lawyers working for Fair Deal for Expats will be deploying similar legal arguments but using evidence to emphasise the human impact of Brexit. The chairman of Fair Deal for Expats, John Shaw - who lives in France - has submitted a statement to the High Court saying the referendum result was a "shock." He is currently undergoing cancer treatment in France. He states: "If my right to access healthcare is either taken away, or compromised materially such that I am not able to rely upon it in the same way as French nationals, I would be unlikely to receive, or be able to afford, the same level of care in France." His lawyers will tell the High Court that the rights enjoyed by British citizens "beyond these shores" are so fundamental that legislation is "required" to take them away. But in legal papers setting out the government's case - released last week - it insists that starting the withdrawal process will not have any impact on British laws and any changes will be decided in future negotiations. The Royal Prerogative is just one of the arguments to be aired in the High Court. There will be heated debates about the 2015 European Union Referendum Act, which paved the way for a referendum. In their legal papers the government states that Parliament passed that Act on the "clear understanding" that the outcome of the referendum would be "respected." If Gina Miller wins the case - it adds - it will not be able to "give effect to the will and decision of the people." Conservative chairman of the European Scrutiny Committee, and prominent Leave campaigner Sir Bill Cash thinks the government has a strong case, saying: "To attempt to revisit the decision by another Act of Parliament is a kind of fraud on the electorate." But lawyers at Mishcon de Reya say the idea was to set up an "advisory" referendum - not a binding one. They state: "Nowhere in the 2015 Act does it specify the consequences that should follow from the referendum result." The biggest weapon in the government's armoury could be that the whole issue is not a matter for the UK courts at all. They says it is a complex decision that must be made by ministers. Sir Bill Cash said: "We could have a situation where judges are imposing a requirement on Parliament, via the secretary of state, to make legislation. "That's outside the rules. The proceedings of parliament are outside the jurisdiction of the court." Lord Chief Justice of England and Wales, Lord Thomas of Cwmgiedd, will hear the case - which is expected to last a couple of weeks. Mark Elliott says it is very hard to know which way it will go. "If the court simply applied existing case law, the government would win. The question is whether the court will go beyond existing territory and treat it as an exceptional situation. The court may develop the law." Putting the legal arguments aside, some Brexit supporters say that the High Court case is a fig-leaf for a political campaign to keep the UK inside the EU. Gina Miller disputes that and argues that Leavers and Remainers should back her case against "prerogative creep." "The idea that a court case can put a halt to Brexit is nonsense and it has nothing to do with altering the timetable. What we are looking for is legal certainty." If the court concludes that Parliament must approve Article 50, that could be a game-changer. The majority of MPs campaigned for the UK to remain in the EU. They could, in theory, vote against the activation of Article 50. But would they risk enormous political and social ructions by rejecting the referendum result? Most members of the House of Lords are also opposed to Brexit. That raises the possibility of another extraordinary scenario - an unelected Lords voting against the wishes of 17.4 million people. If the government loses its case in the British courts, they could eventually go to the European Court of Justice. It raises the possibility of a truly strange scenario - Brexit ministers asking European judges to overturn the decision of the British courts.

I won't have time to explain all of this to them. There was a familiar pain as my eyes adjusted to the current situation. My heart felt like it was going to beat out of my chest. I stood there, gasping for air. I stood in place as I watched a stream of people wearing lab coats rush past. They were all trying to flee the building, as a response to the blaring alarms going off throughout the complex. It's completely and utterly rational to run away from danger. Unfortunately, I don't have the luxury of acting rational right now. The crowd continued to flood through the corridor. It was impossible to power my way upstream. Right arm strung back, with hand clenched into a fist. I'm not one for violence, but sometimes it's necessary. 3..... 2..... 1..... Now! Carefully practiced, timed down to the exact moment, I swung my fist forward, directly in front of me, about 3 inches above my level. I put my whole weight behind that punch. I had to, because it's not exactly easy to knock out a 6'1," 300 lbs security guard with one punch. However, just as planned, I did just that. Frank's whole body relaxed before crumpling to the floor, as the unexpected hit knocked him out cold. At least I hope he was just knocked out. Never had a chance to check to see if he was okay. I swiftly pulled the gun from the holster that Frank was wearing, turned off the safety with a flick of the finger, and fired three shots into the cement ceiling above me. The noise was deafening in the cement echo chamber of a corridor. Just as planned, the noise was even louder than the alarms. The mob of people trying to flee suddenly recoiled in response. Taking advantage of the opportunity I had just created for myself, I rushed forward through the crowd. Most tried to step aside to avoid the seemingly crazed gunman. They seemed even more afraid than moments before. I don't blame them. Within a few moments from firing the shots, I had maneuvered my way to one of the emergency stairways that led deeper into the complex. I swung open the door and rushed inside just as the crowd returned to fleeing for their lives. The stairway was empty, as most of the employees on the lower floors had already been evacuated. I sprinted down the stairs, taking them two and even three at a time. I went as fast as I could until I reached the 34th step down from the 5th basement level door. That one always seemed to slip me up. I took special care to slow down and adjust my pace to avoid that step. Navigating down the rest of the stairs and through the following corridors on the 12th basement floor was relatively easy. I had each twist and turn committed to memory. The next challenge was the large door laden with'Secure Personnel Only' warnings all over. It requires a 12 digit pass code that only the scientists assigned to the lab it protected knew. I happened to be one of those scientists, but I didn't have the time to slow down to input the numbers. As I sprinted towards the door, I raised the gun, took aim, and fired the remaining two bullets into the keypad. Thanks to the practice I had, and a bit of luck, the shots ripped into the circuitry and forced the door to slide open. I slipped through as soon as there was enough space in the doorway. Inside was source of the crisis at hand. The particle accelerator my team had been working on had malfunctioned. Or instead, perhaps it had worked better than we had expected. We were researching anti matter in an attempt to find a way to safely gather and harness it as a possible fuel source for interstellar travel. The keyword in that sentence was'safely'. When it we turned it on for the first time earlier today, everything went to shit. The lab was still filled with my colleagues, all huddled together against the far wall. They knew it was hopeless to run. Once the accelerator's safety measures fail, the resulting blast would decimate half the country. They tried their best in the time they had, but there was nothing else they could to stop it. Luckily, I had all the time in the world to come up with a solution. I rushed through the lab to the main switch board. I knew what I had to do. "Alexandra, get over here!" I yelled. She was one of my interns, and for some reason, always followed my orders when I got to this point. Quick to her feet, she rushed to join me at the console that controlled the mile long machine that contained our impending doom. "Wh-where did you go? How did you Alexandra stammered. She was confused, and rightfully so. Unfortunately, there wasn't much time left. "Listen closely," I said, calmly. "I know how to stop all this but I need you to pay attention and do exactly as I say, without question. Got it?" "I..... yes. Of course." With that, we began the long sequence of inputs that were necessary to save us. To save everyone. I couldn't do it alone, as it required at least two people to get past multiple of the security protocols. Under so much pressure, Alexandra did great. She did just as I ordered, and everything was going smoothly until the final moments. It all came down to this. "On three, I'll increase the energy input to the max, while you hit that large red button to your left," I said. She quickly turned to me, shocked. "ONE!" "W-wait, what!?" She was freaking out. "JUST DO IT! TWO!" "THREE!" I shoved the slider all the way forward, and she..... hesitated. Fuck. This was the farthest I had gotten, and in the final moment, that one moment of hesitation made the difference. It was all over for her, our fellow scientists, and half the country. It was not, however, over for me. Just as the blast went off, I closed my eyes and focused. I knew what I needed to do differently. What to say to her. I knew how to save everyone..... I won't have time to explain all of this to them. There was a familiar pain as my eyes adjusted...

This study explores a combined RF and hybrid RF-Free Space Optics (FSO) system in which numerous mobile users send their data via RF connections to a relay node (for instance, a small cell base station), and the relay then transmits the info to a destination (such as a macro cell base station) using a hybrid RF-FSO backhaul link. Both the relay and the destination apply multiple antennas during RF link transmissions and receptions, whereas each mobile user operates with a solitary antenna. The RF connections function as full-duplex vis-à-vis the FSO connection but half-duplex relative to each other, meaning that only one of the user-relay RF link or the relay-destination RF link can be active at a time. In this configuration, we derive the ideal resource allocation strategy for dividing the RF bandwidth resource among the RF links. Our numerical findings validate the efficiency of the suggested communication framework and its superiority over previous methods utilizing solely one kind of backhaul link.
