Fine-tuned pre-trained language models can suffer from severe miscalibration for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) data due to over-parameterization. To mitigate this issue, we propose a regularized fine-tuning method. Our method introduces two types of regularization for better calibration: (1) On-manifold regularization , which generates pseudo on-manifold samples through interpolation within the data manifold. Augmented training with these pseudo samples imposes a smoothness regularization to improve in-distribution calibration. (2) Off-manifold regularization , which encourages the model to output uniform distributions for pseudo off-manifold samples to address the over-confidence issue for OOD data. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing calibration methods for text classification in terms of expectation calibration error, misclassification detection, and OOD detection on six datasets. Elementals with pink eyes held green fire in their palms and watched it dance to the rhythm of the world. Shaman blew powder into the air that turned into sparks and colors, making pictures of the future or the past. Beasts would prowl, left alone and respected by the people. They were great and terrible beats, some huge and feline, they had gnashing teeth and thick armored skin, their eyes glowed orange like demon fire, but they left well enough alone if they weren't disturbed. Some said the king controlled them as he did all things, they were all connected, and a part of each other, and the king would never bring harm to his people. Other creatures roamed the land outside the crater, spreading out in the flat plains. Huge furry monsters with long powerful legs like elephants but twice the size rose from the ground, they were scaly with long snouts and longer flitting purple tongues that would taste the air for their small slits for eyes brought no real awareness. They breathed fire on occasion when the moon was just right, and their cries were heartbreaking in their loveliness. There were strange birds with feathers as sharp as knives that filled the air in great numbers. Their cries were painful and their spit burned. With unpleasant temperaments they were often part of the stories parents told children to frighten them into behaving. The kingdom was vast, and not without violence, yet it was well established on the continent and usually on good terms with the neighboring lands. They were a mecca for animals that provided tasty meat, and the magical gemstones that lay under the earth made them profitable to trade with. The jungles to the west provided them with wood and plants when it was needed, and deserts brought strange power that was found need under the sand. Everyone provided a function, and often rulers would become jealous and greedy, starting wars for land and prestige. The king was always reluctant to send his people to battle without reason, but when they fought they were a sight to behold. Long legs and strong arms would deal devastating blows to opponents as they bathed in the bloodlust, destroying their enemies. They had no had war in a long while. On this day an emissary from north region traveled through the streets, down into the crater and into the palace. He looked upon the King and trembled at the sheer force of wild power that pressed into his skin, taking the breath from his lungs. " There is trouble in the far north. " He begins simply. These people were never ones for fanfare or unneeded formalities. He had been advised that the King did not enjoy wasting his time. " They grow more aggressive, sending scouting parties into our lands. Their water leviathans attack our boats and dry up the rivers. " His tone was slightly desperate as he thought of the people of in his land slowly wasting away from dehydration. " Our Queen sends her love and asks for your warriors. Too long has this enemy coveted our lands, long ago our ancestors agreed they would have the far north, free to explore the new lands, and yet they move south. They pray to wicked gods of wrath and destruction and they will not stop until the world is theirs, even if it burns as they take it. " The king sits upon his throne, made of ice and stone. His eyes are black and bottomless, overly wide and eerie. He sits in silence, only tapping his finger against the arm of his chair rhythmically to a beat only he could hear. Suddenly his eyes fall closed and his head tilts to the sky. He breathes in a deep breath and holds it in his lungs. The air around him vibrates and everyone in the vicinity clutches their heads as their skin grows too tight. It was an eternity in a moment before he opened his eyes and smiled a crooked dark smile that promised death and darkness. His calm spoke volumes and the emissary knew that this man, if he was even a man had just communicated with the earth itself. " I know this enemy. We have aided your Queen before and our love runs deep and strong. " He stands to an impossible height and his blood red wrap crosses his shoulder and trails onto the ground. His steps make the stone quake and the vines crawling over the throne reach out desperately towards him, beckoning their king back. He lays a hand on the emissary's shoulder and forces him to rise. He looks into his eyes, still smiling a terrible smile, and the man was afraid. " I have thought long of this even before your arrival. " The king says softly, yet it seems his voice comes from all corners of the room. " I am not rash. " A murmur of arrogance rumbles from the other elders. " Tell your queen we will go to war. "

The portrayal of John's historical narrative has undergone significant transformations throughout history. Early medieval chronicles penned during or soon after his reign served as the initial sources. Among these were Richard of Devizes, William of Newburgh, Roger of Hoveden, and Ralph de Diceto, who documented John's reign's formative years, displaying a mixed perspective – critical of his behavior during Richard's rule yet somewhat favorable toward the start of John's reign. However, credible narratives of the middle and late periods of his reign are scarce. Gervase of Canterbury and Ralph of Coggeshall are the primary sources; their depictions of John's kingship were unfavorable. Posthumous accounts substantially shaped John's negative reputation, with Roger of Wendover and Matthew Paris contributing significantly. The latter asserted that John sought Islamic conversion for military support from Muhammad al-Nasir, an Almohad ruler – a claim now discredited by modern historians.

John Culshaw's family, who lost him in a stabbing incident in Wigan in 1993, were not informed that his remains, specifically his stomach and liver, had been preserved by Greater Manchester Police (GMP) after two autopsies. Over 50 other families have also been informed their deceased loved ones' body parts were stored by the police force. GMP deliberated on whether to reach out to these families for several months prior to doing so. Mrs. Jennifer Shaw, John's mother, expressed her dismay over the delay, stating, "He's my son. And he's been left – half of him." She would have consented to the use of his organs had she been consulted.

The discovery of the retained body parts came about due to an audit of the ex-Forensic Science Service in 2014, during which more than 180 samples, including significant organs, from crime victims in Greater Manchester were identified as being in police custody. Since 2006, it has been against the law to take or preserve human tissue without the families' approval following a scandal at Liverpool's Alder Hey Hospital involving the covert removal of organs from hundreds of deceased infants. The preserved specimens held by Greater Manchester Police were obtained prior to this legislation.

Assistant Chief Constable Debbie Ford commented, "When we became aware of the samples, we realized that this delicate matter would never just be about adhering to the rules or the law. For this reason, we sought guidance from numerous stakeholders, including community and religious organizations, as well as our internal Ethics Committee. After thorough consultation, it was determined that we possessed both an ethical and moral obligation to address this situation."

The Turing Machine is the paradigmatic case of computing machines, but there are others, such as Artificial Neural Networks, Table Computing, Relational-Indeterminate Computing and diverse forms of analogical computing, each of which based on a particular underlying intuition of the phenomenon of computing. This variety can be captured in terms of system levels, re-interpreting and generalizing Newell's hierarchy, which includes the knowledge level at the top and the symbol level immediately below it. In this re-interpretation the knowledge level consists of human knowledge and the symbol level is generalized into a new level that here is called The Mode of Computing. Natural computing performed by the brains of humans and non-human animals with a developed enough neural system should be understood in terms of a hierarchy of system levels too. By analogy from standard computing machinery there must be a system level above the neural circuitry levels and directly below the knowledge level that is named here The mode of Natural Computing. A central question for Cognition is the characterization of this mode. The Mode of Computing provides a novel perspective on the phenomena of computing, interpreting, the representational and non-representational views of cognition, and consciousness.

Most of the literature on neural network quantization requires some training of the quantized model (fine-tuning). However, this training is not always possible in real-world scenarios, as it requires the availability of the full model and the original training data. Moreover, even if we are able to train the quantized model, it might not be easy to deploy it in the end system due to its proprietary nature (e.g., in neural network accelerators). In this paper, we study the performance of different state-of-the-art quantization schemes in the case when we have no training data and no access to the full model. We show that it is possible to match the accuracy of the full-precision model for some classification tasks in a scalable way without any training. Our approach is a generalization of the "quantization-aware training" proposed in and for 3-bit weights to a generic number of quantization bits. Furthermore, we show that, in certain cases, the resulting quantized model is deployable in proprietary neural network accelerators.

You're misinterpreting why astronauts feel microgravity. It's not due to their distance from Earth, but rather their state of freefall. If you constructed a tower reaching the ISS's altitude and stood on a scale at its pinnacle, you'd discover you weighed approximately 90 times your Earth-bound weight. Imagine the foundation beneath you suddenly crumbled. Instantaneously, according to the scale, you'd weigh nothing. This is analogous to astronauts and the space station, except they're moving so rapidly laterally that the Earth's curvature keeps them touching the Earth or maintaining a constant altitude. However, at the Moon's orbit, Earth's gravitational pull is notably reduced. Using Newton's law of gravity, you can determine that each kilogram of lunar material experiences less than 0.003% of the force of a kilogram on Earth's surface. Although Earth's gravity is weakened in this region, it still manages to keep the Moon in orbit. The Moon orbits significantly slower (1.0 km/s) compared to the ISS (7.7 km/s), and Earth's gravity has 28.5 days to influence its orbit rather than 90 minutes.

During the Hellenistic period, many different schools of thought developed. Athens, with its multiple philosophical schools, continued to remain the center of philosophical thought. However Athens had now lost her political freedom and Hellenistic philosophy is a reflection of this new difficult period. In this political climate, Hellenistic philosophers went in search of goals such as ataraxia (un-disturbedness), autarky (self-sufficiency) and apatheia (freedom from suffering), which would allow them to wrest well-being or eudaimonia out of the most difficult turns of fortune. This occupation with the inner life, with personal inner liberty and with the pursuit of eudaimonia is what all Hellenistic philosophical schools have in common.

Following the impact of light waves on retinal receptors, small electric impulses are generated in the optic nerve. Considered as a conduit, the optic nerve transports these impulses towards the brain's visual cortex. Upon arrival, the brain initiates a recognition process, comparing current inputs with stored memories and past responses. Electrical activity ensues throughout the brain as it identifies patterns by assessing color groups, object sizes, and myriad other nuanced details. The optical center employs a sophisticated associative network to distinguish and categorize these patterns as distinct objects. Subsequently, the pattern-recall area of the brain matches these identified objects against stored memories: What prior experiences share similarities with the present perception? Primed memories are then readily accessible for activation upon encountering corresponding stimuli. This intricate process encompasses numerous mental leaps from raw data, such as "That is a mass of red," to conclusions, like "That is a ripe tomato." When recognizing shapes in the sky, this is your brain creating order out of ambiguity. Having prepared a collection of potential matches and roughly determined context, the processed patterns are forwarded to the analytical portion of your brain in a succinct form. In contrast to the comprehensive sequence of "That's a person. That's a red dress. The red dress is nearer than the person. The red dress covers the person. The red dress is static," the condensed representation reaches the thinking section as "The person is wearing a red dress."

While constitutional law concerns the European Union's governance structure, administrative law binds EU institutions and member states to follow the law. Both member states and the Commission have a general obligation to respect the law. In case of disputes between EU institutions or between the EU institutions and a member state, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) is the sole competent institution to resolve such disputes. The CJEU is the supreme court in the area of EU law. The CJEU is based in Luxembourg, but judges sit in panels of three throughout the EU in order to hear cases. The CJEU has two types of jurisdiction. First, it can hear preliminary references, which are essentially questions from EU institutions or member states which ask if a particular action is compatible with EU law. This type of case is inquisitorial in nature: the Court is obliged to give an opinion in the matter, but it is not required to decide on the merits of the case, as is the case in most national courts. Second, the CJEU can hear cases at the request of a member state, where the member state has been sued by an individual or private party. In this case, the CJEU can resolve the case on the merits or the CJEU can transfer the case to a national court. The CJEU can also hear cases which arise from EU regulations or directives. The CJEU consists of 28 judges, who are appointed by the Council of the European Union and the European Parliament. The judges are elected for a renewable term of 6 years. The CJEU's role in the EU judicial system is, in essence, to ensure the uniform application of EU law throughout the EU. The CJEU is not able to issue a ruling that differs from the position of the European Commission or the Court of Justice. The CJEU is, therefore, essentially bound by the positions of the Commission and the Court of Justice, and it is only in very rare circumstances that the CJEU can issue a different ruling. The CJEU has no power to create new EU law. All legislation is drafted by the Commission, who puts the legislation to the Council of the European Union and the European Parliament for approval. The CJEU can annul European legislation where the legislation is incompatible with EU law. This is the only way in which the CJEU can actually limit EU law. The CJEU is not infallible. It is possible for the CJEU to be overruled by the European Court of Human Rights. In addition to the CJEU, member states can bring actions against EU institutions or member states in the national courts. In some cases, member states may prefer to litigate in a national court, rather than in the CJEU, because a national court is usually more familiar with the laws and regulations of a member state than the CJEU. If a member state is sued by a private party in a national court, the national court can issue a preliminary ruling to the CJEU, asking if the action is compatible with EU law. In addition, a member state may be sued in a national court by an EU institution. Member states are, in effect, "sui generis" parties to EU law: the CJEU can issue a ruling against a member state without the member state having to ask the CJEU to do so. EU institutions are therefore often bound by the decision of the CJEU, and they will usually seek a ruling from the CJEU in advance of bringing an action against a member state. The CJEU's role in the EU judicial system is to ensure uniform application of EU law.

A fully automated knee MRI segmentation method to study osteoarthritis (OA) was developed using a novel hierarchical set of random forests (RF) classifiers to learn the appearance of cartilage regions and their boundaries. A neighborhood approximation forest is used first to provide contextual feature to the second-level RF classifier that also considers local features and produces location-specific costs for the layered optimal graph image segmentation of multiple objects and surfaces (LOGISMOS) framework. Double echo steady state (DESS) MRIs used in this work originated from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) study. Trained on 34 MRIs with varying degrees of OA, the performance of the learning-based method tested on 108 MRIs showed significant reduction in segmentation errors (p 0.05) compared with the conventional gradient-based and single-stage RF-learned costs. The 3D LOGISMOS was extended to longitudinal-3D (4D) to simultaneously segment multiple follow-up visits of the same patient. As such, data from all time-points of the temporal sequence contribute information to a single optimal solution that utilizes both spatial 3D and temporal contexts. 4D LOGISMOS validation on 108 MRIs from baseline and 12 month follow-up scans of 54 patients showed significant reduction in segmentation errors (p 0.01) compared to 3D. Finally, the potential of 4D LOGISMOS was further explored on the same 54 patients using 5 annual follow-up scans demonstrating a significant improvement of measuring cartilage thickness (p 0.01) compared to the sequential 3D approach.

In this study, we present a novel approach for creating an image of an object based on specified text attributes, using a pre-existing image as a foundation. Building upon previous research in text-to-image generation primarily concentrating on object appearance, our technique prioritizes maintaining the provided contextual information within the generated image – a first in this domain. To address the challenge, we suggest a multi-conditional Generative Adversarial Network (MC-GAN), capable of managing both object and background data simultaneously. A key element of MC-GAN is a synthesis block designed to separate object and background information during training. This mechanism allows MC-GAN to produce lifelike object images with the intended background while regulating the influence of the background information from the input base image using the foreground details from the text attributes. Throughout its existence, Warsaw has been a multi-cultural city. According to the 1901 census, out of 711,988 inhabitants 56.2 were Catholics, 35.7 Jews, 5 Greek orthodox Christians and 2.8 Protestants. Nowadays it is estimated that 1,500,000 people live in the city. The city has been a seat of government for many years, in the 16th century for the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, in the 18th century the capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and in the 19th and 20th centuries the capital of Poland. The city was also the capital of the Second Polish Republic in , as well as the capital of the Polish People's Republic in . The city played an important role in World War II. On 1 September 1939, it was the site of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, when Jewish insurgents fought for almost a month, despite being heavily outgunned and outnumbered, the Germans ultimately crushed the rebellion. As a result of the war, the city was completely destroyed, and the population was decimated by death, starvation, and deportation. Today the city is Poland's capital and its largest, most populous, and most cosmopolitan. The city's largest and most recognizable landmark is the Royal Castle, a castle built in the 14th century for the Polish kings. The Old Town was built in the 13th century by the King of Poland Casimir III the Great. The Old Town was nearly completely destroyed during the Warsaw Uprising in World War II. The Warsaw Uprising was an insurrection staged in the Polish capital of Warsaw between 1 August 1944 and 2 October 1944, during the German occupation of Poland in World War II. The uprising began when the Red Army had captured the suburbs of Warsaw and the Polish capital was surrounded by the Soviet forces, but was not yet liberated by the Red Army. The insurrection was a response to Nazi Germany's plan to destroy the Polish capital. The Germans intended to destroy the city to prevent the Polish resistance from using the capital as a base for further resistance and a springboard to launch a general uprising, and to make an example of the city and its inhabitants to deter other cities from resisting. The Warsaw Uprising was the most important armed resistance effort by any European capital during World War II. The uprising was led by the Polish Home Army (Polish: Armia Krajowa, or AK), the dominant Polish resistance group, which remained committed to the Polish government-in-exile in London. The AK prepared for the uprising for many months before the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, and was the only armed resistance group operating in the city. The members of the AK formed a military structure based on the Armia Krajowa system that had been set up in occupied Poland at the beginning of the war. In recent decades, a number of profound theorems concerning approximation of hard counting problems have appeared. These include estimation of the permanent, estimating the volume of a convex polyhedron, and counting (approximately) the number of linear extensions of a partially ordered set. All of these results have been achieved using probabilistic sampling methods, specifically Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) techniques. In each case, a rapidly mixing Markov chain is defined that is guaranteed to produce, with high probability, an accurate result after only a polynomial number of operations. Although of polynomial complexity, none of these results lead to a practical computational technique, nor do they claim to. The polynomials are of high degree and a non-trivial amount of computing is required to get even a single sample. Our aim in this paper is to present practical Monte Carlo methods for one of these problems, counting linear extensions. Like related work on estimating the coefficients of the reliability polynomial, our technique is based on improving the so-called Knuth counting algorithm by incorporating an importance function into the node selection technique giving a sequential importance sampling (SIS) method. We define and report performance on two importance functions.

This paper introduces a reinforcement-learning based resource allocation framework for dynamic placement of threads of parallel applications to Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) many-core systems. We propose a two-level learning-based decision-making process, consisting of a user-defined layer and a machine learning layer. The former allows the user to define policies, i.e., a decision-making algorithm to be used in the machine learning layer, while the latter offers a set of available policies, allowing the user to select the most appropriate one for a given application. Our framework is a multi-agent system, where agents are threads of parallel applications and a coordinator is the user. The framework is implemented using a Java agent-oriented programming model, where the agents are implemented using Java threads. We present results from a simulated and a real-world case study. The results show that our framework can dynamically adapt to the underlying hardware, improving the utilization of the cores of the system. We show that, compared to a baseline system that does not take into account the policy-based policy, our framework improves the utilization of the cores by up to 14. We also show that our framework can improve the utilization of the memory of the system. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents a review of the literature. Section 3 presents the design of the framework. Section 4 presents results from a simulated and a real-world case study.

Larger firms - defined as those with over 100 staff - were more likely to be attacked than smaller counterparts, said the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), which surveyed 1,200 companies. Its report found 42 of larger firms had been the victim of a cyber attack, compared with 18 of smaller ones. The business group has urged companies to do more to protect themselves. Just a quarter of the firms the BCC surveyed said they had put in place security measures to protect themselves against hacking. "Cyber attacks risk companies' finances, confidence and reputation, with victims reporting not only monetary losses, but costs from disruption to their business and productivity. "Firms need to be proactive about protecting themselves from cyber attacks," said BCC director-general Adam Marshall. Household names including Yahoo, eBay and TalkTalk have all fallen victim to major cyber attacks. Last year, Tesco Bank reported losing PS2.5m in an unprecedented breach at a British bank. The law requires organisations to have appropriate measures in place to keep people's personal data secure. Next year data protection regulation will be extended, increasing businesses' responsibilities to protect personal data. "Firms that don't adopt the appropriate protections leave themselves open to tough penalties," warned Mr Marshall.

One of the primary challenges of visual storytelling is developing techniques that can maintain the context of the story over long event sequences to generate human-like stories. In this paper, we propose a hierarchical deep learning architecture based on encoder-decoder networks to address this problem. To better help our network maintain this context while also generating long and diverse sentences, we incorporate natural language image descriptions along with the images themselves to generate each story sentence. We evaluate our system on the Visual Storytelling (VIST) dataset and show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on a suite of different automatic evaluation metrics. The empirical results from this evaluation demonstrate the necessities of different components of our proposed architecture and shows the effectiveness of the architecture for visual storytelling.

From approximately the next three centuries, Scotland was ruled directly by the British Parliament, located at Westminster, as well as its successor, the UK Parliament. The absence of a Scottish Parliament continued to be a significant aspect of Scottish national pride. Proposals for a "devolved" Parliament emerged prior to 1914; however, they were put on hold because of the onset of World War I. In the late 1960s, there was a surge in Scottish nationalism, leading to calls for self-rule or even separation from the UK. As a result, in 1969, the Labour government under Harold Wilson established the Royal Commission on the Constitution, with the main goal being to investigate methods for granting greater autonomy to Scotland within the confines of the unitary state of the United Kingdom. The commission published its findings in 1973, proposing the creation of a Scottish Assembly with the power to legislate on most domestic matters in Scotland.

The most unnerving part of Aurora's day was catching a glimpse of herself in the mirror. She had long ago grown accustomed to seeing the identical faces of women and men that lived today. It all started many years ago with customer dissatisfaction. People would all wander into a supermarket with their different faces, different hands and different shades of skin and they'd spend their precious minutes looking for a perfect banana or a perfect tomato. Scientists threw hours into making these minutes less stressful by creating tomatoes that were identically beautiful. Then they did the same for bananas. Soon people wanted their faces to have the same treatment as well as their children's. It wasn't long until the gentle erosion of time had etched the old faces away entirely. Everyone looked the same and that was going to be the end of it. Every few years, an unfortunate day arrived and the process wouldn't go perfectly with, say, a child born with a single large, unusual freckle under their right eye or, god forbid, eyes green like a long extinct species of sour apple. With Aurora, one of the most extraordinary differences had occurred. When she emerged into the world, she had the traditional blue eyes, the blonde hair, but her skin was a deep brown, like the forgotten soil. Her parents, with their identical peachy faces looked to one another like a confused person in a mirror. They had signed the form much like every other parent, knowing but not considering the risk that old, strong genes could manipulate the process and leave them with a truly unique baby. Parenting a unique baby used to be a difficult road but with the Museum open and a rising interest in these "deformities," a couple could stand to make a great sum of money from the simple sale of their child. This was preferred to raising the accident themselves and many simply funneled the funds back into another attempt at the process, hoping blindly that the genes wouldn't warp the identical face they desired once again. Aurora spent her childhood by herself in a tiny playpen in a large hall of the museum. She never saw children like herself because every living soul who passed through the room looked exactly the same. Children parroted their parents' excitement. "Have you ever seen skin like that in real life?" they'd exclaim. "The poor thing, all alone," a pair of women would lament. From Aurora's side, it was impossible to tell who was mother and child, sister and sister, sometimes even brother and mother looked frightfully similar if dressed the same. Even more impossible to imagine was the concept of family itself. The only ones closest to her were the ones who fed her and even she had trouble telling if they were the same person or not with each passing day. As she grew older, she began to take stock of her room. She examined the bed as they studied her. She grew frustrated at receiving the same meal every morning, noon and night with the same identical fruit from the uniform markets that had grown very popular. She knew very little of the surrounding rooms but knew the doors to them well; heavy as they were, people hungrily threw them open every other minute or so. She couldn't speak because no one had ever taught her, but she knew that she was the brown girl. That's what people called her and the words hung proudly above her pen. Her body grew more unique every day. Her curls were difficult for people to wrap their confined minds around. She had freckles that littered her face, each like a hidden star on a foggy night. She elongated, her neck longer and more beautiful than anyone in her crowd of clones. Her curves expanded from her over the years with seismic energy, new mountains and valleys unlike any seen in years. In all this time, no one had taken a genuine interest in her. Not more than a few half-hearted glances or the occasional long stare like one might experience at a zoo. The young boy who first called her Aurora looked like all the others. Apart from his museum uniform, it'd be hard to spot him in the crowd if not for the way his eyes never let go of her. Their strong grip. When she slept, she usually slept alone behind locked doors, smothered in air conditioning. Waking to the sound of shuffling feet, she hears murmurs about the brown girl and starts her day. The day he called her Aurora, she had stirred early. Even though she'd spent her whole life being watched, this felt different. It was like he had taken his eyes and touched her skin with them. In stolen moments, they would begin the day. For the first time in her life, she was able to learn about the inside of a person. And Jon's insides were the same color as hers as far as anyone knew, but who knew what color his soul was. When she finally spoke her first words, they were questions and Jon told her what she wanted to know. He explained the girl with no eyes in the room to her left, the incredibly small boy with black hair in the room to the right. He avoided the subject of what laid outside the walls of the Museum and practically ran from the room to escape the conversation about the sum of money that she was worth, the price of admission, and what it would take to buy her freedom. He would put his finger to her mouth and tell her not to let anyone know that she could speak. Maybe he feared losing her or maybe he feared losing the easy money the Museum offered. Once the pair had gotten close, it became difficult..... exploring new emotional terrain when forced to stay on separate sides of the room. They shared those traditional blue eyes, but her soil skin kept her behind a fence and rotten fruit had begun to take seed beneath those pores. She resented that she could close her eyes and love his insides but, upon looking at him directly, could only see the waves of identical faces that jeered at her for years. In the mornings, she wouldn't want to wake early to see him anymore and separately they would cry identical tears. He was a child and so was she. She told him that she knew he had to marry another girl who looked like him and have babies who looked like him. He told her that he loved her and she knew he only loved the skin. Her life hadn't given her the opportunity to explore the same rooms that welcomed his face. So when he left the job and her behind, it was a surprise that she wished to keep the name. One day, after white face and white face washed over her, she would say her name aloud to her audience. Confused spectators would read the plaque in front of her pen, wondering how she learned to speak. Children pointed their sharp fingers and remarked loudly that they didn't want a speaking exhibit. The employees brought Aurora new fruit to shut her up, but this made her speak louder. Eventually patrons no longer wished to see the Brown Girl and having earned them a sizable amount of revenue, the Museum happily opened her pen and said "Good Luck." Pulling the door open, she tiptoed past the blind girl who would never read the banner above her tiny cell. Another heavy door led to a room where a tired creature with two blonde haired heads rested clumsily. Siamese was printed in beautiful calligraphy across the wall. Room after room of people behind tiny little fences. Finally she reached the entrance and made her way outside where the world looked like it was covered in fresh snow. Everyone looked at her like she was gon na melt their world with her heat and she worried deeply that she'd never know another person's insides again for even she was frightened by her own face.

A problem is regarded as inherently difficult if its solution requires significant resources, whatever the algorithm used. The theory formalizes this intuition, by introducing mathematical models of computation to study difficult problems. Demonstrate an understanding of how the theory of computation is used to model and analyze the computational complexity of algorithms and problems. Given a natural language problem description, understand how it can be translated into a mathematical model of computation. Know the classes of problems that are considered to be inherently difficult, and the complexity classes that correspond to these classes. Know what are the main limitations of the P vs NP problem, and what are the implications of these limitations. Have a basic understanding of the relationship between the complexity of an algorithm, and the resources required by the algorithm. Be able to use this theoretical knowledge to improve algorithms and algorithms' analysis. This is a theoretical course, with a large practical component. In the practical part, you are expected to experiment with different models of computation, such as the deterministic Turing machine, the random Turing machine, and the nondeterministic Turing machine. You are also expected to create a complexity class for your own problem description, and to study this class by solving instances of it, and studying the best known algorithms for this class. You are also expected to give a talk, based on the work you do in the practical part.

Modelling the physical properties of everyday objects is a fundamental prerequisite for autonomous robots. We present a novel generative adversarial network (Defo-Net), able to predict body deformations under external forces from a single RGB-D image. The network is based on an invertible conditional Generative Adversarial Network (IcGAN) and is trained on a collection of different objects of interest generated by a physical finite element model simulator. Defo-Net inherits the generalisation properties of GANs. This means that the network is able to reconstruct the whole 3-D appearance of the object given a single depth view of the object and to generalise to unseen object configurations. Contrary to traditional finite element methods, our approach is fast enough to be used in real-time applications. We apply the network to the problem of safe and fast navigation of mobile robots carrying payloads over different obstacles and floor materials. Experimental results in real scenarios show how a robot equipped with an RGB-D camera can use the network to predict terrain deformations under different payload configurations and use this to avoid unsafe areas.

In this paper, we consider the expected blocklength of variable-length coding over the binary symmetric channel (BSC) with noiseless feedback. Horstein first proposed a simple one-phase scheme to achieve the capacity of BSC. Naghshvar et al. used a novel extrinsic Jensen-Shannon (EJS) divergence in a sequential transmission scheme that maximizes EJS (MaxEJS) and provided a non-asymptotic upper bound on the expected blocklength for MaxEJS. Simulations in this paper show that MaxEJS provides lower expected blocklengths than the original Horstein scheme, but the non-asymptotic bound of Naghshvar et al. is loose enough that lies above the simulated performance of Horstein scheme for a BSC with a small crossover probability. This paper proposes a new expression for MaxEJS expected blocklength that is a tight approximation of simulated performance. This expression is developed by exploring a genie-aided decoder (GAD) whose expected blocklength will always be larger than MaxEJS and can be approximated by two random walks. We conjecture that even with these two approximations, the expression may still be an upper bound on blocklength as suggested by the simulation results.

Clear or coated glass is commonly found in most light bulbs. Bulbs with coated interiors contain kaolin, a white, powdery clay substance. Kaolin, or kaolinite, is a fine, chalky clay, applied electrostatically within the bulb. This process scatters the bulb's emitted light, resulting in a softer, more uniform illumination. Manufacturers may incorporate pigments into the kaolin to modify the bulb's final light emission. Kaolin-diffused bulbs are frequently utilized in indoor lighting due to their gentle light quality. In contrast, other types of colored bulbs, such as those used for parties, Christmas trees, and decorative purposes, derive their hues through colored glass produced by incorporating dopants like cobalt (for blue) or chromium (for green). Neodymium-infused glass is sometimes employed to generate a more authentic light appearance.

One method to decelerate your computer is neglecting to defragment your hard drive. Since files are typically partitioned into small segments and scattered across the disk, your system must search various locations to assemble the entire file whenever you access it. By defragmenting your hard drive, these segments are relocated adjacent to one another, allowing your computer to avoid scouring the entire disk for each fragment.

Another approach to impede performance is by accumulating an extensive number of files on your desktop (URL0). During system startup, your computer retrieves the icons for each individual file, which can significantly prolong the boot-up time.

The transformation of short, overlapping, and possibly flawed DNA fragments from ecological samples into precise depictions of the concealed microbiomes' genomic structures is referred to as metagenome assembly. Current advanced methods necessitate powerful computers with extensive shared memory and struggle to manage contemporary metagenome data sets that surpass Terabytes in volume. This study presents MetaHipMer, a novel metagenome assembler boasting superior quality and performance. MetaHipMer utilizes a refined de Bruijn graph technique coupled with a custom scaffolding methodology, which generates extended scaffolds and adapts to metagenomic quirks. MetaHipMer is optimized for parallel processing using Unified Parallel C language, permitting smooth operation on both shared and dispersed memory architectures. The experimental findings indicate that MetaHipMer either equals or excels over existing top-tier tools regarding accuracy. Furthermore, MetaHipMer effectively manages large parallelisms and successfully tackles formerly insoluble metagenome challenges. By employing MetaHipMer, we have achieved the first complete assembly of the Twitchell Wetlands dataset, comprising 7.5 billion reads and occupying 2.6 TBytes.

There are infinitely many primes, as demonstrated by Euclid around 300 BC. There is no known simple formula that separates prime numbers from composite numbers. However, the distribution of primes, as well as some properties of prime numbers, have been extensively studied and there are many important results in number theory related to primes. In the 1910s, New York-based filmmakers were attracted to Jacksonville's warm climate, exotic locations, excellent rail access, and cheap labor. Over the course of the decade, more than 30 silent films shot in or around our city are known today as "lost" movies. Jack Dreyfus takes a look at them this week: After the Civil War, Jacksonville was an emerging railroad hub with lots of space for new tracks. The first train arrived here on October 1st 1871 from Chicago. By 1888 when Florida became its own territory, there were nearly 100 miles of track that stretched along what is now downtown St. Johns County - all owned by Jacksonville Transportation Company Limited. In 1889, JTCL merged with other companies into Atlantic Coast Line Railroad (ACLR) which would become one of the country's leading railway systems. On September 26th 1899, ACLR chartered the T.P.B.J., named after Thomas Payne Brown Jr., who led their efforts during Reconstruction. Later that year they bought out local competitor Stuart Jones owned lines, creating Greater Jacksonville Railway Company in 1901. As trains moved steadily through this area, so did film crews. The 1920s saw many great silent movie stars make appearances in the Sunshine State. Tallulah Bankhead starred opposite John Gilbert in 1917's "Heavenly Twins." Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, Orson Welles, Mae West and Binnie Barnes made cameos throughout the decade while Mary Pickford filmed her last role alongside Douglas Fairbanks Sr. in 1926 before moving back to Hollywood permanently. But it wasn't just famous faces behind the cameras; it also put some of America's top directors on location too. Others followed suit making movies including "A Fool For Love" (1925), "Night Nurse" (1928) and "Dynamite Dick" (1929). All three feature films about athletes premiered in theaters across Duval county. As the Great Depression hit, production slowed down drastically. But even though many studios had closed shop, many independent producers continued to shoot localized features locally using screenwriters from places like Pittsburgh who knew how to tell stories set outside major cities. Renowned director C. Aubrey Smith moved his office to Main Street in 1924 where he wrote over a dozen scripts for productions shooting in town. He directed two here including 1932's "Barbary Coast" featuring Betty Grable who lived nearby. By the mid 1930s, things started looking up again thanks largely to Warner Bros. Pictures. They began buying rights to popular novels such as "Tarzan Of The Apes" which allowed them to create easily marketable series. It didn't hurt either that Florida proved itself another favorite destination for filmmakers especially ones working on Westerns. There were several here including 1935's "Small Town USA" based loosely on Cecil Fielding's book "Lady Chatterley's Lover" starring George O'Hara and Louis Calhern among others. The studio experimented with different genres filming both comedy and horror shorts here. One of those comedies was 1937's short titled "Wackyland" featuring Laurel And Hardy playing circus clowns. According to the Yesteryear blog, the majority of these early films never found distribution due to poor sound quality which is why many remain completely unknown today only appearing occasionally on TV airings. With renewed interest in the industry rising nationwide, along with increased funding, major corporations wanted in on the action. Galicia was spared the worst of the fighting in that war: it was one of the areas where the initial coup attempt at the outset of the war was successful, and it remained in Nationalist (Franco's army's) hands throughout the war. While there were no pitched battles, there was repression and death: all political parties were abolished, as were all labor unions and Galician nationalist organizations as the Seminario de Estudos Galegos. Galicia's statute of autonomy was annulled (as were those of Catalonia and the Basque provinces once those were conquered). According to Carlos Fernandez Santander, at least 4,200 people were killed either extrajudicially or after summary trials, among them republicans, communists, Galician nationalists, socialists and anarchists. Victims included the civil governors of all four Galician provinces; Juana Capdevielle, the wife of the governor of A Coruna; mayors such as Anxel Casal of Santiago de Compostela, of the Partido Galeguista; prominent socialists such as Jaime Quintanilla in Ferrol and Emilio Martinez Garrido in Vigo; Popular Front deputies Antonio Bilbatua, Jose Minones, Diaz Villamil, Ignacio Seoane, and former deputy Heraclio Botana); soldiers who had not joined the rebellion, such as Generals Rogelio Caridad Pita and Enrique Salcedo Molinuevo and Admiral Antonio Azarola; and the founders of the PG, Alexandre Boveda and Victor Casas, as well as other professionals akin to republicans and nationalists, as the journalist Manuel Lustres Rivas or physician Luis Poza Pastrana. Many others were forced to escape into exile, or were victims of other reprisals and removed from their jobs and positions.

There is a vast amount of research that supports the idea that triggers are a real thing and that they can significantly affect individuals. The issue isn't due to a subpar phone; instead, it's the insufficient shielding on the phone's speaker. In earlier phones and networks, a technology called TDMA (time division multiple access) was utilized. Although these devices transmitted signals via several hundred MHz radio waves, identical to modern networks, the interference picked up by the speaker would be ineffective. Even if audible, it would be too high-pitched for animals or humans to perceive. However, TDMA's significance lies in how it allows users to communicate over a frequency channel in brief intervals. Each user is allotted a specific duration to interact with the tower before the next user's turn begins. This switching doesn't take place at MHz frequencies, but rather in the lower kHz range, which speakers can reproduce and humans can listen to up to 20 kHz. In essence, your phone broadcasts MHz radio waves but modulates them on a kHz interval to adhere to tower regulations. Poorly shielded speaker amplifiers and the modulation's interaction result in the speaker resonating with the cellular signal, leading to the perceived sound. Contemporary phones avoid this problem since they employ distinct networks that no longer rely on TDMA, thereby ceasing to modulate radio waves at audible frequencies.

" Hello Mrs. President. " " Hello Mr. - " Hillary glanced at her calendar " Smith ." His appointment was for 2 whole hours. This gentleman must be quite important to occupy so much of her time. " Have you become accustomed to your new chair yet? " he asked with a smile " Well, it's only been a week and I've spent the entire time getting filled in on all sorts of issues, now that my security clearance has been upgraded. " she said, hoping she did not come across as too complaining. " I'm afraid this is another one of such meetings. " Mr. Smith said apologetically. " Oh, I'm sure it's not too bad. Most of what happens in here is really just the continuations of old problems my husband used to tell me about. " " He wouldn't have heard about this issue, as we didn't know about it before 2002. " he said. " Also, I should remind you that this subject is on a strictly need-to-know basis, so you might not want to discuss it with your husband. " Hillary almost chuckled at his little cliche, but something told her that this was serious. The man before her was very well composed and obviously experienced. He did not seem to be impressed with meeting the president for the first time. " So what is this about? My calender only mentions your name and that you are a scientist of some unspecified sort. " she said. " Well, that is true, although I would put more on my business card, if I had one. I am the director of a research institution that was founded in late 2002 to examine an object of alien origin. " he said. Hillary knew that many scientists mused about the possibility of aliens, but she had never been interested in that discussion. She knew she should probably be excited about the fact that alien life was apparently confirmed, but she had gotten used to the president-routine now and quickly got on with the practical details. " Okay. Interesting. How expensive is it and what results have you come up with? " she asked bluntly. " It is very expensive. Currently we are using about 100 billion dollars annually, and it used to be higher. " he said. He looked down for a short moment and then continued. " And as for the results, we are only working on containment, and it is successfully being contained. ." That was a large number. She should have noticed such an amount of money in the budgets. " I am pretty familiar with the government finances. How do you manage to get that amount of money? I'm pretty sure I haven't seen'Alien research' on any of the budget proposals. " she said with a smile. " We get it through the military spending of the State Department. " he said. Well the State Department spending did go up 350 billion between 2002 and 2010 but.... " But how did you get it while the war in Iraq was going on? " she inquired. " The war wasn't as expensive as reported. So we just got the extra overhead. " he replied. Hillery hoped this wasn't the only reason they had gone to Iraq. " Okay. You said you were working on containment only? What kind of object is this? " " Yes, " he said " The object is a perfect cube about 1 meter across. We discovered it in the middle of a meteor crater surrounded by a 5 meter thick spherical shield. The inner part of the shield was made of gold and the outer part was made of a very heat resistant and durable alloy. " Hillary didn't care much for the technical aspects, but it seemed well rehearsed, so she didn't interrupt. " But although the shield was very resistant against blunt force impact, it was easy enough to cut open. So in 2004, we did. We accounted for everything, and prepared for the worst. Even if the cube had been made out of antimatter, the bunker would have contained the explosion. At first, after we opened the sphere, it was rather anticlimactic. Just a black cube, covered in a slimy substance. After a few minutes our initial analysis showed that the substance contained an acid, perfect for dissolving the explosion-proof container we had made. We quickly encapsulated it in a plastic container, that the acid should have been inert to, but after a few minutes the substance changed properties and started dissolving the plastic. " he explained. Mr. Smith shrugged his shoulders and continued. " We ended up placing it inside the original gold container again. " That did sound anticlimactic. " So I guess that accounts for the expenses up to 2004. What did you do afterwards? " Hillary asked. " Well, after we had closed up the gold shell, we detected an extremely small vibration from inside. It turns out, that the substance contained micro machinery which was drilling through the gold. This seemed strange since it could have done that before we brought it in. However, it became clear that this object was harvesting energy from the environment and using this to break down the gold. We discovered it because it drilled far less in the gold after we turned off the lights when replacing the shield. " Mr Smith explained. " Soon after it completely stopped drilling. We hoped that it meant that it had run out of energy, which could perhaps allow us to do more experiments on it. But after a few months of being in the same container, it suddenly started making its microscopic holes in the gold like it was drilling through butter. We just barely avoided a containment breach, and afterwards we found out, that it had probably harvested energy from combination of two things. A small thermal gradient, and vibration energy from a motor running nearby. " " A thermal gradient? " Hillary asked with one eyebrow raised. Now she had let him talk uninterrupted for long enough. Scientists often seemed to have a habit of sliding into an overly technical jargon when they had been talking for too long. " Sorry, it's when there are two different temperatures on each side of an object. It can be used to generate energy, but it's usually in so tiny amounts that - " " Okay ," Hillary interrupted before he could get going again. " So it seems like it wants to escape, and you are trying to contain it, although it's proving to be difficult. " " Yes, but the fact that it suddenly started storing its energy instead of constantly drilling, implies that it understands, that it is being contained and it is getting smarter about escaping. This caused us to ramp up the security. There now are quite a lot of layers of different protection mechanisms in place. " Mr. Smith clarified. Hillary could see the difficulties, but it did not seem to make sense. Why was it trying to escape? " Have you tried communicating with it? " She asked. " Well, we have tried. We drill small holes in the gold shield to interact with the object and send in signals. Mostly low power, low frequency communication, as we don't want to give it energy. So far the only response we have gotten is dissolving equipment. " he said while shrugging his shoulders again. " We don't know what it's for or why it's here on earth. We do have some ideas, and they seem to universally conclude that keeping the object isolated from its surroundings is the best course of action. " " Can you elaborate on the ideas? How can you possibly conclude anything from an object that doesn't communicate? " Hillary asked sceptically. " Well, we know it was sent to earth in a shell that isolated the object. So someone, somewhere thought that sending it without a prison was a bad idea. The question is, why not just throw it into the sun, if they didn't want it to be free? Were they afraid that it would harvest all the energy instead of breaking? But then why not send it out of the galaxy? " Mr. Smith mused. " Maybe it is intelligent and destructive. The civilization that banished it might be so peaceful, that they could not get themselves to sentence it to death as they should have. " " It could also be a friendly gift, wanting to help create peace on earth and the only reason it doesn't just explain this to us is because it doesn't have enough energy to maintain coherent thoughts. The shield might just have been a wrapping to protect it from the dangers of interstellar travel. But who is going to give the order to release it and see if it is indeed merciful? " " Maybe it's like a timed bomb; when monkeys get smart enough to open it, it will kill them all. Whoever sent it could be afraid of competition between intelligent species. And they just hadn't expected anyone to be as cautious as us. There is just no way to really know " Hillary agreed. The choice was flipping a coin with all of humanity at risk. Heads; it is peace on earth, tails; it is destruction of mankind. Earth is well enough off not to flip that coin. " Thank you for the briefing, please continue your work. " she said. Mr. Smith bowed politely and left the room.

Some dairy farmers have said they face going out of business if prices they receive for their products do not rise. They have held protests at supermarkets to show their frustration and demand governments intervene, but so far there has been little response from the federal government or state leaders. The cost of production varies across different states in Australia because of differences between seasons with warmer weather in southern areas resulting in less feed being required compared to cooler northern locations where winters are colder requiring more feeding of animals which leads to higher costs. These variations mean that some farms will suffer losses while others can make significant gains. The National Farmers Federation (NFU) says its members have seen an average 4 per cent fall in milk production since 2013 due to low animal profits and rising input costs - once again highlighting how commercial terms differ from smaller independent dairies. The NFU also say it is possible farmers could go into liquidation unless urgent action is taken. In western NSW alone, according a report by the Sydney Morning Herald on Monday, dairy farmer Paul O'Sullivan had lost 158,000 as his herd dropped 10 per cent over the past five years to just 59 cows. Mr Sullivan started milking calves this year after operating half-time last season when he was forced to sell 21 head of cattle. He now fears he may be facing the same fate next year, despite regularly selling off most of what remains. "If I'm paying down my mortgage today in order to keep me afloat then none of these kids are getting into college," he told Fairfax Media. His financial situation worsened dramatically during May's drought when the South West Slopes received only two thirds of its expected rainfall with many parts receiving no rain at all prompting him to lose nine sheds worth around 30,000 each plus thousands of dollars spent fixing leaking roofs.

Until the early 1980s, industry was a major source of water pollution. Although many plants and factories can be found along the Rhine up into Switzerland, it is along the Allee des Neues Darmstadt in Germany that most of this septic waste goes down stream to the sea. The river is also heavily polluted with the solid waste generated by people who live or work near the river banks such as manure, excrement and a variety of garden products. The industrial sector has developed very rapidly since the early 1990's when new technologies were introduced which made it possible for large industries to operate in areas lacking adequate sewage treatment systems. Results from municipal sewerage studies show that in Berlin there are approximately 3 million residents living within 1 kilometer of a major wastewater treatment plant while in Munich over 2 million reside close enough to the wastewater plant to have significant environmental impacts from seepages and overflows. Industrial effluents flow directly off site through sewers into storm drains and will eventually continue their journey through the environment at an accelerated rate. Industrial waste contains about 70 percent dissolved organic matter (DO) which poses serious health risks to humans, animals and aquatic life if not processed prior to discharge. If untreated these pollutants may cause harmful effects to rivers, lakes and oceans. The majority of industrial activities occur on riverbanks where people spend much time during the day due to the proximity to waterways. Overfishing, loss of habitat and other social problems associated with human activity around water bodies create pollution challenges. The River Severn is marked by the presence of numerous industrial sites including chemical production facilities, textile mills, paper mills, glass manufacturing units and power stations. All defensive actions aimed at identifying, intercepting, and neutralizing adversaries seeking to violate friendly airspace constitute Defensive Counterair (DCA) (JP 1-02). In harmony with Offensive Counterair (OCA) operations, DCA's primary objective is to safeguard an operational territory free from aerial and missile perils. The DCA mandate incorporates both proactive and reactive shields. Proactive defense signifies the strategic application of minimal aggressive responses and counterstrikes to obstruct the enemy from gaining control over a disputed zone or position (JP 1-02). This category embraces ballistic missile defense and aerospace threat mitigation, encompassing point defense, region protection, and security for significant aerial assets. Reactive defense entails non-aggressive steps taken to diminish the likelihood of harm inflicted by hostile activities, without instigating confrontation (JP 1-02). Comprising elements such as early warning systems, chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear safeguards, disguise, fortification, restoration, dispersal, backup, and adaptability, countermeasures, and clandestinity, these passive defenses function to lessen the impact of potential assaults.

Researchers have discovered a new Linux backdoor called Symbiote that uses novel evasion techniques to conceal its presence. It is able to scrub any sign of infection from the file system when it is running and also uses steganography to hide its malicious code inside .PNG image files. The Symbiote malware was discovered by researchers from security firm ESET. It is designed to inject its code into legitimate processes on a compromised machine. The malware consists of a backdoor module that runs in the background and a dropper module that injects its code into a legitimate process, in this case, the xrdp process that is used to allow remote desktop access. The xrdp process is run as root and is designed to interact with the xrdp daemon using the D-Bus inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism. "After being injected, the malware hooks into the D-Bus interface for the Xrdp process. This allows the malware to control the xrdp daemon," the ESET researchers said in a report. The malware communicates with a command-and-control (CC) server over a non-standard HTTPS port. Symbiote doesn't use any polymorphic code obfuscation techniques, but its steganographic capabilities and the fact that it can scrub all signs of its presence from the file system might make it difficult for users and security products to detect. "One of the main reasons this malware is hard to detect is that it hides its presence in the file system," the ESET researchers said. "During the infection process, the malware creates a tmpfs (RAM-based) file system in the runuser1000gvfs directory." The malware creates a file called .cache on this RAM-based file system. The contents of the .cache file are encrypted with AES-256-CBC, but this is done to hide the malware's configuration data and not the malicious code itself. "The malware code is executed directly from this tmpfs file system," the researchers said. "It also stores all the log files generated by the malware in the runuser1000gvfs directory." When the malware is done executing, it wipes the contents of this directory and unmounts the tmpfs file system. This effectively removes all traces of its presence in the file system. ESET malware researcher Lukas Stefanko believes that the malware is most likely used in highly targeted attacks. He noted that the CC server identified so far is only reachable from IP addresses in Brazil. "However, the malware is not 'Brazil-exclusive, he said. "It can be easily adapted to attack any region in the world." In a blog post, Stefanko also noted that the xrdp RDP server is enabled by default on many Linux distributions, making it an attractive attack vector for malware writers. Symbiote is not the first malware to use steganography to conceal its data. A malware program called DarkHotel used this technique to hide its code inside images. Another piece of malware that was distributed through a similar supply-chain attack was the recently patched Drupal flaw. Geneticists engaging in population studies have debated if the notion of a population could serve as a foundation for redefining race. To accomplish this, it's essential to establish a clear-cut definition of what constitutes a population in this context. Remarkably, biologists have yet to agree on a standard population definition. Despite its significance in ecology, evolutionary biology, and conservation biology, most population definitions are based on descriptive characteristics like "a collection of organisms belonging to the same species inhabiting a specific area during a designated period." Waples and Gaggiotti distinguish two main categories of population definitions: those rooted in the ecological perspective, and those grounded in the evolutionary perspective. Instances of these definitions include:

1. Ecological Perspective: A population is defined as a set of interbreeding individuals of the same species, living in a specific area, and interacting with one another and their environment.
2. Evolutionary Perspective: A population is characterized as a group of organisms from the same species that share a common gene pool and undergo natural selection processes.

Along the eastern coast of Australia lies a prolonged mountain chain (the Great Dividing Range), resulting in moist oceanic air being lifted (orographic uplift), cooling, condensing, and subsequently producing rain, thereby fostering forested regions on its wet side. Conversely, the western side of the range, despite belonging to the same geographical region, experiences minimal rainfall due to the absence of such a topographical feature, creating a rain shadow effect. The west coast itself lacks comparable mountain ranges, causing incoming oceanic air to bypass the necessary lift and precipitation needed for forest development. While temperature, geological, and soil variances contribute to the scarcity of forests in the west, the primary cause remains the orographic influence of the mountain range.

Horizontal direct effect, which applies to non-state parties, does not extend to Directives, as ruled by the Court of Justice. Regarding the broader query, why do these localities bear such unpredictable titles? I presume you're American. In Europe's ancient towns, establishments weren't meticulously designed but evolved gradually over several centuries. Initially, there were no authoritative bodies determining suitable labels for locations. If a high court convened on a particular street, it became known as Chancery Lane. Should there be a district primarily inhabited by Jews, it was called Old Jewry. Markets could be Cloth Fair or Haymarket. Prostitution-prone streets took on names like Cock Lane or Gropecunt Lane. People didn't mince words; they simply denoted what they observed. Over time, the city transformed, and names morphed accordingly. For instance, Elephant and Castle derives its title from an inn mentioned in the oldest regional records. The term "Elephant and Castle" originated from a coaching inn, first recorded in the Court Leet Book of the Manor of Walworth on 21 March 1765. Previously, the location housed a blacksmith and cutler. The cutlers' guild emblem featured an elephant carrying a castle on its back – possibly symbolizing a howdah – due to the utilization of elephant ivory in handles. Similarly, Blackfriars, located behind Ludgate Hill, was presumably named after the Dominican monks who transferred their monastery there from Holborn during the 13th century. Monks donned black robes, giving rise to the moniker 'friars.' Another hypothesis suggests that Blackfriars gained its name due to its proximity to the old Ludgate, an eastward extension of Fleet Street. The etymology of Ludgate is uncertain; it may stem from flood gate, fleet gate, or postern gate, or from the Old English 'hlidgeat' or 'ludgeat,' translating to postern, swinging gate, or black gate.

Should the ice front of Totten Glacier recede approximately 150km from its present location, scientists predict a subsequent runaway reversal, causing it to advance inland by 200-250km. This potential outcome stems from an analysis of the geology beneath the ice stream. While most major glaciers in East Antarctica remain comparatively stable, Totten is an exception, exhibiting an annual thinning rate of around 0.5 meters, primarily due to warming ocean waters melting its floating front.

Researchers led by Alan Aitken have examined the consequences of Totten's ongoing shrinkage. By studying gravity and magnetic data encompassing the entire drainage basin supplying the glacier, they identified key features indicative of historical ice behavior. Notably, the sedimentary rocks at the modern ice front and in deep fjord interiors display significant erosion, suggesting prolonged contact with moving ice. However, the mid-region holds greater intrigue, as the relatively thick sediments imply brief historical residency of ice fronts in this area and an inherently unstable rock bed dip that encourages glacier retreat.

Professor Martin Siegert of Imperial College London explained to BBC News, "Our findings indicate that when the ice margin begins to withdraw, it does so rather quickly to a new, stable position much farther inland. Our modeling suggests this would result in the loss of ice equivalent to 1.5-2 meters of sea level rise." Historically, Totten retreated to the deep interior of its France-sized catchment area.

Under the proposals, all MPs would continue to vote on all key stages of legislation. MPs will debate the changes on 15 July, Mr Grayling said, and the system will be changed using the rules - known as standing orders - that dictate how Parliament conducts its business. With more powers set to be devolved to the Scottish Parliament after September's independence referendum, Tory MPs have said it is not right that MPs representing Scottish constituencies can continue to determine laws affecting England only. Mr Grayling told MPs that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland were getting a "stronger voice" and that it was "only fair" to do the same for England. The Speaker will be asked to certify which bills or parts of bills relate to England or England and Wales only, he said. There will be no changes in the House of Lords, Mr Grayling said. But where Lords amendments are certified as England or England and Wales only, a "double majority" system applies, meaning it will need a majority of both the whole House of Commons and MPs representing English or English and Welsh constituencies. Tablet computers will be used to count MPs' votes as they walk through the voting lobbies so officials can instantly register whether they have used their veto in votes where the "double majority" rule applies. To jeers from opposition benches, Mr Grayling said "Today we are answering the West Lothian Question," a reference to the constitutional anomaly that lets Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland MP at Westminster vote on measures that only apply in England. ABC HD (stylized as "ABC HD is a high definition simulcast feed of ABC that broadcasts in the 720p resolution format; it was launched on September 16, 2002. Unlike its CBS, NBC and especially Fox counterparts, ABC airs its HD programming in letterboxed widescreen for programming that is offered only in the 16:9 (4:3 for news and EI programming) aspect ratio, which is downscaled to a 480i 16:9 format with the black bars at the sides of the screen removed for standard definition viewers; this was because of the lack of HDTV programming available at the time of its launch. During the summer growing season, phosphate is at a high level. It has a vital role in the breakdown of the sugars manufactured by chlorophyll. But in the fall, phosphate, along with the other chemicals and nutrients, moves out of the leaf into the stem of the plant. When this happens, the sugar-breakdown process changes, leading to the production of anthocyanin pigments. The brighter the light during this period, the greater the production of anthocyanins and the more brilliant the resulting color display. When the days of autumn are bright and cool, and the nights are chilly but not freezing, the brightest colorations usually develop.

The subject matter is captivating, involving dimensions of scale and productivity. Mice share anatomical resemblances to scaled-down elephants. Despite having proportionally sized hearts, their heart rates decrease rather than remaining constant. Surprisingly, I can estimate the heart rate of creatures as vast as a whale or a wombat based on their weight, utilizing the one-quarter power rule (14). This scaling principle applies not only to heart rate but also to other aspects:

* Metabolism (caloric intake)
* Lifespan
* Brain size vs. intelligence
* Required oxygen
* Number of offspring throughout their lives

This pattern extends beyond the animal kingdom and encompasses plants, organizations such as ant colonies and corporations, and even cities. In larger cities, the pace of life is quicker, and the average lifespan of a corporation can be predicted based on its size. All exhibit exponential growth, on average.

The underlying cause behind this phenomenon? These entities, from mice to elephants, humans, trees, and cities, must distribute resources to every component of their structures. As mass increases, delivering blood (nutrients and oxygen) to each cell becomes essential. With an established cardiovascular system, an intricate network of tubes is necessary to reach every cell – mirroring how every house must be accessible via a road system. Every road, including driveways, must connect to a dwelling. Essentially, this structure exhibits fractal properties – a recursive, self-similar design that retains consistency across various scales (such as the branches of a tree).
