Make bedtime routine for them and make sure they're in bed at the same time each night. [substeps] Include extracurriculars like soccer and dance class in this schedule, as well. 2) Schedule naps. Your children need to spend time on their own during the day - the more time you give them alone without an adult watching over them, the better. This will let kids get rid of pent-up energy before nighttime comes around again. If your child is particularly needy or cranky in the early hours after a nap, try putting him down earlier than usual so he's still tired when it gets dark outside. Keep sleep schedules consistent throughout the week (if possible), which allows older teenagers to begin relaxing into a normal pattern, too. [substeps] Napping helps kids focus and play effectively later on, because both those things are important factors in academic success. 3) Get exercise! For most teens, getting enough physical activity is easier said than done; some students find it fun but others never want to go out with friends or do sports themselves unless it involves working up a sweat and sweating off any extra calories. Try making a point of walking together regularly while shopping, cooking dinner or going to school. Being active can help improve mood, decrease stress levels and even boost workout motivation. Even just 15 minutes of light exercise daily could have long-term benefits for teens. [substeps] Getting plenty of movement boosts cognitive performance and prevents infections from viruses that thrive on sedentary lifestyles. It also makes your teen less likely to develop chronic illnesses such as diabetes, high blood pressure and obesity, all known risk factors for heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes. 4) Establish healthy eating habits. A lot of parents think having a meal plan, menu card or grocery list means that kid's meals come out perfect every single day. But if everyone follows these basic guidelines, your kids' diets won't be filled with junk food: Avoid added sugar. Sugar spikes insulin production in our bodies a couple times per hour, leaving us feeling hungry longer afterward. Studies show sugary drinks contribute nearly 20 percent of total calorie intake among U.S. adolescents aged 12-17 years old.[substeps] Cutting back on soda pop and other sweetened beverages will not only make your kids healthier but save money by preventing weight gain. Make lunchtime supervision optional. Kids who don't feel controlled by adults tend to eat junkier foods and skip breakfast. And research suggests teens learn how much food they should consume from what they see at restaurants.[substeps] So turning away from school lunches altogether may encourage healthier choices. And helping kids prepare their own lunches might increase nutritional value since they'll know exactly what goes inside the sandwich. [substeps] 5) Teach responsibility. Don't expect your teen to take care of everything in his life right now. Instead ask him to pitch in around the house. Give him chores that are small enough to keep him busy yet big enough to teach responsibility. Quiz him on math problems before giving him dishes to wash, then settle scores over dinner. These kinds of assignments foster independence in teens and support family dynamics. 6) Make bedtime routines specific to your child. At first glance, establishing a strict bedtime isn't necessarily helpful. In fact, many studies suggest that kids whose parents impose rigid rules about when they must fall asleep wind up sleeping worse. However, individualized bedtimes that meet your teen's needs work best. Some families choose to ban television at bedtime in favor of reading books. Others stick strictly to age-appropriate bedtimes. The key here is to create routines that correspond closely to your child's development stage. You don't want to force a child to start sleeping through the night until grade school age, just to make him too sleepy in college. [substeps] If your teenager doesn't mind staying up late playing video games, read him a book instead to make sure you've set aside sufficient time for relaxation after homework has been finished. Or maybe turn off computers 30 minutes before bedtime instead of relying solely on "screen timeout" programs that promise nothing more than unplugging a device temporarily. 7) Be supportive. Teens often struggle with balance between home responsibilities and social obligations; setting boundaries and enforcing discipline becomes increasingly difficult once a person reaches adolescence. Helping young people maintain challenging routines is essential for reaching maturity. Plus, there's no reason why you shouldn't enjoy your teen's accomplishments alongside her!

Pregnant women are more susceptible to contracting malaria due to weakened immune systems, according to the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG). Malaria poses potential threats to both the mother and fetus, including miscarriage, stillbirth, and premature labor. Transmitted through mosquito bites, malaria presents symptoms such as fever, chills, headache, muscle pains, vomiting, and diarrhea. Although there have been no recorded deaths from malaria among pregnant or recently pregnant women in the UK over the last ten years, the RCOG reports an increase in inquiries from concerned mothers. Approximately 1,500 malaria cases and ten fatalities occur annually in the UK. To minimize the risk of infection, the RCOG advises against non-essential travel to regions with high malaria prevalence, including extensive portions of Africa, Asia (including China and India), Central and South America, sections of the Middle East, and certain Pacific Islands. For unavoidable journeys, the college encourages women to consult specialized malaria clinics for guidance on protective measures. These precautions include using insecticide-treated bed nets, taking antimalarial medications, and practicing mosquito bite prevention methods. Philippa Marsden, chair of the RCOG's Patient Information Committee, emphasizes the importance of informed decision-making, stating, "Although the risks remain relatively small, it's crucial that women are well-informed." Cath Broderick of the RCOG Women's Network adds, "Women experiencing symptoms after returning from high-risk countries and suspecting malaria should consult a healthcare professional promptly and disclose their travel history." Symptoms may manifest up to a week after being bitten.

It's been a bit of an annus horribilis for the internet and all of us who frequent it. In the past year, the world wide web has faced several challenges that have impacted our daily lives, from cybersecurity threats to misinformation and online censorship. One of the biggest threats to the internet this year has been the rise of cyberattacks. In just the first six months of 2021, there were several high-profile hacks that affected millions of people around the world. From the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack to the Microsoft Exchange Server breach, these cybersecurity incidents have caused disruptions in supply chains, energy systems, and governments, and have highlighted the need for stronger online security measures. Misinformation has also been a major problem on the internet this year. The COVID-19 pandemic sparked a deluge of fake news, conspiracy theories, and hoaxes that have been widely shared on social media platforms. This information can be dangerous, as it can influence people's perceptions and behavior, and can harm public health efforts. Social media companies are struggling to keep up with this onslaught, and are being pressed to increase their content moderation practices. Another issue affecting the internet, particularly in countries with authoritarian regimes, is online censorship. Governments in countries like China, Russia, and Iran have increasingly used the internet to control information and suppress dissent. This has led to the blocking of websites, censorship of social media platforms, and even the arrest of online users who criticize their governments. Despite these challenges, there have been efforts to make the internet a better place. Online activism and social movements have gained widespread attention through platforms like Twitter and Instagram. Advocacy groups are working to protect users' privacy rights and push for responsible tech policies. And tech companies are developing new tools and approaches to combat online harms such as misinformation and cybercrimes. As we approach the end of 2021, it's clear that the internet remains an essential part of our lives, but one that we must continue to monitor and safeguard. By holding tech companies accountable and demanding responsible policies from our leaders, we can help ensure a safer and more secure online world for all.

Huge amounts of digital videos are being produced and broadcast every day, leading to giant media archives. Effective techniques are needed to make such data accessible further. Automatic meta-data labelling of broadcast media is an essential task for multimedia indexing, where it is standard to use multi-modal input for such purposes. This paper describes a novel method for automatic detection of media genre and show identities using acoustic features, textual features or a combination thereof. Furthermore the inclusion of available meta-data, such as time of broadcast, is shown to lead to very high performance. Latent Dirichlet Allocation is used to model both acoustics and text, yielding fixed dimensional representations of media recordings that can then be used in Support Vector Machines based classification. Experiments are conducted on more than 1200 hours of TV broadcasts from the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), where the task is to categorise the broadcasts into 8 genres or 133 show identities. On a 200-hour test set, accuracies of 98.6 and 85.7 were achieved for genre and show identification respectively, using a combination of acoustic and textual features with meta-data.

Internal combustion engines are very complex and giving a simplified ELI5 answer really doesn't do it justice. Remember that when a manufacturer reports horsepower, they are reporting peak horsepower, meaning the most power the engine makes over it's rev range. To avoid getting too heavily into technical terms, imagine this.... Try flooring your car at 1500rpm, then try it again at 4000rpm, since your car most likely has a power curve that makes more power at higher RPM's, you will accelerate more quickly when you floor it at 4000rpm. That is because your engine is making less power at 1500 rpm. Saying that two cars make "300hp" is not very telling if one makes 300hp at all revs, and the other produces 300hp at a very high rev and doesn't make much power at other times. There are many reasons why some manufacturers choose to use large displacement engines. One of the best reasons is what we just went over, often times a large displacement engine can produce a more even power curve. This is not always true, but it is easier to make an engine with a large displacement have a balanced power curve. This is great for all kinds of driving because being able to accelerate quickly from a low rpm is useful for road driving and racing. Another reason is simplicity and weight. Weight? What? I thought that bigger displacement meant heavier! Not quite. Smaller displacement engines often use turbo chargers to help boost their power and efficiency. This is good, but turbo chargers add their own weight, take up space, and usually come with supporting units like inter coolers that take up more weight and space and will affect the car's center of gravity as well as a host of other driving characteristics. The third reason why large displacement engines are used is because they usually place less stress on components. Without diving into the combustion process, understand that making a small displacement engine produce the same horsepower as a large displacement engine makes it more "high strung." Components are exposed to higher pressures and higher stresses. This with the added complexity of turbo chargers means that they can wear out more quickly (2.0L turbo charged Mitsubishi Evolutions are a good example of this) and be less susceptible to adverse conditions. Since the components are less stressed in a large displacement engine, they can also be made cheaper, making service cheaper. Furthermore, a relatively unstressed engine is easier to modify to produce more power while an already high strung engine might be at the peak of its abilities without heavily sacrificing reliability. Large displacement engines have drawbacks, they often use more fuel and produce more emissions. A turbocharger that they might lack increases efficiency. However, do not confuse large displacement with exterior weight or size. There is much more to this. Notice that I try to use "usually" as much as possibly because there are very many exceptions. Engineering an engine is a complex process and like all engineering, compromise is the key. For instance, first we propose a novel greedy strategy called "optimal greed" that automatically learns optimal policies resulting in optimal gains while performing similar tasks than previous state-of-the art methods cite6. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) is a scientific intergovernmental body under the auspices of the United Nations, set up at the request of member governments. It was first formed as an independent organization in 1990 and re-established in 1997 after a period of internal turmoil within its membership. On January 1st 2007 the IPCC expanded to include the European Union's climate services following the launch by the executive body of the European Commission of the "Climate Action Plan." On April 21st 2011, the IPCC met for the third time since forming, with most countries signing onto the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (policies formulated by 194 governments, which were adopted in December 2015). The meeting agreed that a new assessment of emissions must be issued every five years from now until 2028; this will indicate whether global warming has slowed or sped up, according to scientists' estimates.

In the presented study, we suggest a hybrid parallel programming strategy for resolving the two-dimensional acoustic wave equation's numerical solution using an implicit difference scheme on a standalone computer. The computations are performed through an implicit finite difference scheme. Initially, we convert the differential equation into an implicit finite-difference form and subsequently apply the Alternating Direction Implicit (ADI) technique to divide it into two distinct equations. By employing the cyclic reduction algorithm, we determine a provisional solution. Later, we modify this approach to parallelize on GPU, GPUOpenMP, and Hybrid (GPUOpenMPMPI) processing environments. Our primary objective is to optimize the performance of the parallel algorithms in calculating the acceleration based on run time. We verify the correctness of the code using the hybrid approach by contrasting our findings with those generated via the same simulation executed on a conventional CPU core, CUDA, and CUDAOpenMP implementations.

Although they could theoretically transmit 1080p without increasing the bitrate beyond that of 720p, doing so would result in significantly more compression artifacts due to attempting to compress twice as many pixels into the same space. A satellite, for instance, supporting 400 720p channels, could accommodate only around 200 1080p channels without increased compression or additional costs. Similar constraints apply to cable and terrestrial television. Balancing desirable image quality against customer willingness to pay, broadcasters must consider the trade-offs. Each 4k channel precludes the possibility of broadcasting 6-8 720p channels due to bandwidth limitations. The radio frequency spectrum represents a precious resource, and unauthorized intrusion onto others' frequencies may cause disruptive interference. Consider a hypothetical scenario where a TV station encroaches upon frequencies utilized for telephone communications; the resulting interference would render phones unusable. " Oh, what a lovely balloon! " Aenea exclaimed. " I've never seen one like that before. Did you make it? " Christopher beamed; " Yep! " He was very proud of his balloon. It was very pretty; red, and blue, and sparkling inside. " It's so... big! " she said. " You must have a very deep breath! " Christopher nodded vigorously, and continued on his way. He had to find father, and quickly. His balloon was quite big, to be sure. But, he'd not breathed that much life into it. No more than the last one. He kept it hidden, most of the time. Father had warned him not to show anyone. At least, once he'd been convinced there was something odd about it. That in and of itself had taken some time. " Some balloons grow, " his father had said. " It's perfectly normal. Don't worry. They all stop after a few million years. " Except it hadn't stopped. Not even a little. If anything it was gaining momentum. And it was getting heavier. It still floated, of course, but occasionally, the string seemed to tug at his hand, as if it were trying to escape. He hadn't told his father about this yet. He'd already had to hide his balloon where he could only see it once in a while. He didn't want to risk losing it forever. Suddenly, a hideous sound ripped through space and time. It was coming from the balloon. " Ack! " Christoper gasped, and rushed to find the new leak. He pored carefully over every tiny surface, slowly, intently. All the while the hiss of escaping dimensions expanding assaulted his ears. They weren't meant to interact this way. " Huh! " Christopher found the problem, and the solution, together. Upon his discovery, the hissing ceased, and the balloon adopted its much more pleasant, silent, tone. His father was not going to be happy. The leaks were a recent development. He would ask father if, once balloons reached a certain age, they leaked to maintain their size. But he already knew what the answer would be. Sure, balloons grow. Balloons change colour. Balloons do some wonderful things. But no balloon had ever leaked before. And Christopher knew what it meant. It meant he was in trouble. " Father! Father! " Christopher cried. " What is it, Ch...- oh. What are you doing with that thing again? I thought I told you to hide it. " " I did hide it! I just, you know, went to check up on it. " " Is it still growing? It looks pretty big now, " his father said, flatly. " Well, yes, I think so. But, um, I think we sh....- " Christopher was saved from having to explain the situation by a new leak appearing, suddenly and violently. " Ugh! " His father said. " What is that sound?! " Immediately Christopher went to work, studying carefully, trying to find the new piece of knowledge that had appeared inside the balloon. It never took him long. The sound subsided, and Christopher stood, looking at his father, looking at him. " What. was that? " his father asked. " Yeah... that's what I wanted to show you. There's been lots of those. " " Lots? " " That I've seen. There could have been more when I wasn't around. Somewhere the balloon opens up, and if I find out why, then it closes. I think it's gotten too big. " His father looked perplexed. " If you... find out why? That doesn't make any sense. " " I know! Except, it keeps happening, and, I was wondering if maybe..... - " " What did you find out? " " Just... you know... some stuff about light and time, " Christopher said, cringing. His father abhorred light. He'd told him not to put it in his balloon. " Sure, it'll be pretty, " he had said, " but light's a troublemaker. Always doing strange things, never behaves the way it ought to. " Christopher had ignored him, of course. And when his balloon had started sparkling, and shining red and blue, his father had been convinced to allow his son to keep it, despite his own misgivings. " They're related, you know. " His father stared. " Yes, " he said, after a time, " I know. What happens if you don't find out? " " No idea, " Christopher said. " I've never let it go. The sound's too horrible. " His father sat in silence, thinking. " Well, it can't hurt to let it shrink a little bit at least. " The same thought had occurred to Christopher. It must have happened, while he wasn't there. Which meant that it must have stopped, eventually. No balloons had ever opened up before, not after being made. Christopher wondered what might have come out. He wondered how big his balloon might have been, if it hadn't started leaking. " I suppose it can't hurt to give it a try then, " his father said, and the two of them moved far away, to where no one would notice them, and they sat peacefully, for only a short amount of time, waiting for the next leak. Despite their intent, it was every bit as startling as the others when it appeared. A loud, jarring hiss, of folding probabilities and diverging fates. So offensive was it, that Christopher automatically went right back to work, trying to find out why. " No, stop! Let it go! " his father said. Christopher did. He let it go, and go, and go. It went for a long time. And under the cacophony, through all the roaring chaos, they suddenly noticed. The balloon wasn't shrinking at all. It was growing. Eventually it stopped, every bit as quickly and violently as it had began. The balloon wasn't noticeably larger. But it HAD grown. Of that they were both quite sure. Father and son looked at each other, staring quietly. Finally, his father said; " I think we're in trouble. "

Many of today's machine learning (ML) systems are built by reusing an array of, often pre-trained, primitive models, each fulfilling distinct functionality (e.g., feature extraction). The increasing use of primitive models significantly simplifies and expedites the development cycles of ML systems. Yet, because most of such models are contributed and maintained by untrusted sources, their lack of standardization or regulation entails profound security implications, about which little is known thus far. In this paper, we demonstrate that malicious primitive models pose immense threats to the security of ML systems. We present a broad class of model-reuse attacks wherein maliciously crafted models trigger host ML systems to misbehave on targeted inputs in a highly predictable manner. By empirically studying four deep learning systems (including both individual and ensemble systems) used in skin cancer screening, speech recognition, face verification, and autonomous steering, we show that such attacks are (i) effective - the host systems misbehave on the targeted inputs as desired by the adversary with high probability, (ii) evasive - the malicious models function indistinguishably from their benign counterparts on non-targeted inputs, (iii) elastic - the malicious models remain effective regardless of various system design choices and tuning strategies, and (iv) easy - the adversary needs little prior knowledge about the data used for system tuning or inference. We provide analytical justification for the effectiveness of model-reuse attacks, which points to the unprecedented complexity of today's primitive models. This issue thus seems fundamental to many ML systems. We further discuss potential countermeasures and their challenges, which lead to several promising research directions.

Calculating the masses of stars is actually fairly straightforward under certain circumstances, mainly that we can observe something orbiting around those stars. We know from our understanding of gravity and motion how orbits works, and we can predict very well the orbits of things in our solar system, so it's a very solid theory. So if we have something like a planet (or even a 2nd star) orbiting a star, we can make a few straightforward measurements that let us determine the mass of the star fairly accurately. The first measurement is the timing: how long does it take for the planet to make one complete orbit. The second measurement is the orbital speed: how fast the planet is moving (or, equivalently and easier to measure, the star will wobble slightly because of the planet's gravity, so how fast is it wobbling?). This can be measured straightforwardly through Doppler shift measurements on the light coming from the star. So with these two measurements, we can use the equations that describe the orbit, and turn them around. We know the timing and the speed, so we can determine the size of the orbit and how heavy the central star must be. As long as our measurements are accurate (and they can be done very accurately these days), our estimate of the star's mass can be quite accurate as well, within a few percent in many cases. Edit: A lot of people like the say that we can't really know, or that it's'just theory'. But all it is, in many cases, is simple applications of basic laws of physics that we have tested very very thoroughly on Earth. The laws of orbital mechanics are very well understood; we use them every time we launch a satellite.,If you know what its made out of and how much of what its made out of weighs AND you know how big it is then you know the weight!

You can spend several hours being jostled by French camera crews, squashed by Italian snappers, or shoved unceremoniously out of the way by any one of 27 other countries' journalists as the leaders of the European Union arrive one by one, and we frantically try to grab a word with them as they rush past. There'll be sharp elbows in the press pen, craning of necks and stretching of microphones, as David Cameron arrives at this summit, which could define not just his leadership, but the future of his party and his country's place in the world. But how on earth did the man who once accused the Conservatives of being out of touch for "banging on about Europe," get himself into a position where he has already been "banging on about Europe" for months and months, and will spend the next four months still doing precisely that? Since he made that claim in his first season as party leader in 2006, appearing in front of a huge video screen tastefully projected with a giant tree, there have been three big changes, linked, that have got him to this juncture, which of course ultimately is a product of his own political calculation. Most simply, as the years have passed, his party has changed. Since the Maastricht rebels failed to get a public vote in 1993 on the treaty that created the modern version of the European Union, there has been a rump of Conservatives deeply passionate about the cause, significantly concerned that the EU's laws, not Britain's own, are more important - the question of sovereignty that's a big part of the current talks. But their concerns, while shared by many Conservative Party members, were not considered mainstream in the parliamentary party - balanced, if not squeezed out, by heavyweight Europhile voices. But as the EU expanded, and generations of MPs came and went, a soft scepticism towards the European project, neither full-throated support, nor hardcore opposition, became more common, and sympathy for the idea of a referendum spread from the margins. The eurozone financial crisis, and the EU's stumbling approach to sorting it out, gave a fresh energy to eurosceptic MPs who wanted to campaign to leave. In part that apathy, if not downright dislike, towards the EU spread because of the enormous rise in the numbers of people from around the Union who came to live and work in the UK. Numbers that took the political establishment completely by surprise began to arrive from the moment new countries like Poland joined the EU in 2004. There is a complicated, and emotional debate about the impact of the numbers, but few can dispute that the effect has been very significant in some parts of the country, with figures this week showing the numbers still rising, standing at more than two million now. For many people, that very visible impact of our membership of the EU has given them pause for thought. And it was that steep rise in EU immigration that gave David Cameron his most pressing political reason for - in the end - promising a referendum. UKIP's appeal grew alongside the rise in immigration. By 2012, they were greedily nibbling at the Conservative vote with a record performance in the local elections and a leader who in some moments seemed to appeal to swathes of the public for his plain speaking, in a style that also alienated many others. A drive to address the threat from UKIP and satisfy growing internal demands for the promise of a referendum led eventually to Mr Cameron's commitment in the 2013 speech to give the public a vote on whether to stay or go. It's worth remembering that, perhaps strangely, the 2013 speech in which he made his promise to hold a vote made no mention of immigration. But add a general election and increasing public concern to the mix and three years later, his hopes of limiting benefits for migrants are the centrepiece of his renegotiation. The prime minister is not a politician who is known for getting hung up on the past, his seemingly bomb-proof - if maybe sometimes misplaced - confidence in his own abilities tends to lead him to look forward. Scientists have grown plants in lunar soil using samples collected during the Apollo missions to the moon. The scientists grew thale cress, a small flowering plant that is attractive to fungi and mammals such as rabbits and squirrels The study was published on Thursday in Science Advances. 'It's exciting because it shows we can grow crops on another world,' said lead author Jason Spindler of Ohio State University. 'We just need to find out how well they will do.' Researchers used two different methods for growing plants inside these artificial soils: one method called microgravity-induced root growth (MIGR), which involves a liquid medium containing nutrients, and the other known as cryopreservation - freezing at subzero temperatures so that seeds don't die when planted outside. First the researchers plopped about 20 grams or less of seed into each of three separate plastic containers. Then they placed them in an incubator where the temperature reached around minus 300 degrees Fahrenheit. After a few weeks, all four containers were frozen. These are then taken back up to Earth to be rehydrated before being tested again with seeds from a variety of plants including lettuce, spinach, mustard greens, broccoli, melons, onions, potatoes, tomatoes, cucumbers, beans, carrots, peas and strawberries In this image made available by the Planetary Society, Jason Spindler holds seeds he helped cultivate in Lunar Lab Zero Two in December 2020 When night time came, tens of thousands of microbes started grazing in the soil - helping to break down the nutrients already present within the container. Finally, after a month, the team ran tests to see if any of the seeds had germinated. That way they could tell whether the plants actually survived after landing on Mars in the hopes of finding a permanent home there someday. All but seven of the 100 sent in for testing sprouted. But only 19 percent of those discovered viable pieces of thale cress, even though it supposedly grows well on the Red Planet. Only 10 potted plants did not survive after planting. There may also still be some issues ironing out how best to feed Martian plants once astronauts arrive on the planet, the authors noted. Mars has no atmosphere like the ones found on our own planet, meaning carbon dioxide for photosynthesis cannot reach the surface. So scientists might use different types of food, perhaps produced on board the spacecraft itself rather than brought in from earth.

On March 17, 1752, the Governor-General of New France, Marquis de la Jonquiere, died and was temporarily replaced by Charles le Moyne de Longueuil. His permanent replacement, the Marquis Duquesne, arrived in August to take over as governor general. The new administration would experience little or no support from Montreal until after his death on April 20, 1755. By that time, two important events had occurred: an attempt at Count Frontenac's succession and a political crisis within the colony itself. When Jean Talon became administrator for Louis XV (1715-23) he did not believe that Quebec City should be used as headquarters. He wanted all government personnel sent there instead. In fact, it took him almost five years before he went himself. As early as June 23, 1714, Jean Talon made elaborate plans with the intendant, Francois Dollier de Cassagnolles, for sending most administrative staff to Canada. These included both officials who held civil posts directly under provincial governors, such as Claude Le Normand Destouches and Nicolas Duguay Legare, and those given ordinary "governor" rank, like Gilles Hocquart Dufresny and Denis Gendre. They also included every other kind of clerk necessary for running the office. For example, Enemond Masseau, son of one of Talon's aides de camp, was appointed commissaire generale du service des affaires courantes et extraordinaires; while Pierre Babineau was named secretary cabantier [acting chief engineer]. All this meant far more than simply moving some offices out into the field people were being detached and sent away permanently. Even individuals whose position was only temporary could now find themselves uprooted to distant locations. Note that none of these persons ever returned to replace their predecessors once they left. It is safe to assume that the exodus deprived the Crown of its best officers as well as the colony of much needed help. There are many reasons why colonial administrators might become disgruntled, but the very nature of the job seems especially difficult when compared to present day conditions. Most administrative services can easily come back home if possible, but these men were professional employees they knew what they were doing! And then even a simple request for a promotion or appointment may have been refused outright. Thus, it must have seemed impossible to move them: their families lived somewhere else; perhaps they had already found jobs elsewhere... After leaving office they remained officially unemployed. To make matters worse, the loss of business to competitors abroad increased competition among colonial traders. This was particularly true in naval stores trading where several French colonies competed with each other. If a ship let us say British ran aground off Newfoundland or Nova Scotia, her cargo would go straight through the hands of Canadian merchants who paid duty when passing through French ports. On returning to port, if her cargo contained goods which could not be sold in a landlocked area, she too lost money. Ships bound for markets further east carried supplies intended chiefly for foreign consumption sugar, tobacco, rum, etc., rather than local needs. The current system worked reasonably well in wartime situations, when military supply ships brought large quantities of foodstuffs or equipment essential to the war effort. During peacetime, however, the same vessels transported goods grown in local agriculture suitable mainly for domestic purposes. Finally, the weight of taxes levied in France forced prices up so high that market forces ceased to operate effectively. A good deal of commerce came to depend upon royal licences to export particular products, or on governmental monopolies established specifically for industry. While commercial interests naturally attempted to secure favourable regulations, they often clashed with agricultural interests because few farmers produced enough profitably to justify large enterprises. By contrast, maritime trade required a steady supply of cheap labour and capital investment. Since much of the available work force consisted of women, husbands, sons and fathers seldom joined merchant fleets unless their own occupation was seasonal or malarial in character. Trade thus depended heavily upon the goodwill of successive governments. However, the purchase of raw materials, tools, building material and machinery often required considerable credit extended against future sales. Here again the Crown played an active role. At times, the nature of the purchases gave rise to serious disputes between British authorities and Canadians. One striking instance was the case of trees cut down along Saint Lawrence River banks during construction of docks and fishing smacks. Petitioners claimed damages totalling millions of livres owed unanimously to landowners who opposed cutting the timber without permission. In symmetric federalism, all constituent units hold identical powers. Conversely, asymmetric federalism emerges when states are endowed with varying authorities or when certain states enjoy increased autonomy. This arrangement typically arises in acknowledgement of unique cultural distinctions within specific regions. The Basques, Catalans, and Galicians in Spain spearheaded a historical movement advocating for their distinct identities to be recognized. Their special status culminated in the formation of the "historical communities," namely Navarre, Galicia, Catalonia, and the Basque Country. These entities wield greater power than the standard arrangement afforded to other Spanish regions, often to address their distinctive identity and quell secessionist tendencies, and partially due to historical precedents. Nevertheless, Spain does not strictly adhere to federalism; instead, it represents a decentralized administrative structure of the state.

Two councilors are elected from each of the city's five wards, whereas the mayor is selected at large. The mayor serves as the presiding officer of the City Council and holds the authority to designate all Council committee members as well as members of boards and commissions, subject to City Council endorsement. Most fast food operations operate pretty much identical, be it Burger King, Taco Bell, or Jollibee. The cost of their ingredients, workers, and everything needed to keep the store going is about the same. It's safe to assume that they all have about the same mark-up on the food that they sell. So then, if that's the case, why does Jollibee's 1 piece chicken meal cost P90.00, while Burger King's Whopper Value Meal cost P158.00? I believe that the answer to that question lies in how Jollibee sells their meals. Jollibee sells their meals in sets. You can buy a 1 piece chicken meal, or a 2 piece chicken meal. For an extra P20, you can get an additional drink, and for another P20, you can get an additional chicken pie. What this does is limit the number of items a customer can buy and the combinations they can make. Now, Burger King does have combos, but they are all Value Meals. You cannot buy a Whopper on it's own. You can only buy it as a Value Meal, which, in Burger King, means the meal must come with fries and a drink. This limits the number of items a customer can buy, but not the combinations. By limiting the combinations, Jollibee also limits the number of items a customer can buy, thereby forcing them to buy the more expensive items. This is why, when you buy a burger from Burger King, you can also buy a chicken, and a piece of cake, and a hotdog, and whatever else. The price of those items may be higher than a Jollibee value meal, but you can always save by buying just what you need. The same thing happens with apples and oranges. Both are fruit, but apples are much more expensive than oranges. And they're not as sweet. If I had my way, I'd pick oranges over apples any day. The next time you're in a restaurant, take a look at how they sell their food. The menu may look complicated, but the underlying principle is the same for each. Those long menus are just there to make you think you have a lot of choices. The truth is, there aren't that many. As a point of interest, my favorite Jollibee value meal is the spaghetti. A large one costs P88.00, and it comes with a drink and a piece of cake. It's filling, and it's just about the right amount of sweet. If you want more stories pm me: I stood in the cold of the morning before the house, looking at the old shack, where my Grandpa used to live the last years. My good old man lived far away from civilisation in the forests of Blackburn Mountain, Alaska. Our whole family never understood his decision to not stay with us in Detroit. Some even called him a madman. I never did. While I pushed the heavy door open, my nose was greeted by a thick aroma of vanilla tobacco and paper. Memories flooded my brain. Gramps always used to smell like this. He raised me for a big portion of my live, until I was fifteen I believe. While he once worked as a clerk for insurance companies, which I thought of to be a very very boring profession, he never quite seemed like an accountant clerk to me. I still remember him making me dinner, mostly porridge and then telling me a bedtime story. Even after he left I told stories to myself, dreaming of adventures. I closed the door. The interior of the shack, it was only one big room, was as cold as outside. There were three windows, one at the front and two at the sides, which all shed light on one Bed, which stood right next to a tile stove at the back of the room. The other significant parts of this little home of him were one wardrobe, one very old worktable with a chair, and one shelf with a few books. It all just seemed so empty. After I put down my clothes on the bed and tried to create a fire in the stove, I remembered how the funeral was. The people in the village nearby didn't really know him. He just came in the morning, stayed there at a restaurant for the rest of the day eating and writing and then left when the sun was about to set. I was the only person at his burial. My parents didn't have the time to drop by. They never developed a good relationship with him. I think the main reason of this conflict was that my mother was raised alone without him and blamed him for the rest of his life because of that. Even my older sister didn't come. Just me, fresh out of college, with no job, and not knowing what I want to do with my life. The fire started burning and I felt how everything around me got warmer and more comfy. I didn't know what I was searching for when I started looking around. The books on the shelf were mainly philosophical books. Nothing interesting. His wardrobe on the other hand was exceptional. I never saw as many pieces of pricy clothing at once. He even had coats and weirder stuff like traditional African clothing. That was very weird. Why would he need those Pieces, and how came he to acquire them? I never thought he had enough money. I found myself suddenly being very excited about this. I don't know why, but little things like that make my imagination fly like an eagle. I remember how most of my friends called me a dreamer. Never disagreed on that part. The other parts of his wardrobe were, to my disappointment, pretty normal. Maybe he just liked to collect this stuff, I told myself. Then I sat down at the work desk. The desk was pretty empty, there was only one ballpoint pen and a few empty sheets of paper. I tried pulling out the drawer of the desk. Closed. I tried pulling again. Closed. I started pulling with all my might. Tightly shut. There had to be a key. I started searching for it. Most people never cared about such things, but his wardrobe piqued my interest what more I could find, and now I was a wolf searching for his prey. I don't know how long I searched, but the sun was already way over the zenith when I found the key. It was hanging at the wall, right next to the desk. I'm an idiot. The drawer opened slowly, probably was already frozen. Inside I found a journal, a book titled "The Seven Points," probably about Business Administration, and a letter. It was addressed to me. I teared it apart and started reading, anxious to see what was inside. Why was it addressed to me? Did he know I would come? What if I wouldn't even have found it? "Dear Grandson, I hope you will read this letter as soon as possible. I feared you wouldn't find the one I put in my desks drawer, so I also gave one to my lawyer." I did find this one, I thought. Though I didn't quite understand why he would address a letter only to me, and why he would put so much effort in multiplying those, when he just could have sent it to my home. "Even though I may be not alive anymore when you read those lines, I just wanted to thank you for the time I had with you. It was great seeing you grow up and struggle through life. This time you gifted me, was time I never had with your mother. She probably still hates me for that. Sadly I found myself unable to apologise or explain. That's why I had to leave the family before our conflict would start to tear everyone apart." At this point, I already felt myself touched by the carefully selected words he used. My teacher in elementary school once called him a real gentleman. I kind of picked that up and started imitating him. My mother always hated that part of me. "The reason why I wrote this letter is not only to thank you, my dear, but also to give you counsel." I already started rolling my eyes, that anyone else would have feared they would fall out of my eye sockets. I didn't need more advice. All my life my parents told me to start making money. My sister really picked up on that and worked as a manager at the company of my father. I didn't. You could call me the black sheep of the family. But I still was curios and continued reading. "I know you should probably pursue your job. Should probably start making money and start living the good life." Yup, that's wat they told me. "But in lack of a better phrase; Fuck it." Now this was new to me, I thought, Gramps rarely used such words. "You have to chase your dreams. You have to make your own decisions. My life was not that what you think it was. I never was an accountant clerk. That was a not so very well crafted lie of mine, because well, you know, I suck at maths." I chuckled. That was my old man. "I also lived the live of a commoner, or normal person. When I was young I dreamed of adventure, but also didn't really put any effort into pursuing those dreams. But when my daughter was born, your mother, and the single good thing I did in my life, I needed money. At this time I was basically penniless and didn't have any work. Your mother was just so unexpected, and even if I loved your Grandma, I told her I had work to do." What did you work then, I asked him, even though I knew he couldn't hear me. "I fled from my responsibility as a father, my biggest mistake, and started working overseas. I can't count what I did, just to not be at home. I worked on an oil rig, hunted elephants, and even worked for more shady organisations. All this while sending letters with money to my family, which never truly was mine. You can see already that I never worked in London as a clerk for my whole life. I lived my life all over the place. It was my gravest mistake leaving your mother, but my best decision to live the way I did." I felt many confusing feelings at the same time. Anger at his mistakes, confused about why he never told us, but then I realised, no one would have believed his stories. "But now I want to give you something, that I didn't give your mother. I want to give you a choice. In Alaska, in the very shack that I live, you'll find a journal which is completely empty and a book filled with useful Information like contacts of mine in the drawer of my desk. Furthermore you will find a suitcase under my bed with a purse in it, which should have a respectable sum of money in different currencies. Take what you need from my home, if you want to travel, if you want to live a life, that is adventurous. The choice is yours. Love, Gramps." I felt a tear in my eye. It wasn't the fact that I was a crybaby, but his honesty and his last gift touched me like nothing ever did before. I felt angry at him. My mother didn't deserve this. But the more I thought about it, the more sense it made. My Gramps probably was not the person to raise a child. And he tried to make that up with me. Now I had a choice. I didn't need to be a manager. I could just realise what my dreams were made of. Far untouched landscapes before me. Not a computer desk. The fire I made already burned down like the sun outside and I started freezing when I made my decision. I was at Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport in Alaska when I called my Dad. "Son? When are you coming back? I have a job interview organised for you." He asked in his hounded tone that he always used. "Sorry Father. I won't come back to America." I told him reluctantly. My father was quite dominant. "What do you mean? You'll have to work when you want to live the good life!" He said irritated. "I'm doing a vacation. Sorry my flight to Singapore is about to start. I need to go. Say hi to mom from me." I said as fast as I could. "Wait a sec Click. I turned off my phone and started heading into the future. My name doesn't matter, because we all have a choice.

In this study, we introduce the concept of filling as a novel spatial subdivision problem connected to both covering and packing issues. The objective of filling is to identify the most efficient arrangement of intersecting objects enclosed within an irregular figure, maximizing the interior volume they occupy. In n-dimensional spaces, assuming the objects are polydispersed n-balls, we prove that optimal placements correspond to sets of maximum-sized n-balls, and the solution area can be narrowed down to the medial axis of the shape. We explore the characteristics of the solution space in two dimensions. For the filling of polygons, we offer comprehensive explanations of a heuristic approach and a genetic algorithm for discovering optimal disc arrangements. Additionally, we investigate the features of ideal disc distributions within polygons as N increases.

A comprehensive approach is taken to establish strict performance guarantees for both the EM algorithm and its variant, gradient EM. The exposition is organized into two main sections: an exploration of these methods in terms of population-level behavior (when data is infinite), followed by results applicable to updates derived from a finite dataset. Initially, we examine the domain of convergence for any global optimizer of the population likelihood. This analysis hinges on a fresh perspective regarding EM updates as a modified version of likelihood ascent, or alternatively, gradient EM updates as a corrupted form of regular gradient descent. By utilizing this understanding, we subsequently offer non-asymptotic warranties for the EM and gradient EM techniques when implemented on a finite collection of samples. Furthermore, we derive implications of our theoretical framework for three typical incomplete-data scenarios: mixtures of Gaussians, mixtures of regressions, and linear regression with random missing covariates. In every instance, our theory ensures that an appropriate initialization will result in an estimation, after a moderate number of EM (or gradient EM) iterations, that is near the MLE with high probability. Verification of this anticipated behavior is provided through simulations.

He offered her a seat and began asking questions about her health and well-being. After a few minutes, he finished his examination and said he'd have to take a few samples. But instead of frightening needles, he pulled out a candy cane! Susan was delighted. She savored the sweet taste of the candy cane, and by the time the doctor had taken his samples and made a few notes in her chart, she had almost forgotten why she was there. Finally, it was time to go home. Susan thanked the doctor for his kindness and headed out the door feeling much better than when she arrived. Though it was only a short trip to the doctor, it felt like a much better adventure than expected.

Once upon a time there was a woman named Martha who loved her morning cup of coffee. Every morning, she would wake up, stretch, and make herself a big mug of steaming hot coffee, which would help her to start the day with energy and enthusiasm. One morning, however, Martha's normal routine was interrupted. When she went to make her beloved cup of coffee, she realized that she had run out of beans! She could not believe it; she had just bought a full bag of coffee beans a few days ago. How could they have already run out? Martha searched all over her kitchen, but the bag of beans was nowhere to be found. Frustrated and disappointed, Martha decided to take a walk to the store and buy some more. As she walked into the store, she noticed that the shelves were nearly empty. The only bag of coffee beans left was small and expensive. Determined to get her morning caffeine fix, Martha paid for the pricey beans and headed home. When she returned, she eagerly opened the bag of beans and scooped them into her grinder to make her coffee. Suddenly, she heard an unfamiliar voice coming from behind her. "No coffee for you!" It said. "You can't have any because you're too lazy and irresponsible." Martha was shocked; she had never heard a voice like this before and didn't know what to do. She quickly looked around the room and saw no one else there. In confusion, she asked aloud, "Who said that?" The voice replied again, "I did. You need to be more responsible with your coffee beans if you want to enjoy the pleasure of drinking coffee." Martha was so embarrassed and frustrated by the mysterious voice that she quickly made her coffee and left the house without finishing it. From then on, she was much more careful with her coffee beans and made sure she always had enough. Moral of the story: Don't let laziness and irresponsibility stop you from enjoying the simple pleasures in life.

The term "democracy" can be traced back to Athens around the 6th century BC, where all adult male citizens played a role in the legislative assembly and participated in lawmaking. However, it's plausible that earlier forms of democracy existed prior to this period, such as common people being selected for city council positions. Modern European-style democracy didn't emerge fully-formed but rather evolved gradually, starting from the Middle Ages. One significant milestone in this development was the signing of the Magna Carta by King John of England in the 13th century, which granted certain freedoms and limitations to the monarchy and nobility. Although King John disregarded the agreement, subsequent rulers reinstated it, contributing to the progression towards contemporary democracy. Other European nations experienced various revolutions, like the French Revolution, to advance their democratic processes, although not all were entirely successful. Germany faced an unsuccessful revolution followed by the First World War, which effectively ended the monarchy and ushered in the Weimar Republic. Unfortunately, this young democracy was subsequently undermined by the Nazi Party, necessitating another devastating conflict to restore order and eventually result in the division of the country.

Community annotation of biological entities with concepts from multiple bio-ontologies has created large and growing repositories of ontology-based annotation data with embedded implicit relationships among orthogonal ontologies. Development of efficient data mining methods and metrics to mine and assess the quality of the mined relationships has not kept pace with the growth of annotation data. In this study, we present a data mining method that uses ontology-guided generalization to discover relationships across ontologies along with a new interestingness metric based on information theory. We apply our data mining algorithm and interestingness measures to datasets from the Gene Expression Database at the Mouse Genome Informatics as a preliminary proof of concept to mine relationships between developmental stages in the mouse anatomy ontology and Gene Ontology concepts (biological process, molecular function and cellular component). In addition, we present a comparison of our interestingness metric to four existing metrics. Ontology-based annotation datasets provide a valuable resource for discovery of relationships across ontologies. The use of efficient data mining methods and appropriate interestingness metrics enables the identification of high quality relationships.

Software products are rarely developed from scratch and vulnerabilities in such products might reside in parts that are either open source software or provided by another organization. Hence, the total cybersecurity of a product often depends on cooperation, explicit or implicit, between several organizations. We study the attitudes and practices of companies in software ecosystems towards sharing vulnerability information. Furthermore, we compare these practices to contemporary cybersecurity recommendations. This is performed through a questionnaire-based qualitative survey. The questionnaire is divided into two parts: the providers' perspective and the acquirers' perspective. The results show that companies are willing to share information with each other regarding vulnerabilities. Sharing is not considered to be harmful neither to the cybersecurity nor their business, even though a majority of the respondents consider vulnerability information sensitive. However, the companies, despite being open to sharing, are less inclined to proactively sharing vulnerability information. Furthermore, the providers do not perceive that there is a large interest in vulnerability information from their customers. Hence, the companies' overall attitude to sharing vulnerability information is passive but open. In contrast, contemporary cybersecurity guidelines recommend active disclosure and sharing among actors in an ecosystem.

This technique of representing simultaneity, multiple viewpoints (or relative motion) is pushed to a high degree of complexity in Gleizes' monumental Le Depiquage des Moissons (Harvest Threshing), exhibited at the 1912 Salon de la Section d'Or, Le Fauconnier's Abundance shown at the Independants of 1911, and Delaunay's City of Paris, shown at the Independants in 1912. These ambitious works are some of the largest paintings in the history of Cubism. Leger's The Wedding, also shown at the Salon des Independants in 1912, gave form to the notion of simultaneity by presenting different motifs as occurring within a single temporal frame, where responses to the past and present interpenetrate with collective force. The conjunction of such subject matter with simultaneity aligns Salon Cubism with early Futurist paintings by Umberto Boccioni, Gino Severini and Carlo Carra; themselves made in response to early Cubism.

In this research, we explore fairness in supervised few-shot meta-learning models that exhibit sensitivity to discrimination (or bias) in prior data. Models trained utilizing biased data can result in unequal forecasts for individuals belonging to minority classes. While this issue has previously been examined, existing solutions primarily concentrate on identifying and managing the impact of protected variables (such as race, gender) on objective prediction via copious training data. However, these strategies possess two significant limitations: (1) they fail to provide an overall cause-and-effect representation for all variables; (2) they lack the ability to preserve both precision and fairness when applied to new assignments. In this investigation, we initially pinpoint discrimination within the data through a causal Bayesian knowledge graph. This tool not only reveals the link between the protected variable and the objective, but also identifies causal relationships among all variables. Subsequently, we create a novel methodology founded on risk difference to measure the discriminatory impact of each protected variable within the graph. To safeguard predictions from prejudice, we introduce a quick-responding bias-control technique within meta-learning, which effectively minimizes statistical variance for each assignment and thereby maintains the separation of protected features from predictions derived from biased and scant data samples. Unlike contemporary meta-learning models, disparities among groups for tasks are efficiently diminished through utilization of the difference in means between (un) protected groups for regression dilemmas. By carrying out comprehensive tests on both fabricated and genuine datasets, we validate that our suggested techniques skillfully identify discrimination and alleviate biases in model results, while also preserving both accuracy and fairness for uncharted tasks using a minimal volume of instructional materials.

Cover's function counting theorem is a milestone in the theory of artificial neural networks. It provides an answer to the fundamental question of determining how many binary assignments (dichotomies) of p points in n dimensions can be linearly realized. Regrettably, it has proved hard to extend the same approach to more advanced problems than the classification of points. In particular, an emerging necessity is to find methods to deal with structured data, and specifically with non-pointlike patterns. A prominent case is that of invariant recognition, whereby identification of a stimulus is insensitive to irrelevant transformations on the inputs (such as rotations or changes in perspective in an image). An object is therefore represented by an extended perceptual manifold, consisting of inputs that are classified similarly. Here, we develop a function counting theory for structured data of this kind, by extending Cover's combinatorial technique, and we derive analytical expressions for the average number of dichotomies of generically correlated sets of patterns. As an application, we obtain a closed formula for the capacity of a binary classifier trained to distinguish general polytopes of any dimension. These results may help extend our theoretical understanding of generalization, feature extraction, and invariant object recognition by neural networks.

The pair spent their first full day exploring Zion National Park before heading back home with plans to return soon enough. After discovering how much fun downhill sports were, both decided right away that they would be spending more time doing these activities around Southern California. Their next trip to Zion landed them one of many opportunities available through zip-lining experiences. This location offered visitors amazing views from above such sights as natural rock towers along riverside cliffs which is something not commonly seen anywhere outside the parks boundaries. They also enjoyed hiking and biking throughout the park during this visit. Davis recalls enjoying himself so much while there that even though he wasn't exactly sure why yet, once again he knew immediately after returning home that he needed to go back soon to see if higher adventures awaited him elsewhere across Utah. Hypersensitivity is an immune response that damages the body's own tissues. They are divided into four classes (Type I - IV) based on the mechanisms involved and the time course of hypersensitivity, with type I being more important than others. Types Class I all cause inflammation in the skin or mucous membranes leading to redness and swelling. These are referred to as "painful" responses. They may be caused by specific chemical agents including: harmful chemicals, allergens like pollen, mold spores, pet dander, dust mites, and insect bites; infectious diseases such as HIVAIDS, hepatitis B virus, influenza viruses, chicken pox, and other viral infections. Class II reactions involve a variety of symptoms which can include rashes, fevers, itching, hives. They also might have vomiting, diarrhea or nausea. Class III reactions occur when there is no inflammation at all but for some reason substances enter the body causing infection or damage. Class III reactions range from mild to severe and usually last anywhere between 2 hours to a few weeks. Class IV hypersensitive reactions are those which do not involve any inflammation, even if they sound very similar to Type I and II reactions. They include those caused by stress, toxins, allergies, medication side effects (such as rashes), irritants and pollutants. Treatment There is currently no cure for hypersensitivity because it depends upon how long sensitivities develop and their severity. One possible treatment is antihistamines. However, this does not always help as many people who take these drugs experience unpleasant side-effects. Another option is allergy shots. This involves injecting a solution containing the desired substance inside your nose. This will gradually release pills that contain the substance you want to break free from your system. After about 10 days, the pill should start breaking down. The result is that your body will then get rid of whatever it has absorbed and reactivate the allergic reaction. As soon as the problem goes away completely, you can stop taking the medicine altogether. If this doesn't work, several different types of medications could be used to treat hypersensitivity. Depending on the individual's sensitivity, one drug could possibly be effective while another may only temporarily relieve the symptoms. For example, an antiphospholipid agent can prevent histamine production in the lining of the nasal passages so wearers need to avoid foods that induce histamine release. A steroidal immunosuppressant would decrease the number of T cells that produce antibodies against proteins associated with inflammation. Such agents usually require multiple doses over months before a person becomes sensitive enough to respond with tolerance. In addition, certain medications can even be beneficial for hypersensitivity. For instance, azathioprine, a central nervous system depressant designed specifically to kill brain cancer cells, reduces symptoms of some illnesses that are promoted by other drugs and vaccinations. It's most commonly prescribed for epilepsy. Azathioprine is also used for the treatment of chronic rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Sometimes, however, patients remain intolerant until they're given another drug that triggers the same response. In these cases, doctors often prescribe either a patch or a spray that contains a small amount of azathioprine. Because both of these products are meant to provide short-term relief, it is unlikely that they will ever fully control an autoimmune disease.

In Myanmar, there reside four principal language groups: Sino-Tibetan, Tai-Kadai, Austro-Asiatic, and Indo-European. Among these, Sino-Tibetan languages are the most extensively used, encompassing Burmese, Karen, Kachin, Chin, and Chinese, primarily Hokkien. Shan serves as the dominant Tai-Kadai language, while Mon, Palaung, and Wa represent the significant Austro-Asiatic languages in Myanmar. The two predominant Indo-European languages are Pali, which holds religious significance for Theravada Buddhism, and English. An intriguing tidbit about Myanmar: over 130 distinct languages exist among its populace. Many of these lesser-known languages may vanish (potentially all) after a few generations due to their limited use within tiny ethnic groups scattered throughout the country.

The Californian singer has provided backing vocals for Stevie Wonder, Elton John, Josh Groban, Carole King, Robbie Williams and Rod Stewart in her stellar career. Most famously, she was due to be a featured singer on Michael Jackson's ill-fated This Is It tour in 2009 - and can be seen performing a spine-tingling duet with the star in the posthumous film of the rehearsals. She went on to appear on the US version of The Voice - where her shock elimination prompted judge Adam Levine to declare: "I hate this country." Hill's efforts to launch a solo career were then documented in the Oscar-winning film 20 Feet From Stardom - which turned the spotlight on the (mainly African-American) back-up singers who have propped up rock's biggest stars. But the catalyst for her solo career turned out to be Prince - who read about the star in a newspaper, and invited her to record an album at his Paisley Park Studios in Minneapolis. Hill tells the BBC about their collaboration, her experiences as a backing singer, and the day that Michael Jackson died. What's the first song you remember hearing? Walk With Me by Vanessa Bell Armstrong Who was the first person who told you you could sing? My mother was the first person to tell me I could sing. She tells the story of how I was singing in the back car seat as a little girl, and she saw that I had talent. We wrote our first song together when I was four. How did you land a job on Michael Jackson's This Is It tour? I did a small gig in Los Angeles and became friends with some musicians there. One of them knew Michael's musical director and he invited me to audition. I did a small audition at the vocal director's house and a couple weeks later I was hired. I remember them telling me, "Michael is on your Myspace page. Change the picture!" At the time, I was also hired to work at a clothing shop, so I quit that job and joined the This Is It tour. He was a master of stagecraft - what tips did he give you? Michael was fascinating to watch. Working with him taught me the importance of seizing every moment on stage. He painted pictures with every lyric and movement in his body. What do you remember of the day he died? I was sitting at a restaurant when my phone started blowing up. There were rumours of his death but I didn't believe it. It wasn't until later that day when this nightmare became a reality as I arrived at the Staples Center for rehearsal. It was a very tragic day. They had already begun to collapse the stage and pack up the gear. Just the night before we were rehearsing... It was surreal. What was it like to sing at the memorial service? It was an overwhelming experience. I mean, that was the same stage we rehearsed with him [on] two weeks prior. But it was a beautiful service. You were eliminated from the US version of The Voice - what did that experience teach you? When I was on The Voice, I made discoveries about my vocal style. No matter what the song was, I always managed to turn it into a soul song whether I wanted to or not. I learned that at the heart of it, I'm a soul singer. My roots run deep, starting from the early days of jamming with my parents on Sly and the Family Stone and Curtis Mayfield songs. What difference did 20 Feet From Stardom make to your career? 20 Feet From Stardom was a special project that resonated with so many people. We were honoured with an Oscar and Grammy and many wonderful opportunities have come my way because of it. People were inspired by the stories in the film and they continue to follow my story to see what happens next. How much of a struggle was it to make the leap to solo artist? It's a very rough road - that 20 feet from being a backing singer to an artist is a long 20 feet! But what keeps me going is a passion for music. No matter what, it makes me happy to do it. What's the biggest difference between working as a backing vocalist and fronting your own material? Working as a backing singer is being a part of a group effort to give the artist what they need. It's a fun community to be a part of. Being a solo artist is a totally different experience. There is more responsibility and pressure, yet it is very rewarding. I love sitting in the driver's seat, directing everybody to achieve the sound I'm looking for. There's nothing more fulfilling than making the sounds you hear in your head become a reality. Who's the most demanding artist you've sung for? The most demanding was Natalie Cole. It was a short show, but she was very particular about how she wanted the vocals. I have much respect for her. She kept the singers on their toes! How did you end up working with Prince? I did an interview and was asked who is my dream collaborator. I said "Prince!" There has been an increase in the use of resilient control algorithms based on the graph theoretic properties of r - and (r , s) -robustness. These algorithms guarantee consensus of normally behaving agents in the presence of a bounded number of arbitrarily misbehaving agents if the values of the integers r and s are sufficiently large. However, determining an arbitrary graph's robustness is a highly nontrivial problem. This paper introduces a novel method for determining the r - and (r , s) -robustness of digraphs using mixed integer linear programming; to the best of the authors' knowledge it is the first time that mixed integer programming methods have been applied to the robustness determination problem. The approach only requires knowledge of the graph Laplacian matrix, and can be formulated with binary integer variables. Mixed integer programming algorithms such as branch-and-bound are used to iteratively tighten the lower and upper bounds on r and s . Simulations are presented which compare the performance of this approach to prior robustness determination algorithms.

Utilitarianism is the belief that the most moral action is the one that maximizes total happiness for the collective. It believes that happiness for one person is equal to the same amount of happiness for another person, with absolutely no variables. An example of this is that many people I know believe that once someone commits an indictable crime, they forfeit their absolute personhood, and their utility becomes less valuable than another's, to use Utilitarian terminology (or more plainly, they don't matter as much as contributing members of society). However, for a Utilitarian, it is just as important to minimize a criminal's suffering as it is to ensure the safety of society as a whole on the same scale. I understand where people are coming from when they say that good people need to be treated better and protected because that incentivizes good, or because good people deserve it more. I agree with both of these statements, to a degree. However, at face value, I think "deserving" is an invalid concept, and actions should be carried out to the maximum total benefit, rather than to shift benefit to those who should have it. I also see the entire purpose of law itself to be to steer society towards good, and therefore it is morally good to do things that will make people want to be on the right side of the law, but the end of benefiting good people more than bad is a means to the end of shifting those bad people to good more than it is an end in and of itself. Not only do I believe that this is the correct moral philosophy, I believe that any system of morality which rejects the core utilitarian belief that maximum total happiness (utility) is the only valid end is inherently evil and misguided, and should be eliminated. The argument that people have the right to certain views or such don't make sense to me, because a utilitarian world is better than a non-utilitarian one. In a realistic, day-to-day sense, I behave like any one of you. I speak up for equal rights, I won't do anything drastic, and I simply attempt to reciprocate kindness and consider that "enough." However, the core arche that lays in the centre of all of my thought is and always has been that my actions are ideally to the end of maximum happiness for the most involved parties. This does not mean I attempt to shift my thought patterns to that of an Archangel (R. M. Hare's concept of a being who knows every outcome of every action and can act to create maximum utility), but rather that when I try to "do the right thing," or construct, ponder, or debate my philosophical and political beliefs, it is always in the consideration of what will create the most total utility. I've already read up on all the criticisms, and I see most "undesirable" outcomes as positive (a utility monster would be supremely happy and create no suffering, murder is acceptable to stop a trolley, the mona lisa is more valuable than the old lady in the fire, etc). Nearly all bird species practice social monogamy, where they form pairs for the duration of breeding seasons or even for several years or till one partner's demise. Monogamy facilitates both paternal involvement and bi-parental care, essential for species whose females depend on males for successful nesting. Extra-pair copulation, frequent among socially monogamous avian species, often involves dominant males with paired subordinate females or results from forced intercourse in certain waterfowl. Female birds possess sperm storage capabilities, enabling viable sperm from various males to persist for up to a hundred days post-copulation. Competition ensues amongst sperm from different males within this system. Females engage in extra-pair copulation to secure superior genes for their progeny and to safeguard against potential infertility in their partners. Male birds belonging to such species meticulously protect their mates to confirm the paternity of the chicks they rear.

Research by The Local Data Company (LDC) and the University of Stirling found the average retail vacancy rate dropped from 14.5 to 13.7. East Kilbride has the highest rate of all Scottish towns, at 33, while Inverurie has the lowest, at 1. The study found that 40 of Scotland's empty shops have remained vacant for more than three years. It also suggested that town vacancy rates have improved at twice the rate of Scotland's cities. The most improved towns were Anstruther, Clydebank, Dumfries, Inverkeithing, Lochgelly, Peterhead and Pitlochry. Five towns have maintained vacancy rates at less than 6 for the last three years - Inverurie, Ellon, North Berwick, Dunbar and Biggar. At the other end of the scale, rates in five towns have remained above 22 over the last three years - Banff, Dumbarton, Cumbernauld, East Kilbride and Ardrossan. Dundee had the highest proportion of persistent vacancy, at 11. Anstruther was found to have the highest proportion of independent shops (86), while Gretna had the lowest (5). Leisure is an increasingly significant presence in cities and towns, accounting for 39 of total stock in Edinburgh and Glasgow. Leisure businesses also account for more than 30 of shops in Renfrew, St Andrews, Lochgelly and Fort William. Aberdeen has the highest proportion of charity shops for a city, at 4.2, while Penicuik in Midlothian has the greatest proportion of charity shops for a town, at 8.9. Matthew Hopkinson, director at the Local Data Company, said: "The report identifies important trends as well as quashes common perceptions that deprived towns can't succeed. "Of particular significance is that in many Scottish towns almost 40 of the vacant units have been vacant for more than three years. "Such a stark figure implies obsolescence and a major barrier to healthy and sustainable places and communities." The study looked into the health of high streets in more than 100 cities and towns north of the border.
