The investigation was led by Scotland Yard and involved numerous police forces across the UK. The teenager was arrested on suspicion of breaching the Computer Misuse Act, and his release on bail comes after he was questioned by detectives from the Metropolitan Police's Cyber Crime Unit. In a statement, TalkTalk said: "We're grateful for the swift action of the police in making an arrest in connection with the cyber attack on our website. We continue to work closely with the authorities and are committed to doing everything possible to secure our customers' data." The company has since pledged to invest 40m in improved IT security following the breach, as well as to overhaul its website and customer service procedures. TalkTalk has also faced criticism from customers who claim that the telecoms provider was slow to respond to the breach and did not do enough to protect their personal data. A number of class-action lawsuits have since been launched against the company, claiming damages for those whose personal information was compromised. TalkTalk is just one of a growing number of high-profile companies to have suffered a major data breach in recent years, highlighting the need for increased online security measures to protect personal information. The case is ongoing, and it remains to be seen what further action will be taken against those responsible for the alleged data theft.

There are two ways to think of light when looking at something. It either generates light itself, like a light bulb or the sun, or it's showing reflected light, like a mirror or some glittering surface. That difference is important because we can't see directly into objects that reflect lights. We have to look into them through other things - like mirrors and windows. In this chapter you'll learn about three different kinds of lenses: convex lenses, concave lenses, and prisms. Convex A convex lens focuses all rays coming from one point (an object) onto the same spot on its opposite side where another ray comes in for focus. If you're using an ordinary camera with film, the type of lens then used to stop down as much light as possible before exposing your photos will be called "a zoom." This means there are adjustments available so you can get close-ups without blowing out shadows too badly. You might also use such a lens if you want more depth of field than would otherwise occur, which lets the whole scene come forward while making parts stand apart nicely. For example, you could take a photo of someone sitting outside during the day but make their eyes appear bigger by focusing just on those positions in front of her face. The overall effect wouldn't happen naturally unless she were inside a room with no window behind her; we'd never notice how small they looked until she was backlit. As a descriptive term, zoom lenses may not mean anything to most people, though. Zooming has been around since photography began, but today's compact lenses don't typically open up and close down the diaphragm automatically when changing magnification. The wideangle setting makes everything closer together and includes all points within half a degree of the center point. Field of view extends to 90 degrees horizontally, 72 degrees vertically. In contrast, a typical telephoto shot subjects include only what appears near the edges of our vision. Objects beyond a certain distance become blurred in perspective. Our eyes aren't trained to do this kind of detail work very well anymore because modern technology provides better images, but in the days of glass plates we had low-quality copies made whenever needed so we didn't need to confuse ourselves over whether any details really existed or weren't simply optical illusions. This study introduces a novel multi-antenna encoding method referred to as Space-Time Index Modulation (STIM). In STIM, data is transmitted via antenna selection in the spatial domain, time slot utilization in the time domain, and M-ary modulation symbols. The decision to use or leave empty a time slot within a frame's framework conveys slot index information. Furthermore, antenna index bits are encoded into each occupied time slot by engaging a single antenna from the pool. M-ary symbols are transmitted over the active antenna during an occupied time slot. Our analysis focuses on a cyclic-prefixed single-carrier (CPSC) system undergoing frequency-selective fading channels. The results indicate that STIM delivers superior performance compared to traditional Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) for identical spectral efficiency and single transmit RF chains. Additionally, low-complexity iterative techniques for decoding high-dimensional STIM signals are provided.

We study fairness in supervised few-shot meta-learning models that are sensitive to discrimination (or bias) in historical data. A machine learning model trained based on biased data tends to make unfair predictions for users from minority groups. Although this problem has been studied before, existing methods mainly aim to detect and control the dependency effect of the protected variables (e.g. race, gender) on target prediction based on a large amount of training data. These approaches carry two major drawbacks that (1) lacking showing a global cause-effect visualization for all variables; (2) lacking generalization of both accuracy and fairness to unseen tasks. In this work, we first discover discrimination from data using a causal Bayesian knowledge graph which not only demonstrates the dependency of the protected variable on target but also indicates causal effects between all variables. Next, we develop a novel algorithm based on risk difference in order to quantify the discriminatory influence for each protected variable in the graph. Furthermore, to protect prediction from unfairness, a fast-adapted bias-control approach in meta-learning is proposed, which efficiently mitigates statistical disparity for each task and it thus ensures independence of protected attributes on predictions based on biased and few-shot data samples. Distinct from existing meta-learning models, group unfairness of tasks are efficiently reduced by leveraging the mean difference between (un) protected groups for regression problems. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets, we demonstrate that our proposed unfairness discovery and prevention approaches efficiently detect discrimination and mitigate biases on model output as well as generalize both accuracy and fairness to unseen tasks with a limited amount of training samples.

On April 18, 1985, a few months after taking his Senate seat, Kerry and Senator Tom Harkin of Iowa traveled to Nicaragua and met the country's president, Daniel Ortega. Though Ortega had won internationally certified elections, the trip was criticized because Ortega and his leftist Sandinista government had strong ties to Cuba and the USSR and were accused of human rights abuses. The Sandinista government was opposed by the right-wing CIA-backed rebels known as the Contras. While in Nicaragua, Kerry and Harkin talked to people on both sides of the conflict. Through the senators, Ortega offered a cease-fire agreement in exchange for the U.S. dropping support of the Contras. The offer was denounced by the Reagan administration as a "propaganda initiative" designed to influence a House vote on a 14 million Contra aid package, but Kerry said "I am willing..... to take the risk in the effort to put to test the good faith of the Sandinistas." The House voted down the Contra aid, but Ortega flew to Moscow to accept a 200 million loan the next day, which in part prompted the House to pass a larger 27 million aid package six weeks later.

"Fatah?" chirps Claybill. He rises slowly from his learning creche, pale, blond brow curled in reproach. "There's a year missing." I smile, sliding off my black and chrome symbiote-handler's gauntlets. Claybill eyes me a moment before responding: "We've been on the road for years now," he says. "Allowing three months of vacation into your schedule might be reasonable if you were on Earth. But we're not here to enjoy ourselves. We don't have time for leisurely entertainment anymore." The General turns back toward the desk where the Commandant is typing furiously. "And that boy needs someone who can help him understand what happened yesterday so that it doesn't happen again." The Commandant has stopped typing and looks up as Claybill speaks. The man looks angry, but there are no wrinkles between his eyebrows. Perhaps he sees nothing unusual about this request or about Claybill's tone. Maybe he knows something I don't know. His face remains impassive until he meets my glare with equal intensity. Then he crosses over the room to stand beside me arm-in-arm. I wait still longer than I should, wondering whether the General will demand an explanation. Instead he places both hands flat against my chest and stares into my eyes. The General is one of those men whose weight makes any inadvertent movement difficult; even such familiar gestures like holding hands take effort. But when I feel myself being squeezed tightly underneath his gaze, I let go instantly. My hands drop down to rest at my sides, palms facing forward. A minute later he begins talking, speaking slowly and deliberately. "I am very concerned about your son's behavior yesterday," he says solemnly. "He has obviously gone through something traumatic and frightening and dangerous. It would do him good to talk. This situation cannot continue indefinitely. You must find out why he did these things and how they were accomplished." My mouth falls open wide enough to reveal my teeth. There could hardly be anything worse than having an entire platoon under military guard because you killed ten people. Or maybe there could be... But God only knows what he went through that day! And to think that he may never see the light of day again.... It isn't fair, I tell myself firmly. What was he supposed to think? That he'd had an accident? Like some little kid falling down the stairs, except that kids aren't sent to prison for killing their classmates - ever, unless they're terrorists. And the kid didn't look like a terrorist. At least none that I saw. So instead of helping him get home safely after wounds received during combat operations, instead of bringing him food and clothes and blankets to keep warm as soldiers tend to do, instead of just waiting around to make sure all his medical needs are met, I'm going to turn him over to two former Gestapo officers! I hate what these incidents have done to us as a species, the way our priorities seem to have changed since 911. No wonder violence seems more attractive to young boys everywhere these days. Now, instead of protecting them, we try to destroy them. Do these guys actually believe that's going to work?! Even if it does, do they really want their children growing up thinking they need to kill twenty-five innocent people every single day to prove themselves worthy of respect? They're clearly looking for answers, although I doubt they'll find much of value lying dormant within Claybill's mind. Even if he tells them everything he remembers, I expect they won't be able to put together a coherent theory based on it. Not without replaying every second of the explosion in slow motion while playing it backwards... which would probably end up giving them a migraine headache. Unfortunately, there's not much else I can say. As far as questions go, asking him how many people died was pretty mindless. If he hadn't witnessed it himself then there's simply no way to answer that question objectively, given the impossibility of the task. But I suppose I could ask him if anyone got hurt besides him, assuming they survived the explosion intact. How does one broach that particular topic casually? With one hand? It seems that, for once, the others are right behind me regarding this issue. Several seconds pass before the Commandant gives a curt nod. He turns back to his computer screen. I spend several minutes trying to figure out exactly what kind of questions I should pose to Claybill next. Nothing seems appropriate. In an effort to combat preventable diseases, 23andMe will start testing customers for diabetes and other health conditions with their Health and Ancestry Service test. The test will not indicate whether or not a customer has the disease, but will indicate whether they are at risk of getting it. The FDA has now approved this genetic health risk report as a direct-to-consumer genetic test. The FDA believes that this test can help people make decisions regarding their health and lifestyle. 23andMe will test for genetic health risks for BRCA1BRCA2 (selected variants), late-onset Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, celiac disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, early-onset primary dystonia, factor XI deficiency, Gaucher disease type 1, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, hereditary hemochromatosis, and hereditary thrombophilia. The test will also screen for drug responses, including: CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2A6, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP3A4, CYP3A5, and VKORC1. These genes impact how well people metabolize drugs such as warfarin, Coumadin, Plavix, and clopidogrel. The test will also screen for the following diseases: Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), celiac disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, primary dystonia, factor XI deficiency, Gaucher disease type 1, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, hereditary hemochromatosis, and hereditary thrombophilia. Women who carry genetic mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes are at increased risk of developing breast and ovarian cancer. Men with these mutations also have an increased risk of breast cancer, and may be at increased risk of other cancers. 23andMe will also report a person's carrier status for the following diseases: Bloom syndrome, Canavan disease, cystic fibrosis, Fanconi anemia group C, Fanconi anemia group G, familial dysautonomia, Gaucher disease type 1, glycogen storage disease type 1A, hereditary hemochromatosis, Mucolipidosis type IV, Niemann-Pick disease type A, Rett syndrome, and Tay-Sachs disease. The BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations can be passed down from either parent, and the child of a parent with one of these mutations has a 50 chance of inheriting the mutation. If a person's test results indicate that they are a carrier of one of these mutations, it does not mean that they have or will develop the disorder, but rather that they can pass the mutation down to their children. According to the FDA, this test will give people information about possible mutations that are linked to increased risk for conditions that could be avoided or effectively treated. For more information about 23andMe's new service, visit their website. The FDA encourages consumers to check out their webpage: Think Before You Spit! Think Before You Spit! Will answer any questions you may have about genetic testing and what results might mean.

Predicting the physical transformations of common objects is essential for self-governing robots. In this study, we introduce Defo-Net, a groundbreaking generative adversarial network capable of estimating shape alterations under exterior pressures from a sole RGB-D image. Based on an Invertible Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (IcGAN), Defo-Net is honed using a dataset derived from a physical finite element model simulator. This architecture retains the versatility of GANs, permitting it to replicate the entire 3-D visualization of an object based on a singular depth perspective and adapt to uncharted object arrangements. Unlike conventional finite element strategies, our methodology offers swiftness suitable for real-time applications. We put Defo-Net to the test in the domain of secure and brisk mobility of load-bearing mobile robots navigating diverse hindrances and floor coverings. Real-world experimentation confirms that a robot furnished with an RGB-D sensor can employ the network to forecast terrain modifications under varying load setups and steer clear of hazardous zones.

Move blocking (MB) is a widely used strategy to reduce the degrees of freedom of the Optimal Control Problem (OCP) arising in receding horizon control. The size of the OCP is controlled by the number of prediction steps and the control horizon. The computation time of solving the OCP grows exponentially with the control horizon, while it increases linearly with the number of prediction steps. In this paper we present an algorithm to reduce the computational time of the solution. We propose to split the control horizon in two or more sub-horizons, adding new constraints to link them together. Each sub-horizon can be solved independently, using MB, but the resulting sequence of control signals will not satisfy the original problem. We use a penalty-based approach to recover the optimality conditions for each sub-horizon without increasing the size of the OCP. The proposed algorithm is tested on several examples, including a nonlinear example, showing that it is able to significantly reduce the computational burden with respect to the standard MB strategy. Reduced jaw strength led to shrinking jaw size, yet the number of teeth remained constant, resulting in overcrowding. In contrast, animals such as dogs and cats possess ample room in their jaws for their complete set of teeth. Another contributing factor could be the shift from a diet primarily consisting of nuts, berries, and meat to one dominated by heavy starches, which resembles sugar and deteriorates dental health. Cavemen likely experienced no dental issues requiring orthodontic correction or toothaches fatal to them because of this ancient diet. Myanmar is home to four major language families: Sino-Tibetan, Tai-Kadai, Austro-Asiatic, and Indo-European. Sino-Tibetan languages are most widely spoken. They include Burmese, Karen, Kachin, Chin, and Chinese (mainly Hokkien). The primary Tai-Kadai language is Shan. Mon, Palaung, and Wa are the major Austroasiatic languages spoken in Myanmar. The two major Indo-European languages are Pali, the liturgical language of Theravada Buddhism, and English. Little known fact about Myanmar is there are more than 130 languages spoken by people in Myanmar. Since many of them are known only within small tribes around the country, they may have been lost (many if not all) after a few generations.

An r -identifying code in a graph G (V, E) is a subset C V such that for each u V the intersection of C and the ball of radius r centered at u is non-empty and unique. Previously, r -identifying codes have been studied in various grids. In particular, it has been shown that there exists a 2 -identifying code in the hexagonal grid with density 4 19 and that there are no 2 -identifying codes with density smaller than 2 11. Recently, the lower bound has been improved to 1 5 by Martin and Stanton (2010). In this paper, we prove that the 2 -identifying code with density 4 19 is optimal, i.e. that there does not exist a 2 -identifying code in the hexagonal grid with smaller density.

Intellectual creations merit protection just as a farmer safeguards his crops or a rancher nurtures his livestock. This concept emerged as early as the October 1845 Massachusetts Circuit Court decision in Davoll et al. v. Brown, where Justice Charles L. Woodbury declared, "Only in this manner can we secure intellectual property, as the exclusive domain of its creator, comparable to his harvested wheat or herded flocks." The idea that "inventions are...possessions" predates this, with France's law of 1791 recognizing, "All novel discoveries belong to their originator; to grant the inventor title and brief tenure over his invention, a patent will be granted for five, ten, or fifteen years." European author A. Nion echoed this sentiment in his 1846 publication, Droits civils des auteurs, artistes et inventeurs.

The 45-55 vote marks the second defeat for Republicans aiming to pass a bill this week to undo the health policy. The vote came a day after the Senate rejected a plan to repeal and replace the health law with a Republican plan. Senators will now consider a "skinny" repeal, which would scale back some of the more controversial provisions. The "skinny" plan would eliminate unpopular parts of Obamacare - the Affordable Care Act - including the individual mandate requiring all Americans to have health insurance coverage as well as a tax on medical devices. If that measure passes, the Senate and House of Representatives would then be tasked with finalising a bill that could still change during negotiations. If successful, the full House and Senate would again have to approve the measure. Seven Republicans opposed the repeal-only plan on Wednesday, which included a two-year delay on a replacement in the hope of finding agreement before that time elapses. The defeat is the latest blow for President Donald Trump, who put repealing Obamacare at the centre of his election campaign, and underscores sharp divisions within the Republican Party over a replacement plan. A proposal to repeal and replace Obamacare with the Better Care Reconciliation Act (BCRA), a Republican plan that was crafted over last two months, collapsed on Tuesday night after nine Republicans voted against it. Republicans have long railed against Obamacare as government overreach, criticising the system for introducing government-run marketplaces, where premiums have risen sharply for some people. The party's proposed alternative included steep cuts to Medicaid, a healthcare programme for the poor and disabled. And it removes Obamacare's individual mandate requiring all Americans to have health insurance or pay a tax penalty. About 20 million people gained health insurance under former President Obama's Affordable Care Act. The non-partisan Congressional Budgetary Office (CBO) found the bill would strip 22 million Americans of health insurance over the next decade. Other attempts to replace Obamacare have failed in recent weeks due to Republican divisions. In an early morning tweet on Wednesday, Mr Trump lambasted Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska for opposing the party's plan, saying she "really let the Republicans, and our country, down yesterday. Too bad!" Mrs Murkowski was one of two Republicans earlier on Tuesday to vote against allowing the debate on healthcare legislation reform to go forward. But her party eked out a victory after Vice President Mike Pence cast the tie-breaking vote which allowed discussion to take place. Senator John McCain, who was recently diagnosed with an aggressive brain tumour, received a standing ovation as he returned to Congress to cast his "Yes" vote. President Trump tweeted his thanks to the Arizona senator for playing "such a vital role" in the vote.

The way it makes sense to me... Let's say I want to turn a bolt 180 degrees. If I use a 1-inch long wrench, my hands won't travel very far to accomplish this goal, because the arc is small. If I use a 3-foot long wrench my hands will move a lot more distance to accomplish the same goal. Sort of like how a block and tackle pulley system makes it easier to lift a weight but means I must use much more rope than the distance I actually want to lift the weight.,Torque is measured in Nm Increasing the radius increases the circumference of a circle. When you increase the distance of which torque is applied, the length of the arc increases. As such, the meters the force is applied to increases. If torque is to remain equal, N must decrease. So when you put all of your strength into turning a 10cm wrench, it does a lot less than putting all of your strength into a 1m wrench.', "It's the law of the lever, which states that if the distance from the handle to the fulcrum is greater that the distance from the fulcrum to the head, the lever amplifies the input force. In the case of a wrench, the fulcrum and head are in virtually the same place so the longer it is, the greater the amplification.

Cats' training revolves around comprehending the core concept of self-motivated desire. To elicit a desired behavior from a feline, one must first stimulate its interest. I instruct cats to retrieve toys. By making the plaything enjoyable when I possess it, and subsequently tossing it some distance away after a brief engagement, the cat typically pursues the "enjoyable item." Following several iterations of this pattern, the cat often starts returning the toy for additional enjoyable moments nearby. With consistent practice, most felines learn to chase and bring back the object: fetching acquired.

In contrast, dogs have been domesticated for considerably longer periods, initially serving roles in hunting and livestock management. Humans tamed wolves due to their pack mentality, swiftness, ferocity, and suitability for our purposes. We cultivated canine companionship for safety reasons and to ensure obedience through selective breeding of amicable and trainable specimens. Cats, however, were domesticated differently. Humans resided in agrarian communities, resulting in an overabundance of rodents threatening their harvests. Cats migrated towards humans due to less fear of these pests, providing mutual benefits: humans profited from their rodent control, and the cats enjoyed proximity to food sources. Consequently, we adopted them as pets and vermin eliminators without extensive training requirements – their primary function was pest management. This disparity in origins and functions explains the distinct approaches to training each species. Essentially, cats' domesticity lags behind that of dogs, leaving them relatively closer to their wild state, occupying our homes. Dogs, being descendants of wolves, retain the instincts of a pack animal. If they are to thrive, they require social connections and clear communication, fostering a strong bond between humans and themselves.

In the Hautes Alpes, they are currently feeding beneath ski lifts on slopes that will soon be covered by a thick layer of snow. But this year the freedom to roam has been curtailed. Somewhere in the dark, dense forests a grey wolf is on the prowl. The wolf was hunted almost to extinction in France in the 1930s but, protected as an endangered species, it is making a surprising comeback. Some 200 wolves have colonised the southern regions of France, divided into about 20 packs. They are believed to have crossed from Italy in the mid-1990s and they are moving ever further north. Lionel Serres has 250 sheep on the mountainside this summer. Each night he pens them in behind electric fences. But the wolf is a cunning predator and so far it has killed 17 of his ewes, while 10 more are missing. Sheep spooked On the day we met, he was busy trying to recover an ewe that had been grabbed by a wolf around the neck. Its fleece was matted, thick with blood. "We have had lots of dead and injured sheep," said Lionel. "The flock is in a pretty sorry state. Some are lame, they are stressed, and some are so frightened they have miscarried lambs." At night the wolf will circle the pens until the sheep are spooked into jumping the electric fences. And so costly are these losses that in recent weeks Mr Serres has been forced to hire another shepherd, who will sleep alongside the sheep at night. He is not the only one with concerns. So angry are the farmers in this region, that on the road to Hautes Alpes, in south-eastern France, on the border with Italy, there are huge signs painted on the road - "NO to the wolf." Two hundred wolves might not sound like a huge problem. But this year there have been almost 600 attacks in which more than 2,000 sheep have been killed. That constitutes a rise of 20 on the same period last year. So, under pressure from farmers and faced with an increasing number of attacks, the local prefect has finally ordered a hunt for one individual wolf thought to be doing much of the damage. Since an anti-hunting code was agreed in 2004, only four wolves have been killed in France. Under the present rules, the wolf can only be shot legally by government marksmen or by shepherds trained and licensed to defend their flocks. Remy Saunier, the chief wolf catcher for the area, is now sending small, nightly patrols into the mountains. 'Mystical animal' "The wolf will always take the easiest prey," he said. "If it's easy he comes back, and that's what he's done here, every other night. We have tried to scare it with lights and noise but it returns. It is only our presence in these mountains that are limiting the wolf attacks. "Most people in France have welcomed the return of the wolf. It is a beautiful, mystical animal. But if these people woke in the morning to find their flock decimated, they might change their opinion." Critics say there is no evidence wolf attacks are out of control and they blame some of these sheep deaths on wild dogs. Moreover, as farmers receive 130 euros (PS115; 190) in compensation for every sheep killed by a wolf, critics claim there is an incentive to exaggerate the problem. Jean-Francois Darmstaedter, the secretary general of Ferus, a French wolf protection agency, says the shepherds need to work harder to protect their sheep - though some shepherds, he points out, are wolf supporters. "Remember there are eight million dogs in France and 200 wolves," he said. "And I would bet there are more dog attacks in these mountains than wolf attacks. In this small region here we have a pack of 15 wolves, and something like 8,000 wild dogs. They aren't always in the mountains, but when they are, they cause a real mess." 'Heading for Paris' Mr Darmstaedter questions why the wolf has inspired such opposition in France. In neighbouring Italy, he says, pack numbers are three or four times as big. But then, the wolf has always provoked fear. In the 17th Century, so afraid were they of wolves, mostly rabid wolves, they were cursed in Gallic folklore by the story of Little Red Riding Hood. At a fair in Marvejols, further to the west, wolf expert Jean-Marc Moriceau is plugging his latest book, titled Man Against the Wolf. "The wolf is a successful predator," he said. "It can move huge distances in search of food. And we can safely assume that in 15 or 20 years' time, if no measures are put in place, then it's possible we will see one or two wolves hunting in the forests 80km to 100km [50-60 miles] south of Paris." Some say the expanding nature of the wolf's habitat will require that more controls are implemented - in France they are calling for a "wolf parliament," in which farmers, supporters, and politicians can all have their say. But the forests south of Paris are probably the grey wolf's limit. Western and northern France are no longer wooded or wild enough to sustain them - which means those who live in Paris, at least, can sleep easily in their beds.

In this paper, we consider a mixed RF and hybrid RFFSO system where several mobile users transmit their data over an RF link to a relay node (e.g. a small cell base station) and the relay forwards the information to a destination (e.g. a macro cell base station) over a hybrid RFFSO backhaul link. The relay and the destination employ multiple antennas for transmission and reception over the RF links while each mobile user has a single antenna. The RF links are full-duplex with respect to the FSO link and half-duplex with respect to each other, i.e., either the user-relay RF link or the relay-destination RF link is active. For this communication setup, we derive the optimal resource allocation policy for sharing the RF bandwidth resource between the RF links. Our numerical results show the effectiveness of the proposed communication architecture and resource allocation policy, and their superiority compared to existing schemes which employ only one type of backhaul link.

Not at all. In fact, the writer Andrew Solomon, who has become known for writing about depression (see The Noonday Demon), has explored depression in non-western societies. He went to remote areas of the world, where he expected to find little depression because of the lack of "problems." Instead, he found that people in these regions had no words for depression, but that they were prone to it. Depression is not a western concept, and people all over the world suffer from it. In fact, the World Health Organization estimates that approximately 154 million people worldwide suffer from depression. Studies have shown that the number of people suffering from depression has increased by 18 between 2005 and 2015. By 2030, the WHO expects that depression will be the leading cause of disability worldwide. As is the case with other mental disorders, there is a stigma associated with depression. This stigma can be even more pronounced in non-western societies. In our western society, the stigma of mental illness is still quite prevalent. This leads many people who are suffering from depression to not seek help, and to suffer in silence. The stigma is stronger in non-western societies, which can lead to a number of problems. A study in South Korea found that 81 of Korean patients who suffer from depression do not seek treatment. In fact, in many non-western societies, people who suffer from depression are often seen as "weak" and "needing to toughen up." Unfortunately, this means that many people who suffer from depression are never treated. Another problem that occurs in non-western societies is that people are often unaware that they are suffering from depression. Without a word for depression, people might not realize that their feelings of sadness are abnormal, and that they need to seek help. Because of the stigma associated with depression, many people in non-western societies don't realize that they are suffering from depression until their symptoms become severe, or until their symptoms last for a long time. By then, the depression can be much harder to treat. Another issue that is associated with non-western societies is the lack of mental healthcare. In countries where the majority of people have no health insurance, mental healthcare is often not covered. Without insurance, people can't afford to pay out of pocket for the care that they need. Mental healthcare can be particularly expensive, and since it isn't covered, people cannot afford to get the help that they need. This, combined with the stigma of mental illness, means that many people never get treatment. There are also fewer mental healthcare professionals, which means that people who need help can't find it. Many non-western countries don't have the resources to train mental healthcare professionals. In addition, western healthcare professionals tend to be older, white, and male. This means that they often don't understand the cultural norms of the people that they are trying to help. Unfortunately, when mental healthcare professionals don't understand their patients, they are less likely to be able to treat their patients. It is clear that depression is a problem in non-western societies. There are fewer mental healthcare professionals, and the stigma surrounding mental illness can prevent people from seeking help. The lack of mental healthcare can also prevent people from seeking help. Fortunately, things are changing. As more and more people in non-western societies realize that mental illness is a problem that needs to be addressed, more mental healthcare professionals are being trained, and more healthcare centers are being built. The World Health Organization estimates that, in 2025, depression will be the leading cause of disability worldwide. The WHO also estimates that, by 2030, depression will be the leading cause of disease burden worldwide. As people realize that mental illness is a problem that needs to be addressed, hopefully the stigma will be lifted, and people who are suffering from depression will be able to get the help that they need.

Multi-dimensional data point clouds' intrinsic dimensionality (ID) is a vital trait to determine suitable machine learning methods and grasp their performance and verification. ID can be assessed globally for an entire data distribution or locally within distinct areas of the data space. This research introduces novel local ID estimators based on linear separability of multi-dimensional data clouds, a feature of measure concentration. Differences among estimators offer insights into their anticipated conduct in real-world scenarios.

In this paper, we present a new multi-antenna modulation scheme, termed as space-time index modulation (STIM). In STIM, information bits are conveyed through antenna indexing in the spatial domain, slot indexing in the time domain, and M -ary modulation symbols. A time slot in a given frame can be used or unused, and the choice of the slots used for transmission conveys slot index bits. In addition, antenna index bits are conveyed in every used time slot by activating one among the available antennas. M -ary symbols are sent on the active antenna in a used time slot. We study STIM in a cyclic-prefixed single-carrier (CPSC) system in frequency-selective fading channels. It is shown that, for the same spectral efficiency and single transmit RF chain, STIM can achieve better performance compared to conventional orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM). Low-complexity iterative algorithms for the detection of large-dimensional STIM signals are also presented.

Revenue is an important financial indicator because it represents the amount of money a company earns from its business activities before deducting any expenses. In other words, revenue is the total income generated by a company, and it serves as the quantitative measure of a company's performance. Revenue is important because it can impact a company's ability to secure financing, attract investors, and grow its business. Investors and lenders will often look at a company's revenue growth over time as an indicator of its potential future earnings and financial stability. Additionally, revenue is used in financial ratios, such as the gross profit margin, which are used by analysts to evaluate a company's profitability and performance. In summary, revenue is a key financial metric that can indicate a company's financial health, growth potential, and value to investors and lenders.

Stabbing victim John Culshaw's remains were retained by Greater Manchester Police without his family's knowledge. Dozens of other families have also been told their loved ones' body parts were kept by the force. GMP said whether or not to contact the affected families was a decision it "agonised over for a number of months." Mr Culshaw, 26, was stabbed to death in Wigan in 1993. His family buried him believing his body was intact, and were unaware his stomach, liver and other tissues had been retained after two post-mortem examinations until police officers visited them in September last year. His mother, Jennifer Shaw, said she wanted to know why it had taken so long to come to light. "He's my son. And he's been left - half of him," she said. "If he'd have died and they'd asked me if they could use the parts to help somebody, then yes. But just to be sat in a lab for 23 years doing nothing, that's just horrendous." The body parts were discovered following an audit of the former Forensic Science Service in 2014, the Manchester Evening News revealed. It found more than 180 samples - including major organs - from victims of crime in Greater Manchester were being held for the police force, which has admitted there could be more body parts unaccounted for. It became illegal in 2006 to remove or store human tissue without families' consent following an investigation at Liverpool's Alder Hey hospital in 1999. Organs from hundreds of babies who died at the hospital were secretly taken. The body parts kept for Greater Manchester Police were removed before that date. Assistant Chief Constable Debbie Ford said: "Once we knew about the samples we felt that such a sensitive issue was never going to be solely about following the regulations or the letter of the law. "For this reason we consulted with a number of relevant people, including community and faith groups, as well as our own Ethics Committee. Following this extensive consultation it was agreed we had an ethical and moral duty to inform the next-of-kin in the vast majority of cases." She said officers had offered a range of options for "sensitive disposal" of the samples, which the force would pay for. However, families have been told some samples could remain unaccounted for "for various reasons," she said. John Culshaw's family will bury his organs in a private second ceremony on Thursday. "Somebody has made a big mistake. Not just me but a lot of other families are suffering as well," Ms Shaw said. "I don't want anyone else to go through this. It's devastating."

New rules come in on 1 January, which will reduce compensation to PS75,000 per person, per institution. Previously the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) protected savings of up to PS85,000 per account. Joint accounts will see protection cut from PS170,000 to PS150,000. The maximum compensation across the European Union is set at EUR100,000, and the British level was reduced as a result of the pound gaining strength against the euro. The precise rate was set on 3 July 2015. At the time, one senior Tory MP described the change as "defective." Although 95 of savers will still be protected, as many as 2.5 million people may not be, according to the FSCS. It is advising savers who have more than PS75,000 in one account, or in one institution, to move their money if necessary. The situation is further complicated by the fact that some registered banks and building societies operate under more than one brand. So it you had PS75,000 savings with HSBC, for example, any additional savings in First Direct would not be protected, as both banks have a joint licence. Savers using Bank of Scotland and Halifax are in the same position. But Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS) and NatWest - although they are sister banks - are both registered separately. So savers could safely have up to PS75,000 in accounts with both banks. "While this should be quite simple to navigate, it's made complicated by the fact that FSCS cover is shared between banks that operate under the same licence," said Hannah Maundrell, editor in chief of money.co.uk. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) publishes a full list of registered banks, and which brands come under the same umbrella. Under the new rules, savers who have up to PS1m in their accounts temporarily - as a result of selling a house, or being made redundant, for example - are also protected. To receive compensation, they cannot have had that cash in their accounts for more than six months. A further warning comes in relation to some foreign banks which trade in the UK, but are registered within the eurozone, such as Germany's Fidor Bank, or Sweden's Handelsbanken. Handelsbanken confirmed that the level of compensation would depend on the exchange rate at the time. So depending on how much EUR100,000 is worth in pounds, savers may get more or less than PS75,000 protection. At the time of writing, that amount is worth less than PS74,000. "With an increasing number of European banks now offering competitive rates, customers need to be aware that not all savings accounts offered in the UK are covered by the UK compensation scheme," said Rachel Thrussell, savings insight manager at Moneyfacts.co.uk.

In light of the growing use of machine learning in critical applications subjected to anti-discrimination regulations or societal expectations, it's essential to prevent predictive models from perpetuating existing biases or discrimination. Recent advancements in algorithmic fairness have focused on applying adversarial techniques to deep neural nets to minimize bias in data while maintaining utility. This study offers new insights into the relationship between demographic parity and joint utility across various populations through the perspective of information theory. We present the initial quantitative analysis demonstrating the tradeoff between demographic parity and joint utility. When population base rates vary, we demonstrate that any method striving for fair representations carries an information-theoretic minimum joint error limit across these groups. To balance our negative results, we also establish that if the best decision functions for distinct groups are proximately aligned, learning fair representations yields accuracy parity - a type of fairness definition stating that error rates are equivalent among groups. Our theoretical discoveries are corroborated via experimentation on genuine datasets.

One way they are doing this is by developing a pill that can be taken instead of the traditional needle-based method of HIV prevention. The current method of HIV prevention, called pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), requires individuals to take a daily pill. However, many people are reluctant to take a pill every day, which can lead to missed doses and ultimately, ineffective protection against HIV. The new pill being developed would only need to be taken once a week, making it a more convenient option for people at risk of HIV infection. Scientists are still in the early stages of development for this new pill, but they are hopeful that it will be an effective way to help prevent the spread of HIV. If successful, this pill could provide a much needed alternative to the current PrEP regimen and help reduce the number of new HIV infections each year.

If you're a beginner in the world of neural networks, you've probably heard of recurrent neural networks (RNNs). RNNs are a type of neural network that is well-suited for modeling sequential data, such as text. In this article, we'll give you a gentle introduction to RNNs and how they work. RNNs were first proposed in the early 1990s by Jurgen Schmidhuber, who is now a professor at the Swiss AI lab IDSIA. At the time, RNNs were not well-understood and were largely ignored by the machine learning community. It wasn't until much later that researchers began to realize the potential of RNNs for modeling complex sequential data. RNNs are called "recurrent" because they perform the same task for every element in a sequence. This makes them ideal for modeling time series data, where each element is dependent on the previous element. For example, consider the following sentence: The cat slept on the mat. Each word in this sentence is dependent on the previous word. In other words, the meaning of the sentence changes as the order of the words changes. An RNN can learn to model this type of sequential data. There are many different types of RNNs, but they all have the same basic structure. An RNN consists of a series of "cells" that process an input sequence one element at a time. Each cell has a set of weights that are updated as the cell processes the input sequence. The weights of the cell determine how the cell will process the next element in the sequence. RNNs can be used for a variety of tasks, such as language modeling, machine translation, and image captioning. In recent years, RNNs have also been used for generating music and painting. Most light bulbs have either clear or coated glass. The coated glass bulbs have a white powdery substance on the inside called kaolin. Kaolin, or kaolinite, is a white, chalky clay in a very fine powder form, that is blown in and electrostatically deposited on the interior of the bulb. It diffuses the light emitted from the filament, producing a more gentle and evenly distributed light. Manufacturers may add pigments to the kaolin to adjust the characteristics of the final light emitted from the bulb. Kaolin diffused bulbs are used extensively in interior lighting because of their comparatively gentle light. Other kinds of colored bulbs are also made, including the various colors used for "party bulbs," Christmas tree lights and other decorative lighting. These are created by coloring the glass with a dopant; which is often a metal like cobalt (blue) or chromium (green). Neodymium-containing glass is sometimes used to provide a more natural-appearing light.

When you install a program it may make other changes than just copy files to your harddrive. If you just delete the files then those changes won't be undone. For example, the installer may create desktop shortcuts, and it may create a variety of entries in the system registry, perhaps registering the application as a handler for certain filetypes (for example, indicating that this application should be launched when you doubleclick on a.mp3 file), and much more. The uninstaller will remove these entries as well as deleting the files. Simply deleting the files won't perform this cleanup. So if the installer made the above registrations then Windows will still try (and fail) to launch the application when you doubleclick on a.mp3 file. And you'll have a shortcut on your desktop which no longer works. Plus whatever other changes the installer made, which you chose not to undo. In short, you've turned your computer into a bit of a mess where some features have suddenly become broken.," "Often times, programs will write new keys to your Registry on your computer. These won't be removed simply by deleting the files. Usually an installer will remove them. Also, some programs have cache and other files located in many various locations around your computer. Unless you know all of these locations, you probably can't find all of them to be sure you've removed 100. But something important to note, installers and uninstallers are both created by the developer. So if they didn't program the uninstaller to remove everything properly, then it won't. There's nothing to enforce the uninstaller doing what it should do. This is why, even with using uninstallers, you will often still have files, settings and registry keys left over from your programs.

"We're really excited about the possibility of using this type of technique," said Dr. Sorin Ticheminov, the lead author of the study published online October 18 in Cell. "It's exciting because most fishes are really weak at prey management; we think it's important and that it is possible to identify these species by looking into them." They were led by Prof. Yushiro Yamamoto, an assistant professor in Japanese botany and coauthor of the paper. "Some animals do more than others - if not better," said the team of researchers who spent months traveling around Central America trying to find out how the species evolved over centuries. Dynamic equilibrium was first described by Galileo who noticed that certain assumptions of Aristotelian physics were contradicted by observations and logic. Galileo realized that simple velocity addition demands that the general case must be true, but at a point in space distant from all other points there is no motion where there should have been. Thus it appears that either the assumption that everything moves has to be modified or the world does not move as predicted. If one assumes uniformity (or simplicity) then such an anomaly doesn't arise because velocities are additive across any spatial distance for equal masses. The idea works well up until very high speeds when relativity comes into play - Newton's laws predict different behavior than Galilean mechanics depending on whether you're moving close to light speed; this led Einstein to come up with special relativity. In contrast, if bodies follow elliptical orbits around each others' centers then even though objects could appear stationary relative to one another they would still exhibit orbital motions regardless of their physical masses due to Kepler's third law. When combined with Plato's dictum "all things tend toward perfect circles," classical celestial dynamics usually leads to circular orbits which preserve invariance under translation. Once Special Relativity became established, the problem of distinguishing between planetary geometries based solely upon mass arose after it was discovered that Saturn had rings. From an abstract geometric perspective these don't seem like something that can physically exist: If we assume conservation of angular momentum then how do we account for the fact that Rings aren't actually just flat planes? This phenomenon challenged many aspects of Newtonian gravity along with observational evidence regarding Kepler's Laws. However attempts to model them initially left behind what some might consider an undesirable property known as static stability - the most extreme example being presented here wherein every aspect of gravitational theory falls apart once planets enter the picture due to deviations from prescribed elliptic paths. Classical Planets successfully addresses both problems while preserving time-honored thinking about why orbits look the way they do without resorting to adding new penalties whenever you try doing more complicated stuff within the orbitals themselves!

This paper provides a comparative analysis of impedance models for power electronic converters and systems for the purpose of stability investigations. Such models can be divided into either decoupled models or coupled models and the paper provides an overview of how to derive and implement these two different approaches. The analysis is carried out for three different converter topologies: the full bridge converter (VSC), the half bridge converter (HSC), and the single phase inverter. The emphasis is on the design principles for the impedance models and the derivation of the different components, as well as on the comparison between different models. The paper is organized as follows. Section II provides a general background on power electronic converters, stability investigations, and the role of the impedance model. Section III describes the decoupled impedance model, focusing on its derivation and implementation. Section IV presents the coupled impedance model, focusing on its derivation and implementation. The paper is concluded in Section V. A power electronic converter is essentially an energy transformation device. The input energy, e.g., in the form of a voltage or a current, is transformed to another energy, e.g., in the form of a voltage or a current. Power electronic converters are used in almost all fields of technology, e.g., for electrical energy production, electrical energy storage, and electrical energy distribution. In all these fields, the stability of the converters is crucial and, hence, a good understanding of the stability is of utmost importance. A general description of power electronic converters and stability investigations can be found in . In stability investigations, the main objective is to analyze the stability of the power electronic system. The first step is to describe the system by means of an equivalent circuit. This circuit is generally based on the concept of impedances and its design requires a detailed knowledge of the converter and the system it is used in. An overview of the different modeling approaches for the impedance model can be found in . This paper focuses on the modeling of impedances for the analysis of power electronic converters. The impedance model can be divided into two different classes: (1) a decoupled model, and (2) a coupled model. The decoupled model is based on the concept that the different components of the power electronic converter can be treated separately. It can be implemented using linear voltage-dependent modeling, nonlinear current-dependent modeling, or both, and the different modeling techniques are explained in Section III. The coupled model is based on the concept that the different components of the power electronic converter interact and, thus, it cannot be implemented using linear voltage-dependent modeling. The different modeling techniques are explained in Section IV. The decoupled impedance model is useful in the case that the dynamic behavior of the power electronic converter is not influenced by the other components. For instance, the voltage and current ripple of the output voltage of a DC-DC converter are independent of the output load, which is assumed to be resistive or capacitive, and the decoupled model is the preferred choice for the impedance model. The coupled impedance model is useful in the case that the dynamic behavior of the power electronic converter is influenced by the other components. For instance, the output inductance of a DC-DC converter influences the dynamics of the voltage and current ripple of the output voltage, and, thus, the coupled model is the preferred choice for the impedance model. This paper is organized as follows. Section II provides a general background on power electronic converters, stability investigations, and the role of the impedance model. Quantum stabilizer codes (QSCs) suffer from a low quantum coding rate, since they have to recover the quantum bits (qubits) in the face of both bit-flip and phase-flip errors. In addition, QSCs have a limited distance, meaning they can only correct a certain number of errors before the code fails. This can make them less suitable for applications that require high error tolerance, such as quantum communication or fault-tolerant quantum computing. Despite these limitations, QSCs are still useful for some applications, particularly when the noise is dominated by one type of error (either bit-flip or phase-flip), or when the number of errors is low. QSCs can also be combined with other error-correcting techniques to improve their performance, such as the use of concatenated codes or the implementation of topological codes. Overall, while QSCs may have limitations, they are an important tool in the field of quantum error correction and have played a significant role in the development of quantum technologies.

In this study, we present a mean-field game with a regularization function incorporated into its one-stage reward function. Our focus is on learning this modified game via an infinite-horizon discounted reward scheme. Through the use of value iteration, we propose a learning algorithm for the regularized mean-field game through fitted Q-learning. Unemployment insurance (UI) is a program created by the federal government that allows workers who lose their jobs to collect benefits when they are unemployed. Each state administers its own UI program, but must adhere to federal guidelines. The unemployment insurance program is funded through employer taxes, and benefits are paid to unemployed workers through state unemployment offices. Unemployment insurance pays benefits to eligible workers who have lost their jobs through no fault of their own, usually due to a reduction in force or other business-related reason. Unemployment insurance benefits provide temporary financial assistance to workers. Most states provide 26 weeks of benefits. In most cases, you will have to file a claim for benefits. You will be asked to give the names of your employers for the past 18 months, your earnings and the reason you are no longer employed. You may be asked to provide documentation to verify your eligibility. You will also be asked to report each week you are unemployed. In the US, there are Federal and state-based unemployment benefits. Federal unemployment benefits are paid by the government and are only available to individuals who were formerly employed by the government or other government agencies. This type of unemployment benefits are a result of the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA). State unemployment benefits are also paid by the government but are a result of state laws. Every state has a unemployment insurance department that is responsible for administering the benefits. Federal unemployment benefits are paid directly to you by the government. State unemployment benefits are paid by the government but are generally disbursed through your state's unemployment insurance department. The amount of federal unemployment benefits you are eligible to receive depends on the amount you contributed to the program through your federal taxes. For all that it may sound attractive to the Scots, Welsh and Northern Irish to have greater influence over their respective economic destinies, presumably that would be less desirable if at a stroke they became poorer. The point is that as and when there is an English parliament for English people - of the sort that the former Tory minister John Redwood has been demanding, and David Cameron seemed to concede today - the financial transfer from England to the rest of the UK may be harder to sustain. So these constitutional reforms will be tricky, if not dangerous - if at least a part of the current glue that holds the UK together is a redistribution of resources from England to the rest, and that glue is progressively removed. Being British right now means in part that public services and living standards are not too far apart in quantum and quality wherever you happen to live. But what if the overhaul of the UK's budget-making or fiscal constitution waters down that glue. How much is at stake? Well, spending on public-sector services per head is highest in Northern Ireland, PS10,900 and it is lowest in England, at PS8,500. The figure for Scotland - beneficiary of the famous or notorious Barnett Formula, which formalises an income transfer from England to Scotland - is PS10,200. So expenditure on public services in Scotland is a fifth higher per person than south of the border, and it is 28 higher in Northern Ireland. In Wales, the increment on public-service spending is 14 - which the Welsh have often complained is too little, compared with the transfer of income to Scotland. Now one way of looking at the scale of the transfer is to look at the amount of income - or what is known as gross value added - generated in each country. So English gross value added per head is highest, at just under PS22,000, and it is lowest in Wales at PS15,400. The English enjoy public-service spending per annum equivalent to under 40 of the income they generate, whereas annual outlays on public services in Wales are equivalent to more than 60 of nationally generated income per head. The ratios for Scotland and Northern Ireland are just over 50 and not far off 70 respectively. In a UK of considerable social and cultural solidarity that prevailed for most of the twentieth century, these sorts of disparities between income and outlay between the nations were relatively uncontroversial: they captured the idea that all UK citizens are in it together, as it were. But today it seems almost inevitable that in David Cameron's brave new world of greater national fiscal self-determination, some English nationalist MPs on the right of the spectrum may increasingly view Wales - and Scotland and Northern Ireland - as de facto socialist paradises excessively featherbedded by the English. That said, if the nations are given much greater control over income taxes - which appears to be what is on offer - could they not pay for whatever public services they feel they need out of these locally levied taxes? Not remotely. Income and other direct taxes per head in Wales raise PS5,564, considerably less than the UK average of PS7,360, and nowhere near enough to cover public service expenditure. There is a similar mismatch between direct income taxes and public spending throughout the UK. Borrowing and indirect taxes, mostly VAT, make up the difference. And there is not the faintest chance that national parliaments will be given the power to increase VAT, because this would be an admin nightmare for businesses and undermine the UK as a frictionless single market. All of which means that it may sound exciting and empowering in Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland to make their own choices about taxing and spending. But it may also be a bit nerve-wracking (or worse) if it provides cover for Westminster to reduce the income transferred to them from English taxpayers.

Smart devices, storage and other distributed technologies have the potential to greatly improve the utilisation of network infrastructure and renewable generation. Decentralised control of these technologies overcomes many scalability and privacy concerns, but in general still requires the underlying problem to be convex in order to guarantee convergence to a global optimum. Considering that AC power flows are non-convex in nature, and the operation of household devices often requires discrete decisions, there has been uncertainty surrounding the use of distributed methods in a realistic setting. This paper extends prior work on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for solving the dynamic optimal power flow (D-OPF) problem. We utilise more realistic line and load models, and introduce a two-stage approach to managing discrete decisions and uncertainty. Our experiments on a suburb-sized microgrid show that this approach provides near optimal results, in a time that is fast enough for receding horizon control. This work brings distributed control of smart-grid technologies closer to reality.

Autism is a mental condition, present from early childhood, characterized by difficulty in communicating and forming relationships with other people and in using language and abstract concepts. Asperger syndrome is a developmental disorder characterized by significant difficulties in social interaction and nonverbal communication, along with restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior and interests. ADHD is a chronic condition marked by persistent inattention, hyperactivity, and sometimes impulsivity. Clear everything up?','Autism is a set (often referred to as a "spectrum of related developments disorders which are primarily characterized by difficulties with socialization. The symptoms vary widely and can include things such as difficulty in reading others' body language, shyness, inability to understand sarcasm, etc. You've probably met autistic people and not known it, but they may have seemed "awkward" to you. The autism spectrum ranges from people with minor symptoms on one end to totally non-functional people on the other. Asperger's is a specific form of autism. ADHD (also known as ADD) is a common disorder which primarily manifests itself as a short attention span, lack of motivation, and inability to focus. ADHD is caused by an abnormally low baseline level of activity in the brain, which causes the brain to constantly try to find new sources of stimulation to raise the baseline to a more normal level. This is why people with ADHD become bored easily. The ADHD brain is like a person who is always hungry and feels the urge to eat constantly because nothing keeps him full for long. This is why ADHD is often treated with stimulants like Adderall which boost the baseline level of brain activity and allows the patient to focus their energy more effectively. Interestingly, people with autism or ADHD also tend to be highly talented in other areas. Some (although by no means all) autistic people are called "savants," and have extraordinary ability in things such as math or memory. ADHD is highly correlated with high levels of creativity.

JPEG 2000, the ISOIEC image coding standard, offers a collection of advanced source coding algorithms for efficient communication of high-resolution images. Its key attributes include scalable embedded coding capabilities, enabling users to generate low-resolution thumbnails from vast data collections or focus on specific areas of interest using minimal resources for communication and rendering. Despite being intended for fixed-precision inputs, the standard's irreversible version is commonly implemented utilizing floating point arithmetic internally. Furthermore, it caters to high-bit depth data and includes Part 2, which supports three-dimensional datasets like multicomponent or volumetric imagery. As a result, JPEG 2000 emerges as a compelling option for large-scale communications coding and visualization of 2D and 3D data generated by scientific simulation software. This paper showcases early experimentation employing JPEG 2000 on scientific simulation data derived from the Parallel Ocean Program (POP) global ocean circulation model, illustrating both its potential benefits and the obstacles that lie ahead for scientific visualization applications.

A study has confirmed that new neurons are still being made well past adolescence, and suggested that older studies that had claimed otherwise were flawed in their methodology. Older studies had tried to detect the presence of a protein, doublecortin (DCX), in the brain months, or even years after the brain matter was preserved - long after the DCX had deteriorated. The new study examined freshly preserved samples and found a large amount of evidence of newly developed cells. There was about a 30 decrease in the presence of newly developed cells from the youngest to the oldest donor samples, whose ages ranged from 43 to 87. Some scientists remain skeptical of the results, claiming that detected DCX levels were not sufficient evidence for newly developed cells, but the scientists in the study say they used very strict criteria when identifying new cells.

Anthropology represents a multidisciplinary field that brings together humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences. It draws on findings from natural sciences, encompassing insights into the origins and development of Homo sapiens, human physiological features, behaviors, intergroup differences, and the ways in which the evolutionary background of Homo sapiens shapes its societal structures and cultures. The roots of anthropology can be traced back to ancient civilizations in Greece and Persia, where scholars sought to explore and comprehend cultural disparities. In turn, anthropology has significantly contributed to the emergence of contemporary interdisciplinary areas such as cognitive science, global studies, and diverse ethnic studies during the late 20th century.

Several modern machine learning (ML) systems are constructed utilizing an assortment of previously trained elementary models, each performing specific functions (such as feature extraction). The widespread adoption of these models streamlines and hastens the creation processes of ML systems. However, due to the majority being provided and managed by unreliable entities, the absence of standardization or oversight over these models carries substantial security ramifications, which have yet to be fully understood. In this study, we reveal that malevolent primitive models pose significant risks to the security of ML systems. We introduce a comprehensive category of model-reuse assaults whereby maliciously engineered models cause host ML systems to behave erratically on intended inputs. Through experimentation on four deep learning systems (consisting of both singular and ensemble systems) utilized in skin cancer detection, speech recognition, facial recognition, and self-governing guidance, we exhibit that these attacks are (i) productive - the target systems exhibit unwanted behavior on the specified inputs with considerable likelihood, as intended by the attacker, (ii) disguised - the harmful models operate identically to their harmless equivalents on untargeted inputs, (iii) adaptable - the detrimental models continue to be productive despite varying system design decisions and fine-tuning techniques, and (iv) facile - the attacker requires minimal familiarity with the data employed for system optimization or evaluation. We offer theoretical explanations for the efficacy of model-reuse attacks, implying the unparalleled intricacy of contemporary primitive models. This predicament appears essential to numerous ML systems. We subsequently explore prospective defenses and their obstacles, leading to fertile research avenues.

Experts reassembled pieces of tiles found amid tons of earth from the site known to Jews as the Temple Mount and to Muslims as Haram al-Sharif. They say the tiles date from the period of the Second Temple, during the time of King Herod about 2,000 years ago. The temple was destroyed by the Romans in 70 AD during a Jewish rebellion. Some 600 segments of coloured stone floor have been found since archaeologists began examining the debris from the hilltop site in 2004. The plateau where the temples stood is the most sacred site in Judaism. It is joined by the Western Wall, venerated by Jews as part of the original supporting wall of the temple compound. Haram al-Sharif (Noble Sanctuary) is also the place where Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad ascended to Heaven, and is the third holiest site in Islam. The archaeologists say the tiles probably came from porticos in the temple's courtyards. Piecing the fragments together "enables us to get an idea of the Temple's incredible splendour," said Dr Gabriel Barkay of the Temple Mount Sifting Project. Experts say they managed to assemble seven potential designs of how the flooring could have looked like. The type of flooring is known as opus sectile, Latin for "cut work," and "considered to be far more prestigious than mosaic tiles floors," according to Frankie Snyder, from the project's team. "The tile segments were perfectly inlaid such that one could not even insert a sharp blade between them," she said. The Temple Mount Sifting Project was established by Israeli archaeologists in 2004 to examine debris dumped by Islamic authorities following expansion work at an underground mosque on the compound. The project attracts thousands of visitors each year who participate in finger-tip searches of the earth and has so far turned up hundreds of ancient relics, including coins, animal bones and pieces of pottery.

The sound of an exhaust is a very complex sound. Basically, there are explosions going on inside the motor. This is the genesis of the sound you hear. However, different factors can affect the actual tone, loudness, and quality of the exhaust sound. Some of these factors include: 1. Exhaust System Design: The design of the exhaust system plays a significant role in the sound produced. The size of the pipes, mufflers, and resonators can all affect the exhaust's tone. 2. Engine Type: Different engine types produce different exhaust sounds. For example, a V8 engine typically produces a deeper and more throaty exhaust sound compared to a four-cylinder engine. 3. Exhaust Manifold: The exhaust manifold collects exhaust gases from the engine and channels them to the exhaust system. The design of the manifold can affect the sound produced. 4. Catalytic Converter: The catalytic converter is responsible for reducing harmful emissions in the exhaust. However, it can also affect the exhaust tone. 5. Aftermarket Modifications: Aftermarket exhaust systems, headers, or mufflers can all alter the exhaust sound produced by a vehicle. In summary, exhaust sound is a complex issue with many variables affecting the tone, loudness, and quality of the sound produced.

This paper proposes a robust adversarial reinforcement learning (RARL) -based multi-access point (AP) coordination method that is robust even against unexpected decentralized operations of uncoordinated APs. Multi-AP coordination is a challenging task, as it requires multiple APs to work together to optimize network performance while avoiding interference and congestion. Adversarial reinforcement learning is a machine learning approach that involves training agents to make decisions in a competitive environment, where each agent is trying to maximize its own reward while also trying to interfere with the other agents' performance. The proposed RARL-based method uses a centralized controller to coordinate the actions of multiple APs in a way that maximizes network throughput while minimizing interference. The controller uses a deep reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize the coordination policy, taking into account the dynamic nature of the network and the presence of competing agents. The RARL approach is particularly useful in situations where there is a high degree of uncertainty, as it allows the controller to adapt its policies in real-time based on the actions of the other APs. This makes the system more robust and resilient to unexpected events, such as malfunctions or unplanned changes in the network topology. Overall, the proposed RARL-based multi-AP coordination method has the potential to significantly improve the performance and reliability of wireless networks, particularly in environments with multiple competing APs.

He asked for bail to be granted with conditions. However, the detective sergeant asked for an adjournment to the case, saying he needed time to consider the application and the fact Mr McCafferty had been arrested on foot of a European Arrest Warrant. Mr McCollum said his client had been in custody for five days but did not object to the request. The detective sergeant said he needed time to consider the application as he wanted to take account of the fact Mr McCafferty had been arrested under a European Arrest Warrant and it had been served by the Northern Ireland Office. District Judge Rosie Watters agreed to the request for an adjournment. Mr McCafferty was released on his own bail of 500 and is due to appear again before the court on June 28.

Ninety-five percent of bird species are socially monogamous. These species pair for at least the length of the breeding season or - in some cases - for several years or until the death of one mate. Monogamy allows for both paternal care and biparental care, which is especially important for species in which females require males' assistance for successful brood-rearing. Among many socially monogamous species, extra-pair copulation (infidelity) is common. Such behaviour typically occurs between dominant males and females paired with subordinate males, but may also be the result of forced copulation in ducks and other anatids. Female birds have sperm storage mechanisms that allow sperm from males to remain viable long after copulation, a hundred days in some species. Sperm from multiple males may compete through this mechanism. For females, possible benefits of extra-pair copulation include getting better genes for her offspring and insuring against the possibility of infertility in her mate. Males of species that engage in extra-pair copulations will closely guard their mates to ensure the parentage of the offspring that they raise.

During the 1950s in the United States, a period of conservative social order prevailed following the traumatic experiences of the Great Depression and World War II. The post-war era brought about an increase in Soviet power and the onset of the Cold War, resulting in a widespread fear of communists and subversive elements. This collective atmosphere fostered a desire to maintain a status quo. Contrastingly, the 1960s marked a significant leftist reaction against the conservatism of the previous decade. Repressed social issues gained prominence, with the Vietnam War acting as a catalyst due to its association with communism and the implementation of the draft. Previously, the American resistance to communism was generally viewed as honorable, but this notion was soon contested. The emergence of hippies in the 1960s was a response to this leftist pushback against the values and societal norms of the 1950s. Their core beliefs encompassed pacifism, free love, environmental consciousness, and drug use. These principles were encapsulated by the popular phrase, "make love, not war," which defied the established Cold War ideology of the time.
