James strolled along the line of chambers; these weren't referred to as jail cells since the inhabitants weren't imprisoned. Instead, this institution catered to mental health patients, and James' wing accommodated the aggressive individuals. Unlike their daytime counterparts, James relished his evenings at the asylum, as the patients were generally tranquil and resting. The soft scampering of rats in the walls, the distant plops from a leaking faucet, the melancholic wind howling through the asylum's crevices in the stones. These sounds were overshadowed by the incessant babble during day shifts. James paid no heed to the patients until he reached the final door on the left. Known as the penthouse due to its elevated position and the city lights visible outside, James glanced inside and observed the solitary inhabitant huddled on his bed, gazing out the window into the abyss. He turned the key in the lock and entered, joining the patient beside the bed and sharing the viewpoint. The moon was waning tonight, casting minimal illumination from its thin crescent, yet the urban lights still gleamed. The streetlights splattered yellow patches on the path leading away from the asylum, forming a speckled ribbon separating the asylum from the cityscape. "Hello James," Bruce mumbled, "It's a beautiful night, isn't it?" "Yes, Bruce," James replied, "I see that. How is your wife doing today?" "She's still deceased, Bruce." This dialogue was a familiar one; they exchanged it nearly every night. Bruce, the most perilous resident within the asylum, posed no threat due to his size or strength. However, his mastery of martial arts and extensive experience navigating the city's treacherous terrain granted him an unparalleled agility and menace using only his bare hands. During Bruce's initial week at the asylum, he had taken the lives of two other patients.

We present Nopol an approach for automatically repairing buggy if conditions and missing preconditions. As input, it takes a program and a test suite which contains passing test cases modeling the expected behavior of the program and at least one failing test case embodying the bug to be repaired. It consists of collecting data from multiple instrumented test suite executions, transforming this data into a Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) problem, and translating the SMT result - if there exists one - into a source code patch. Nopol repairs object oriented code and allows the patches to contain nullness checks as well as specific method calls.

After his coronation, John moved south into France with military forces and adopted a defensive posture along the eastern and southern Normandy borders. Both sides paused for desultory negotiations before the war recommenced; John's position was now stronger, thanks to confirmation that the counts Baldwin IX of Flanders and Renaud of Boulogne had renewed the anti-French alliances they had previously agreed to with Richard. The powerful Anjou nobleman William des Roches was persuaded to switch sides from Arthur to John; suddenly the balance seemed to be tipping away from Philip and Arthur in favour of John. Neither side was keen to continue the conflict, and following a papal truce the two leaders met in January 1200 to negotiate possible terms for peace. From John's perspective, what then followed represented an opportunity to stabilise control over his continental possessions and produce a lasting peace with Philip in Paris. John and Philip negotiated the May 1200 Treaty of Le Goulet; by this treaty, Philip recognised John as the rightful heir to Richard in respect to his French possessions, temporarily abandoning the wider claims of his client, Arthur.[nb 4] John, in turn, abandoned Richard's former policy of containing Philip through alliances with Flanders and Boulogne, and accepted Philip's right as the legitimate feudal overlord of John's lands in France. John's policy earned him the disrespectful title of "John Softsword" from some English chroniclers, who contrasted his behaviour with his more aggressive brother, Richard.

The Book of Discipline is the guidebook for local churches and pastors and describes in considerable detail the organizational structure of local United Methodist churches. All UM churches must have a board of trustees with at least three members and no more than nine members and it is recommended that no gender should hold more than a 23 majority. All churches must also have a nominations committee, a finance committee and a church council or administrative council. Other committees are suggested but not required such as a missions committee, or evangelism or worship committee. Term limits are set for some committees but not for all. The church conference is an annual meeting of all the officers of the church and any interested members. This committee has the exclusive power to set pastors' salaries (compensation packages for tax purposes) and to elect officers to the committees.

I feel like the other answers are missing the point that you want. As said by other posters, your red blood cells literally only carry oxygen to your muscles and CO2 away from them. Imagine your blood cells REALLY want to carry some molecules. For now, imagine we are going back to the lungs. The blood cells have CO2, then. Now, when your blood rushes past the arterioles (very small blood vessels; since they are small, they are very numerous, and the volume:surface area ratio is very small, which makes it much more efficient), that CO2 is switched with the O2. Why? O2 has a much higher concentration near your lungs than it does at your muscles; the molecules want to reach an equilibrium. When there's much more O2 in one side, they actively want to get to another side. I'm sure you've learned of stuff like osmosis and diffusion. This is just osmosisdiffusion through the membranes of the blood vessels. Now, the O2 rich blood will go to your muscular arterioles. There, where there is much more CO2, the O2 will be switched. Now, your muscles have O2 to use, which will be turned to CO2 through cellular respiration (IE, how we turn sugar into energy). However, the blood will now have less O2 and more CO2, and we are brought back to the beginning.,The only "nutrient" that a healthy red blood cell carries to the peripheral cells is oxygen. Basically, it carries oxygen around in a big container inside of it called hemoglobin. When the RBC reaches the capillaries, which are the blood vessels with the smallest diameter, the container opens up and the oxygen diffuses out of the RBC and into the surrounding blood. Then it diffuses into the cells in that immediate vicinity. The way this happens, and the reason that it happens are a bit complex for an ELI5 post but essentially, there are many different conditions that alter how loosely or tightly closed the hemoglobin "container" is. And the conditions in the periphery, where the capillaries are, make it conducive for the RBCs to let go of the oxygen they are carrying.

Moreover, they were more likely to report receiving a wage increase within the past year, with increases often surpassing their rising costs.

Data limitations aren't primarily caused by infrastructure expenses or the need to cover spectrum costs. Although these factors may contribute, the primary motivator is financial gain. Telecom providers aim to generate higher revenues. By implementing data caps, they can offer larger plans with inflated prices and levy additional fees for excess usage. In the United States, this trend boils down to increasing profits at the expense of consumers.

Despite the rationale behind data caps being linked to spectrum and infrastructure constraints, there is no substantial evidence supporting this claim. Here's why:

Spectrum is indeed a finite resource, restricting the overall capacity of data transmission on both cable and wireless networks. However, the amount of data you can download is not limited by the spectrum itself; instead, it depends on the available bandwidth. The misconception arises from the belief that spectrum scarcity necessitates data caps. On the contrary, data caps serve a different purpose.

Another prevalent myth regarding data caps is related to network congestion. Proponents argue that without data caps, overselling – offering more bandwidth than what's genuinely available due to not all users consuming the network continuously – would lead to network congestion as multiple individuals consume excessive amounts of data simultaneously. Yet, congestion occurs when the network bandwidth is completely saturated. Therefore, data caps don't prevent congestion per se but merely provide a mechanism to manage bandwidth allocation amidst oversubscription. Thus, the argument that data caps are essential to address network congestion is flawed. Instead, the underlying issue lies in managing network resources effectively.

A new method for completely automatic knee MRI segmentation to analyze osteoarthritis (OA) employed a unique hierarchy of random forests (RF) classifiers. The initial step involved utilizing a neighboring approximation forest to offer contextual characteristics to the subsequent RF classifier. This second-level classifier took into account local features and generated location-dependent expenses for the LOGISMOS (Layered Optimal Graph Image Segmentation of Multiple Objects and Surfaces) system's layer-wise optimal graph image segmentation of various objects and surfaces. MRIs applied in this investigation were obtained from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) study and consisted of double echo steady state (DESS) images. After being trained on 34 MRIs displaying varying levels of OA, the efficacy of the proposed method was assessed against traditional gradient-based and single-stage RF-derived costs on an additional 108 MRIs, resulting in significant decreases in segmentation errors (p < 0.05). The 3D LOGISMOS approach was expanded to longitudinal-3D (4D), enabling the integration of data from successive visits by a single patient. By incorporating information from all temporal points, this 4D LOGISMOS provided a more comprehensive solution that utilized both spatial 3D and temporal contexts. Validation of 4D LOGISMOS on 108 MRIs from baseline and 12-month follow-up scans of 54 patients demonstrated considerable reductions in segmentation errors (p < 0.01) when compared to 3D. Furthermore, a significant enhancement in measuring cartilage thickness (p < 0.01) was observed when applying 4D LOGISMOS to the same 54 patients using five annual follow-up scans, as opposed to the sequential 3D strategy.

Massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) is a key technology for 5G wireless communications with a promise of significant capacity increase. The use of low-resolution data converters is crucial for massive MIMO to make the overall transmission as cost- and energy-efficient as possible. In this work, we consider a downlink millimeter-wave (mmWave) transmission scenario, where multiple users are served simultaneously by massive MIMO with one-bit digital-to-analog (DA) converters. In particular, we propose a novel precoder design based on signal-to-leakage-plus-noise ratio (SLNR), which minimizes energy leakage into undesired users while taking into account impairments due to nonlinear one-bit quantization. We show that well-known regularized zero-forcing (RZF) precoder is a particular version of the proposed SLNR-based precoder, which is obtained when quantization impairments are totally ignored. Numerical results underscore significant performance improvements along with the proposed SLNR-based precoder as compared to either RZF or zero-forcing (ZF) precoders.

Widespread deployment of the Internet enabled building of an emerging IT delivery model, i.e., cloud computing. Albeit cloud computing-based services have rapidly developed, their security aspects are still at the initial stage of development. In order to preserve cybersecurity in cloud computing, cybersecurity information that will be exchanged within it needs to be identified and discussed. For this purpose, we propose an ontological approach to cybersecurity in cloud computing. We build an ontology for cybersecurity operational information based on actual cybersecurity operations mainly focused on non-cloud computing. In order to discuss necessary cybersecurity information in cloud computing, we apply the ontology to cloud computing. Through the discussion, we identify essential changes in cloud computing such as data-asset decoupling and clarify the cybersecurity information required by the changes such as data provenance and resource dependency information.

The argument presented in my recent [CMV] revolved around the implication of women's inferiority due to the restriction on men dressing as women. While some compelling points were raised, none succeeded in altering my stance. In essence, this perspective contends that such restrictions do not signify women's subordinate status, but rather an inherent female inferiority perpetuated by persistent patriarchal suppression throughout history. Consequently, any gender norm, be it liberating or restrictive, symbolizes male dominance. Thus, the underlying assertion is: Men hold power and subjugate women. If one disagrees with this premise, however, there seems to be no substantial argument beyond "because." This perspective equates believing in pervasive patriarchal oppression as equivalent to religious faith, where "because men are evil; they established patriarchy" serves as a sufficient explanation for various societal issues, including both detrimental regulations for women and supposed freedoms in dress codes. This mindset fosters a culture of perpetual victimhood, yet my intention here is to scrutinize the argument itself. When someone posits that society conveys women's inferiority (an assertion I've rarely encountered), they likely harbor the belief that males wield power as an intrinsic characteristic, making their claim a reflection of the contrary belief. I welcome alternative perspectives capable of challenging my perspective.

In this paper, we consider the joint task of simultaneously optimizing (i) the weights of a deep neural network, (ii) the number of neurons for each hidden layer, and (iii) the depth of the network. More specifically, we propose an optimization method that determines the optimal values for these parameters via a weighted combination of the generalization error and the model size. We show that when trained on image data, the proposed optimization method outperforms a number of other state-of-the-art methods such as Bayesian optimization, evolutionary algorithms, and gradient descent on image classification tasks. In addition, we demonstrate that by training the proposed model on one image classification dataset, we are able to obtain a well-performing model on other datasets, e.g., CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, with minimal training. This is done by using the learned weights of the model on the one dataset to initialize a new model on the other two datasets. As our method can train a model from scratch or fine-tune a pretrained model, it can be considered as a universal image classifier (UIC), which provides an interpretable, efficient, and flexible alternative to other recent methods such as Gatys and Lu et al. . In addition to image classification, our method can also be used to train a model that can generalize across different tasks. We conduct experiments to demonstrate that trained with the proposed method, a model can generalize across tasks such as image classification and semantic segmentation with no additional training data. Finally, our method is easy to implement and can be directly applied to any deep neural network without changing the network architecture. Paper can be found here. Understanding the formation of subjective human traits, such as preference and opinions, is an important, but poorly explored problem. An essential aspect is that traits collectively evolve under the repeated influence of the environment. The impact of the environment is especially strong in situations where individuals differ in the baseline trait level, where preferences and opinions can develop over time in a dynamic context. It is important to understand the underlying mechanisms of this dynamic evolution of opinions, in order to be able to shape opinions in a desired direction, e.g. for the purpose of social manipulation. I will present a game-theoretic model that allows to study the evolution of traits under repeated environmentally-driven interactions. I will show that the social evolution of traits can be driven by a process of 'drift and selection', in which both drift and selection are driven by the repeated environmental influence. I will discuss implications of this model for the understanding of opinion formation, and apply the model to different settings.

If that happens, the ice loss could push up global oceans by 2m, or more. The claim is based on an assessment of the rocks underlying the ice stream. Scientists tell the journal Nature that should the front of the glacier retreat about 150km from its current position, it will then enter a runaway reversal that takes it 200-250km further inland. Most of the big glaciers in the east of the White Continent appear relatively quiescent; Totten is something of an exception. It is experiencing a thinning rate of about half a metre per year, according to the latest satellite measurements. Previous research indicates this is probably being driven by warm ocean water getting under and melting the floating front of the glacier. What Alan Aitken and colleagues have now done is examine a possible future for Totten if the shrinkage continues. They have used gravity and magnetic data recorded over the entire catchment feeding the glacier to understand its past behaviour. They find that the underlying sedimentary rocks at the modern front of Totten are heavily eroded, as are the rocks in fjords deep in the interior of the catchment. The inference is that these sections are where persistent, moving ice has had time to grind down the geology. It is the mid-region, however, that piques the team's interest. Here, the sediments are relatively thick, suggesting that ice fronts have historically been resident in this section for only short periods. This mid-region is also where the rock bed dips inland - a geometry that glaciologists say is naturally unstable and accelerates any glacier retreat. "What this all tells us is that once the ice margin starts to go back, it goes back quite rapidly to a newer, stable position way inland. And if you do that our modelling indicates you will lose ice equivalent to 1.5-2m of sea level rise," co-author Prof Martin Siegert from Imperial College London, UK, told BBC News. The last time Totten retreated to the deep interior of the France-sized catchment was probably in the Pliocene Epoch, he added. "Three-point-five million years ago, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were in the region of 400 parts per million - so about where they are now. The atmosphere was a couple of degrees warmer than it is now, which is in line with what we expect for the end of this century if we do nothing about it. The Pliocene is where we're headed." Even so, the timescale for the far retreat inland would be on the order of centuries, on current trends. The international community has of course committed itself to doing something about climate change, promising at the Paris talks in December to try to keep the global atmospheric temperature rise above pre-industrial levels to "well below 2C." Various analyses, however, suggest a 2.7C increase is a more likely outcome, based on the voluntary national curbs to greenhouse gas emissions promised at the meeting. And that variance could be significant, according to research presented at the recent European Geosciences Union meeting in Vienna last month. Prof Rob DeConto from the University of Massachusetts-Amherst, US, has modelled possible ice losses from the Antarctic continent based on the two temperature figures. For a 2C rise, he found minimal change by the end of this century. On the other hand, for 2.7C he identified ice losses equivalent to many tens of centimetres of sea-level rise. "There's threshold behaviour in the Antarctic ice sheet system," Prof DeConto told reporters at EGU. The concept of prime number is so important that it has been generalized in different ways in various branches of mathematics. Generally, "prime" indicates minimality or indecomposability, in an appropriate sense as the set of divisors (or integers) whose square roots are exactly equal to each other and which satisfy some condition on their sum. For example, a prime number satisfies the Faulkner-Salvin Steinage theorem: A prime number has at least one negative integer, if and only if its sum is at most twice the product of all other numbers. You can also use this theorem for the rule that any two positive integers with nonnegative square root values must have to be prime numbers. One prime number means, among other things, convergence between a tensor function x and a real line that connects the origin to the leftmost point of the unit circle. Russia plans to temporarily disconnect the entire country from the internet in an exercise designed to test the country's internet infrastructure in case of a cyber-war. The test is expected to begin on Monday. Russia's RIA Novosti news agency quoted Russian Defense Ministry spokesman Igor Konashenkov as saying on Friday that Russia's Defense Ministry is planning to test the country's defense system in the event of a cyber-attack on Monday. Konashenkov said that the exercise will include a shutdown of internet service in the entire country. "During the day on Monday, the entire Russian Federation will be offline for several hours," Konashenkov said. "The aim of the exercise is to test the entire internet infrastructure of the Russian Federation, including the country's cyber-defense system." Konashenkov added that the exercise is part of the Defense Ministry's efforts to protect the country's national security and to develop the country's cyber-defense capabilities. "The exercises will be held in different regions of the country," he said. "We're testing our defense system to see how we're prepared to face such a situation." Asked whether Russia was preparing for a cyber-war with the United States, Konashenkov said: "We're always ready for any cyber-attacks, including against Russia." He added that "the United States should also be ready for any cyber-attacks against it." Russia has repeatedly warned of the possibility of a cyber-attack on its territory, although no such attack has ever been launched. The Defense Ministry also said that during the exercise, Russia's air force will test the capabilities of its "cyber-aircraft" and its own capabilities to conduct cyber-attacks. Konashenkov said that the military's goal is to increase the country's ability to protect its military information systems from cyber-attacks. "We're preparing for cyber-attacks on our military," he said.

Many years ago, keyboards used different pins to represent each bit of information. When some keys were held down, a different set of pins would have voltage across them than others. USB doesn't work that way at all. It just sends data back and forth, one bit at a time, very quickly. It's a lot more like sending data across a network. When you hold down multiple keys, it just sends more bytes of data. When you record audio, it's digitizing the audio and streaming the bytes directly to your computer.," "Professional audio is recorded at least 44,100 samples per second, with 24 bits per sample. That's a data rate of around 1060 kbs. USB 2 supports a data rate of up to 480 Mbs. That's around 47 individual microphones all at the same time. It works because USB is a serial communication with high speed switching. Meaning it sends two bits down the data pins, and rapidly switches between which bit is being sent. It switches literally millions of times a second, plenty fast for audio.,The reason you can detect large amounts of keys pressed and record high quality audio is that the USB device is its self a little computer. It has enough circuitry to detect all the key presses and record the audio and then it packages all that data into a single stream of bits, and it's the bits that get sent back and forth over the USB connection. In fact, this data is only sent over two of the four pins. The other two are used only for delivering power to a USB device that doesn't have its own power supply. The reason the microphone can transmit in very very close to real time is that sound is very slow compared to have fast computers are. Sound is a wave of changing air pressure that moves through the air. The higher the tone or pitch, the faster the air pressure changes neutral to high to low and back to neutral. The highest frequency humans can hear is 20KHz which means the air pressure makes that cycle 20,000 times a second. To record this sound a microphone is setup which converts the air pressure into a voltage that swings from low to high and back, just like the air pressure. This changing voltage is then "sampled" by a converter circuit. Sample here just means to measure. So the voltage is measure to see how high it is at a given point. If you do this over and over again, and you do it fast enough, you get enough measurements to recreate the original sound with an amplifier and speaker. To get enough samples to do this, you need to measure twice as fast as the highest frequency in order not to miss the really fast changing voltage. Recall the highest was 20,000 times a second. So we sample at 44,100 times a second. Now lets check some numbers. Each sample requires 16 bits of data and there are 44,100 samples per second so that is 705,600 bits per second. Most USB audio interfaces can record two channels at the same time, and play back two channels at the same time, so now we need to move 2,822,400 bits per second. Sounds like a lot. Except even the slowest USB devices can send 12,000,000 bits per second. So we can do 4 channels of high quality audio and still have 10,000,000 bits per second left over. Now sending audio data to the computer actually uses a lot more of that 12,000,000 bits per second because the audio has to be packaged in a way that the computer understands what it is and where it goes and that's done by wrapping the samples in other data.', "The USB 2.0 (most common) standard has support for data transfer speeds as high as 480 Mbps (more than enough to handle audio and most video input streams). The new USB 3.0 standard supports data transfer speeds of up to 5 Gbps and USB 3.1 supports up to 10 Gbps (which is enough bandwidth to handle just about any multimedia peripheral device you can possibly think of including live 4K video streams, for example). Of the 4 pins in a regular USB 2.0 cable, only 2 are used for data and the other two are used for supplying voltagepower. The USB device has a chip in it that converts the information (e.g. audio information from a microphone or keyboard presses) into packets of data that can be transferred via USB to the receiving device (computer). That's why you don't need multiple wires for carrying different types of data, it all just gets converted into one data stream. Note that newer USB implementations (3.0 3.1) have more than 4 pins to facilitate higher speed data transfers greater bandwidth.

John Bieniewicz, age 44, was struck unexpectedly during a park game on Sunday, resulting in his death in the hospital on Tuesday. Basel Abdul-Amir Saad, 36, has been accused of attempting to inflict serious injury upon Bieniewicz. Authorities may alter the charges following additional investigation. Media reports and a memorial webpage describe Bieniewicz as a skilled referee with experience across various competitions, and a husband and father of two boys. "On behalf of all his friends, we are deeply saddened. Heartbroken. This was an unjustifiable end for a wonderful man," stated Jim Acho, Bieniewicz's friend, to the Associated Press news agency. Eyewitnesses at the Livonia event reported observing Bieniewicz dismissing Saad for complaining about a ruling and receiving a second citation. Player Scott Herkes informed the Detroit Free Press that Bieniewicz was examining the field and was taken aback by the attack. "The referee did not instigate this assault," Herkes stated. "I have never witnessed anything like this in my entire life." Saad allegedly departed the scene following the occurrence, and multiple players obtained his vehicle's license plate number as he exited. Saad's attorney, Brian Berry, shared with local media that his client was cooperating and had surrendered to law enforcement. "There is reason to believe the details of this situation have been distorted in some accounts," Berry wrote in an email to the Detroit Free Press. "Although this tragedy is heart-wrenching, it is essential that we maintain an open mind and await the full disclosure of the facts surrounding this case." This marks the second such fatality within the past two years. In April 2013, a minor player assaulted referee Ricardo Portillo during a football game in Utah. The father of three succumbed to his injuries after a week in a coma. The adolescent subsequently confessed to manslaughter.

The Galician autonomy charter was repealed, along with those of Catalonia and the Basque provinces once they were overtaken. As per Carlos Fernandez Santander's account, a minimum of 4,200 individuals met their demise through extrajudicial killings or summary trials, amongst them republicans, communists, Galician nationalists, socialists, and anarchists. Amongst the fatalities were the governors of all four Galician provinces, their wives like Juana Capdevielle of A Coruna, mayors such as Anxel Casal of Santiago de Compostela from the Partido Galeguista, prominent socialists like Jaime Quintanilla in Ferrol and Emilio Martinez Garrido in Vigo, Popular Front deputies Antonio Bilbatua, Jose Minones, Diaz Villamil, Ignacio Seoane, and former deputy Heraclio Botana, as well as non-aligned professionals including journalists Manuel Lustres Rivas and physician Luis Poza Pastrana, and soldiers who refused to join the rebellion, such as Generals Rogelio Caridad Pita and Enrique Salcedo Molinuevo and Admiral Antonio Azarola, and PG founders Alexandre Boveda and Victor Casas. Numerous others were compelled into exile or suffered further retaliations, losing their jobs and positions.

The Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information said that the social network had not obtained effective approval from WhatsApp's 35 million German users. Facebook bought WhatsApp for 19 billion in 2014. Facebook is facing a 20 million (22.5 million) fine in Germany over the way it acquired user data from WhatsApp. Facebook bought WhatsApp for 19 billion in 2014. In 2016, it announced plans to start sharing user data between the two services, but said it would not do so without obtaining user consent. The Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information said on Tuesday, however, that the social network had not obtained effective approval from WhatsApp's 35 million German users. "We are aware of the DPA's statement of objections and are examining the documents," a Facebook spokeswoman said in a statement. "We will respond in due course." The WhatsApp and Facebook merger generated plenty of controversy when it was first announced. The social network said it would start sharing data with WhatsApp in August 2016, but the European Commission halted the process in August 2017 while it investigated antitrust concerns. That investigation has since been dropped, but the Commissioner's announcement this week shows that privacy regulators are still probing the issue. "Facebook and WhatsApp are independent companies. And that's why we're not able to combine user data," Facebook told the Commissioner in January 2017. "The only thing we're asking for is the number of phone contacts the user has on WhatsApp in order to improve their experience on Facebook." According to the Commissioner, however, WhatsApp users were not informed they would need to agree to new terms and conditions in order to continue using the service. "The requirement of unequivocal consent to the terms of data processing was also not met, as the users did not have a free choice," the office said. Facebook also used "inappropriate" tracking pixels to collect data about WhatsApp users, the Commissioner's office said. Tracking pixels, also known as web beacons, are tiny images embedded in webpages that can be used to collect data. "Facebook has used its dominant position to create a situation in which users had to agree to the processing of their data on a central platform. This has led to a reduction of users' control over their data," the Commissioner said. Facebook didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Robert Guiscard, an other Norman adventurer previously elevated to the dignity of count of Apulia as the result of his military successes, ultimately drove the Byzantines out of southern Italy. He was defeated by Justinian I at the Battle of Pavia in 878 and died shortly thereafter while on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem.[65] In 966, Italian forces were decisively driven from Sicily during the Angevin conquest under Charles the Fat by Stephen II of Taranto,[6869] who soon became emperor after Baldwin III's death.[70] In 1054 he took possession of Rome, which had been left without rulers for more than 500 years since the fall of Hadrian.[71] The Frankish kingdom continued to expand eastward into the Balkans where it met with a series of wars against Bulgarian and Venetian dynasties (976-982) over several large territories; eventually, however, the crusaders lost control over most territory they captured and quickly reverted to the status quo ante bellum. Francia reached its zenith in 1017 when Pope Urban II consecrated Henry V as Holy Roman Emperor. After this time, the Franks began to lose their influence - or so seemed likely at first: in 1135, Frederick Barbarossa completed his reconquest of Saxony[72], but within decades the province was again ruled by a local lord rather than a German king. The same fate visited Silesia in 129798.[73] By 1345 all these lands except Bohemia [74] lay outside the jurisdiction of either France or Germany. Under Louis XI there was some recourse to Byzantine ideas about "national unity," although unlike the Greeks' imperial system Louis did not attempt to enforce such an idea through coercion. As noted above, many of the foreigners who settled in the West considered themselves independent. They lived alongside native peoples who complained that the conquerors treated them differently because they were foreign, often employing force to impose their rule upon locals[75]. Examples included William Rufus, Prince-Bishop of Paris between 1151 and 1198 who established himself throughout Normandy until his defeat near Rouen in 1200 led him back to Paris, and Tancred de Koves, Count Palatine of Burgundy and Duke of Lorraine, whose position in eastern Germany was challenged after Philip II named Staufenberg archbishop of Mainz. These men attempted to extend French authority only to the degree whereby the populace would accept it. When these settlements didn't last long, the Europeans had mixed feelings. A few claimed to be genuine Christians seeking to share Christ's message among pagan nations, but others wanted what they regarded as unfree European land to be theirs alone, using any means necessary. This is seen today especially clearly in Northern Europe. Fortunately for Western civilization, neither the concept nor practice of the Crusades endured uncritically past the 14th century. It has survived in popular culture though largely in fiction.[76] From the Middle Ages, historicism also gained prominence in archaeology, astronomy, geology, botany, geography, linguistics, medicine, mathematics, music, philosophy, politics and sociology. According to historian John Dower: "Historicists saw Latin as simple language based originally on Greek rather than Hebrew, and as a literary form derived equally from Homeric Greece...77] Despite being introduced into the academy with great fanfare and heralded as 'the new science' by Voltaire and Leibniz, Historicism never really caught fire, aside from the beginnings of History as Science before 1900 - especially after World War I - when historians generally started to recognize the importance of scientific methods, data analysis and empirical evidence in the study if history. After the Renaissance, historical studies grew out of maps made possible by cartography, which helped researchers trace the boundaries of medieval kingdoms and empires across Europe. Historians used these markers to find information about political power structures external to those marked on ancient maps including trade patterns and population figures. For example, English chroniclers like Edward Gibbon could show how England rose to become one of the world's largest and richest countries and then collapsed just three hundred years later due to internal conflicts. Maps even allowed for statistical comparisons, showing increasing wealth and urbanization along the continent starting around the middle ages, while decreasing populations occurred primarily in rural areas. Today scientists use satellite images to map changes in agriculture and natural landscapes. At roughly the beginning of the 19th century and continuing until the twentieth century, history increasingly involved the study of social classes and occupations.[81] Historian Thomas Carlyle wrote of the late 18th and early 19th centuries that "history has gone mad and has given birth to an incredible array of scientists called historians... we have learned nothing'. While the Treaties and Regulations will have direct effect (if clear, unconditional and immediate), Directives do not generally give citizens (as opposed to the member state) standing to sue other citizens. In theory, this is because TFEU article 288 says Directives are addressed to the member states and usually "leave to the national authorities the choice of form and methods" to implement. In part this reflects that directives often create minimum standards, leaving member states to apply higher standards. For example, the Working Time Directive requires that every worker has at least 4 weeks paid holidays each year, but most member states require more than 28 days in national law. However, on the current position adopted by the Court of Justice, citizens have standing to make claims based on national laws that implement Directives, but not from Directives themselves. Directives do not have so called "horizontal" direct effect (i.e. between non-state parties). This view was instantly controversial, and in the early 1990s three Advocate Generals persuasively argued that Directives should create rights and duties for all citizens. The Court of Justice refused, but there are five large exceptions.

Thousands of demonstrators flooded the streets to demand Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi's resignation. The controversy surrounding Sisi arose from his sudden decision to cede the Red Sea islands to Saudi Arabia during a visit from King Salman. These barren islands have been under Egyptian sovereignty since 1950. In Cairo, protesters voiced their discontent with "Sisi out" and "We possess the land" chants. Engineer Mohamed Hussein spoke to Reuters, expressing his dissatisfaction with the broader national conditions rather than solely the islands. Some demonstrators also echoed "The people desire the demise of the regime!" - a chant from the 2011 Arab Spring revolution that ousted previous leader Hosni Mubarak - along with "Sisi-Mubarak." At least 80 individuals were detained in Cairo and Alexandria, according to authorities. The White House expressed concern and vowed to closely monitor developments in US ally Egypt. Both secular and religious activists had encouraged protests against the transfer of the uninhabited islands, Tiran and Sanafir, located near the entrance to the Gulf of Aqaba. Sisi defended his decision, asserting that they had historically belonged to the Saudis and Egypt had merely acted as caretakers. "We didn't forfeit our territory; instead, we acknowledged the rights of others," he declared. "No soil was conceded by Egypt; all documentation supports this conclusion." Critics argue that Sisi's clandestine handling of the deal, without parliamentary authorization and post-transaction announcement, was questionable. Some accuse him of striking the agreement in exchange for Saudi financial assistance and investments. In recent months, Sisi has faced mounting criticism on various fronts, including Egypt's struggling economy. Previously popular among the populace due to his win in the 2014 election, Sisi now faces a growing opposition movement.

While it may be understandable that some individuals may feel relief at the ban of controversial subreddits like Coontown, it is important to consider the larger issue of free speech and the impact of censorship. Advocating for the suppression of certain opinions or ideas, even if offensive or extreme, sets a dangerous precedent and can ultimately lead to a restriction of our fundamental rights to express ourselves. Additionally, banning a subreddit does not necessarily eradicate the problematic beliefs that fueled its existence in the first place. Instead, it merely pushes those individuals and ideas underground where they may actually become stronger and more extreme. It is important to address and challenge harmful ideas through open dialogue and education, rather than simply censoring them.

Manufacturing larger engines with greater displacement proves more cost-effective due to the direct correlation between horsepower and RPMs. Faster RPMs require lighter, robust components, necessitating extensive design efforts for optimal intake and exhaust flow. Time-consuming engineering is required for maximum small engine efficiency, unlike building a larger engine. Most responses here are inaccurate, with varying degrees of error. Internal combustion engines are intricate systems; oversimplifying fails to capture their complexity. When a manufacturer discloses horsepower, they refer to the engine's peak power, which represents the highest power generated throughout its RPM range. To grasp this concept without delving into technical jargon, consider the following analogy: Your vehicle likely exhibits a power curve that generates more power at increased RPMs. By pressing the accelerator at 1500rpm and then again at 4000rpm, you will notice faster acceleration at the latter RPM because the engine produces less power at the former. Thus, stating that two vehicles generate "300hp" does not convey significant information if one engine delivers consistent power across all revs, while the other only achieves peak power at high RPMs. Several factors influence manufacturers' decisions to employ large displacement engines. One compelling reason is the generation of a relatively uniform power curve. Although not always applicable, larger engines generally offer a smoother power delivery. This attribute benefits various driving conditions, including road travel and racing, as quick acceleration from low RPMs is advantageous. Additionally, simpler and lighter engine designs are possible through large displacement engines, counterintuitive as it may seem. While larger engines tend to be heavier, smaller engines often incorporate turbochargers to enhance power and efficiency. This improvement comes at the expense of added weight and complexity.

The small town of St. Paul was buzzing with excitement. Everyone in town had heard about the upcoming boxing match between two of the town's best fighters, Nick and Joe. Nick was the hometown favorite. He had been boxing since he was a kid, and had always been considered a natural talent. He was well-known for his hard-hitting punches and lightning-fast reflexes. Joe, on the other hand, was something of an unknown quantity. He had just moved to St. Paul a few months ago and had quickly become a fixture at the local boxing gym. He was smaller than Nick but had a reputation for being incredibly tough and resilient. The night of the fight arrived, and the entire town gathered at the boxing arena. The place was electric with anticipation. When the bell rang for the first round, both men came out swinging. Nick seemed to have the edge, landing several powerful punches and sending Joe reeling. But Joe kept coming back, taking almost every punch Nick threw at him. By the end of the fourth round, it seemed like Nick had the fight in the bag. But then something strange happened. Joe suddenly started throwing wild punches, seemingly without any strategy or control. It was as if he were possessed. Nick capitalized on Joe's lack of control and managed to land a few more punches before the bell. When the decision was announced, Nick had won by unanimous decision. Joe slumped down against the ropes and refused to leave the ring. His corner men tried to talk to him, but he wouldn't respond. After some time, they managed to get him to his feet and escorted him out. As Joe walked out of the ring, someone in the crowd shouted "Bad luck boxers!" It seemed that Joe had been cursed with bad luck, and it had cost him the fight. From then on, whenever Nick and Joe ran into each other around town, the locals would refer to them as "the bad luck boxers."

Quantum annealing (QA) is a quantum computing algorithm that works on the principle of Adiabatic Quantum Computation (AQC), and it has shown significant computational advantages in solving combinatorial optimization problems . QA has recently been extended to general matrix operations by introducing a multipoint thresholding technique called Multi-Objective Quantum Annealing, which allows for the calculation of more than one objective at once using an ensemble of measurement outcomes while preserving the original state before any measurements were performed. This approach has become known as Multimodal QA because multiple objectives can be simultaneously optimized with very different error rates; however, its performance cannot yet match those obtained from QA alone owing to limitations intrinsic to the process itself, such as decoherence with respect to the environment. Although there are several techniques available to reduce this effect, not all have proven effective enough to allow real-time implementation of multimodality. Furthermore, the development of new devices capable of performing multitudinous object analyses may take decades or longer, resulting in unacceptable delay times between problem formulation and solution execution. The goal of our project was therefore to develop novel methods to accelerate the algorithms used in Multi-objective QA so they can be implemented within milliseconds rather than minutes. To accomplish this, we developed two new approaches: 1) A method where solutions are found concurrently across all objectives instead of sequentially, thus obviating the need for global environmental control during multi-objective analysis 2) Methods to reduce coherence noise inherent to the AQC procedure itself through the use of tailored engineered environments

Thanks to numerous musical venues, including the Teatr Wielki, the Polish National Opera, the Chamber Opera, the National Philharmonic Hall and the National Theatre, as well as the Roma and Dramatyczny Theatres, Warsaw boasts a vibrant and varied cultural scene. The city's nightlife is equally colourful and diverse, with everything from sleek and trendy bars, to welcoming pubs and cosy coffee shops. The city's Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is the best place to experience the rich history of the city and a great place to explore on foot. The city's many museums, galleries and monuments are all within easy reach of the Old Town. The city's numerous gardens and parks are also worth a visit. azienki Park is the largest park in Warsaw and is located in the city centre, and the Botanical Gardens are also popular with visitors. Warsaw is a city of shopping. You'll find luxury shops and boutiques in the city centre, and the Plac Trzech Krzyzy (Trzech Krzyzy Square) is home to the best Polish designers. For more affordable shopping, head to Zote Tarasy (Golden Terraces) which houses shops, boutiques, restaurants, a cinema and even an ice-skating rink. Other shopping malls include the Galeria Mokotow and the Blue City and Arkadia Malls. Warsaw's most famous cafe is Cafe Blikle, located in the city centre. This traditional cafe has been serving delicious cakes and pastries for over 100 years. There are also numerous bakeries in the city, the most famous being Barbara on Al. Jerozolimskie Street. Warsaw has a rich and varied nightlife. The city's bars and clubs range from intimate and cosy, to luxurious and stylish. The best time to visit Warsaw is in late spring or early summer, when the weather is warm and pleasant and there are numerous festivals and events taking place in the city. The city is also worth a visit in winter when the city streets are transformed into a fairytale-like landscape thanks to the snow.

Staff at the hospital, run by the Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Foundation Trust (NTW) ordered a pizza on 10 December, but were dismayed when the phrase appeared on the box. Staff told the BBC they thought the 'n-word' was offensive and should be removed. They ordered the pizza in a bid to "celebrate" 100 years of the NHS, the BBC reported. 'Zero tolerance' A spokesman for the hospital said the company, Hotpress Pizza, had apologised for the gaffe. He said the company had not been told to use the term, and added: "The trust has zero tolerance for racism, and we have written to Hotpress to express our concern. "They have apologised and are undertaking an internal investigation." The incident comes amid growing debate about the use of the term 'n-word' in Britain. Last month, an Oxford University study suggested that the word has been on the decline since the 1970s. The study, which examined public use of the word, found that use had declined from 35 per cent in 1972 to 25 per cent in 2011. Peter Ward, a 54-year-old resident of Barnstaple, Devon, and Richard Hiley, a 30-year-old man from Tividale in the West Midlands, were both sentenced at Birmingham Crown Court on Monday. Ward received a sentence of five years and two months, while Hiley was given a five-year term. Both men admitted to offenses involving the possession, distribution, and importation of Class A and Class B drugs. Known online as PlutoPete, Ward operated a business specializing in providing military-grade foil packaging, which claimed to conceal illicit substances from detection, as well as offering new psychoactive substances, or "legal highs." Ward was apprehended by National Crime Agency (NCA) officers in Barnstaple in October 2013 during an international operation aimed at major vendors on dark web marketplaces such as Silk Road. During the search of Ward's rural property, authorities discovered Class A and B drugs and various computers. Subsequent analysis revealed that Hiley, an ex-customer of Ward's, had been contracted by Ward to convert bitcoins into cash. In December 2013, NCA officials raided Hiley's residence in the West Midlands, identifying significant transactions between the two through financial records obtained from Ward. Hiley also confessed to two charges of illegally importing prohibited weapons – specifically, five stun guns – which he asserted were for personal protection. NCA Branch Commander Ian Glover stated: "Criminals and their clients often believe that dark web marketplaces offer anonymity. However, the truth is that law enforcement collaborates internationally to track down and prosecute these individuals." (Source: US Department of Justice)

Pre-trained language models finely tuned may encounter significant misalignment when processing in-distribution and out-of-distribution data due to their excessive capacity. To alleviate this problem, we suggest a fine-tuning approach featuring two kinds of regulation for improved calibration: (1) Intramanifold regulation, generating artificial intramanifold instances via data manifold interpolation. Training augmented with these synthetic samples instills a regularization of smoothness, enhancing in-distribution calibration. (2) Extramanifold regulation, motivating the model to provide consistent probability distributions for extramanifold instances to tackle the overconfident behavior towards OOD data. The results of our experiments reveal that this method surpasses current calibration techniques for text categorization in terms of expected calibration error, misclassification identification, and anomaly detection across six datasets. Scientists from the University of California San Diego have developed a method to create neurons. The technique is able to convert astrocytes, the supporting cells in the brain, into neurons, including three types of neurons with distinct functions - for example, excitatory, inhibitory and neurological. The researchers say that their work provides an alternative to current methods used by neuroscientists who use stem cells in developing new neurons which might otherwise be lost when those cells are destroyed during this process. "Neuroshima," discovered 60 years ago, was one of the first tools scientists employed to create nerve cells containing neurons but it could not produce enough neurons because it lacked sufficient support cells. This problem means that most attempts at making neurons using pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) end up as either 'osteoblasts' - like embryonic fibres - or smooth muscle cells, which do not possess sufficient neuron-producing ability to develop into new neurons. Researchers had previously failed to create neurons using these techniques because they contained insufficient astrocyte survival factors (ASF). In 2001, Dr Liisa Talvi and her team at UCSD identified ASFs in astrocytes and demonstrated they were capable of generating neurons in animal studies. They also discovered that astrocytes provided the necessary nutrients needed to promote neural cell growth. Now, after a series of experiments on human brains, they have found that adding these ASMs can help them generate neurons with particular properties such as excitability, strength and electrical conductivity. These characteristics make astrocytes suitable candidates as targets for controlling neuronal activity through stimulation and inhibition. Professor Talvi said: "We showed that we can direct the development of astroglia when stimulating the vascularization of their parenchyma, the fluid surrounding them. We also discovered that inhibiting the formation of astroglial vesicles via a small molecule antagonist completely changes the shape of the organelles so that they form a different type of neuron. Our research has helped us achieve our goal and advance our knowledge about how astrocytes affect neuronal function and how this affects the development of neurons. This provides us with exciting possibilities where we may use these astrocytes to speed up neuroscientific discoveries and ultimately improve human health."

It's taken me a long time to decide. There are still 5 days for me to change my mind, but as it stands I want to leave the UK's economic injustice, its shoddy governance, and its establishment. I'm going to go through each issue and give a brief overview of the arguments. Then I'll state why I'm choosing Yes, and why I'm not choosing No. Democracy - Nobody from either side argues that Westminster is without fault. On the Yes side they pretend that Westminster is bad because it projects Tory government into Scotland. On the No side they believe that Westminster can be changed for the better from within. They're both wrong. Westminster is anti-democratic in other ways. Not just with the problems of the Lords, Cash for Honours and Expenses: the voting system means that even when Labour gets into power, it is not because Scotland voted for it. First-past-the-post means that there is [bias towards a two-party system] , and the main parties become inevitably more alike as they appeal to centrist, swing voters. And there is no swing in Scotland. It is mainly in the South of England. So it is no surprise that in 69 years of Westminster rule, Scottish votes changed which party received power only once, in 1974. In addition, Westminster steals our best politicians and leaves only numpties like Johann Lamont to hold the Scottish Government to account. If you think those Scottish MPs are doing a good job, over 30 of the 59 voted for benefit caps, and are straying from the ideology of their voter base. Why would we agree to that arrangement? Why, when we have the Additional Member System in Holyrood that is (by voting standards) pure sex, creates representative parliaments, and where coalitions force parties to adopt common-sense policies everyone can agree on rather than top-down ideological reorganisations? Politics - The SNP have created a myth that they are the party of progressiveness, and that independence is the stepping stone to social justice. Many no voters I've spoken to just can't see past Alex Salmond, don't like "nationalism," (the word is used in the same ignorant way socialism is in the USA) and have not thought about the long term consequences of independence on the political discourse. I think the argument that I've heard that Scotland has more in common with the London dockworker than the Scottish baron is absolute nonsense. It ignores the fact Scottish and English politics is diverging. Holyrood does not draw on ethnic identity politics. It draws on Scotland's collectivism. The anti-bedroom tax payment, removing charges and private investment from the NHS, community buying of privately owned land, and free university education stand in stark contrast to austerity and corporate welfare. Meanwhile, UKIP's rise guarantees that Westminster will resemble the worse kind of nationalism more than Holyrood ever could. They stress benefit thievery, not tax-dodging. Immigration, not job creation. That we need to protect ourselves from Putin with Trident and from Islamists with military force. Moreover, the system entrenches establishment, widens the wealth gap and shrinks social mobility. Rather than uniting so the system can disenfranchise as it has done, Scotland is far better off walking away from the corporate agenda, not incrementally coaxing it to what it wants. Defence Foreign Policy - The SNP want rid of trident but want to join NATO, Better Together cry doom at Scotland's defence and lack of influence at the top. Jobs at Faslane could be threatened but the SNP have pledged to re-employ them. We got dragged into an illegal war, and the UK's foreign policy has been nothing but bad news when it comes to the middle east. Having a smaller voice that says good things is better than a large, infinitely belligerent one. Leaving the UK is not going to change what the UK says, so if you like UK foreign policy, don't worry, it's still going to be there. In addition, it will give us a seat on the EU council where the Cabinet secretary stopped the Scottish Fisheries minister from attending , when he is the person with the most influence. EU - This is an shitstorm equal to the economic arguments. Vast quantities of legal opinions on both sides. At the end of the day, given that Scotland holds 25 of the EU's renewable energy potential, 20 of the fishery stocks, and only 1 of the population of Europe, a deal will be struck. Duncan wasn't really convinced that the plan was going to work. Two days ago he was awaiting transfer to a more secure location, which sounded like they were going to "suicide" him if one believed the word around the holding cells, and suddenly yesterday a guard he had seen on duty for the past three weeks handed him a most surprising note written on a napkin during the usual weekly search of his "apartment" as the guards referred to them. The note read: "Tomorrow. Midnight. Be ready. Get rid of the note" After reading it 10 times or more Duncan flushed the note down the poor excuse of a toilet his "apartment" contained and sat on his bed considering the significance of it. It could be a cruel joke or an attempt to find excuses to make his stay even more unpleasant. He had managed to hold his mouth shut as far as the most important information went and that didn't sit well with his hosts. The interrogations had been long and tiresome and they had started to get painful in the last 2 weeks, the scars on his back a testimony to the latter. And yet there he was staring at the guard that handed him the note with something far more dangerous in hand. Another explosion drove him from his thoughts and into action, grabbing the gun and saying "Lead on then." The air was filled with the shouting and running of the other guardsmen who went back and forth above them on the platforms. It was a wide corridor leading to a security checkpoint with always two guards present and the door could only be opened by the key card one of them carried although he didn't know who. There was no way they could approach without being spotted "I hope you have something good planned because I can't think of any way to get through this without getting spotted by your ex-colleagues" whispered Duncan turning to Mr Bond. Say nothing and hide the gun. Do not stop walking before we reach the gate whatever happens. We don't want to give them any doubts." Duncan nodded in agreement, hid his gun and after taking a deep breath to pick up some courage followed Mr Bond. The moment they turned the corner Mr Bond hailed the two guards who looked at him with startled faces. "The Warden wants this one moved. Open the gate quickly." They were at the middle of the way to the gate. "They told us nothing of this change Eddie. We have to check with Taylor upstairs." They were almost upon them. "We don't have time for you to check! In thirty seconds they were running towards a 4x4 with all their might hearing the alarm go off as they reached it. "A helicopter is supposed to meet us two kilometers north of here in three hours" said Mr Bond and motioned Duncan to follow. "So how much did you tell them?" asked Mr Bond as they were making their path through the trees. "Well they know the movements of the rest of my platoon for the past weeks but I managed to withhold the real purpose behind them. Which was? What day is it? Thursday the 15th. Well then tomorrow those guys are going to have the surprise of their lives. We have gathered our forces in secret with my platoon running interference to attack the underground base of operations they maintain to the west part of the valley. Really? How did we learn of it existence in the first place? We captured some key personnel during another mission near the borders of that area. Pure luck. You're right. The study conducted by The Local Data Company (LDC) in collaboration with the University of Stirling revealed that Scotland's average retail vacancy rate declined from 14.5% to 13.7%. Among Scottish towns, East Kilbride reported the highest vacancy rate at 33%, while Inverurie boasted the least, with a rate of 1%. Approximately 40 shops in Scotland have been vacant for over three years. The improvement rate of town vacancy rates outpaced that of cities' rates by a factor of two. The top-performing towns were Anstruther, Clydebank, Dumfries, Inverkeithing, Lochgelly, Peterhead, and Pitlochry. Five towns – Inverurie, Ellon, North Berwick, Dunbar, and Biggar – maintained vacancy rates below 6% for the previous three years. Conversely, rates in five towns exceeded 22% during the same period – Banff, Dumbarton, Cumbernauld, East Kilbride, and Ardrossan. Dundee recorded the highest percentage of persistently vacant shops, at 11%. Anstruther showed the highest concentration of independent stores (86%), whereas Gretna exhibited the smallest (5%). In Edinburgh and Glasgow, leisure businesses claimed 39% of the total stock, and they dominated more than 30% of shops in Renfrew, St Andrews, Lochgelly, and Fort William. Aberdeen held the largest share of charity shops among cities, at 4.2%, and Penicukick, Midlothian, possessed the highest proportion for towns, at 8.9%. Matthew Hopkinson, LDC's director, stated, "This report highlights crucial tendencies while debunking widespread beliefs that struggling towns cannot thrive. Notably, approximately 40 vacant units in various Scottish towns have been unoccupied for over three years, suggesting decay and a significant impediment to flourishing locales and populations." The investigation examined the vitality of high streets in over 100 cities and towns in Scotland.

As the muscles holding the spine straight begin to relax, the spine naturally curves, causing slouching. This problem occurs more often than you think, and it is extremely common for people who have back problems in general to experience this problem. The most common symptoms include: The slouched posture can be caused by any number of factors including body mass index (BMI), weight gain or loss, muscle strength or weakness, low blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol levels, and certain medications such as gastric bypass surgery. Another cause of a slouchy posture has actually been identified, which means that it will not go away unless addressed from an early age. It's called "postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome" (POTS). Though POTS isn't life-threatening, if left untreated it can lead to serious health issues later on in life. If you suspect your posture may be affecting your sleep because you are slouched over all night long then getting some help might be necessary. If you are tired during the day but still find yourself falling asleep with a slumped forward position at night then having a change in attitude towards how you sleep could make a big difference. Here are four tips to consider when trying to solve this issue: Try sleeping on your side instead of your back, though it may take a little time to get used to. Have one pillow under each arm so that you don't have to try too hard to adjust your body to place itself across either side of the pillow. Put a blanket over both sides of the bed so that if you do need to decide where you want to sleep it would be easy enough to lean into the blankets without worrying about hurting your head due to length. Finally, put pillows between your knees - putting them slightly off center will allow you to raise your legs up higher while keeping them below your chest. Doing this should keep you from slumping sideways on your mattress. In order to maintain proper alignment and balance throughout your day, you must also make sure that your back is in good shape. A perfectly healthy spine helps to support the rest of your body, and can even prevent you from suffering debilitating conditions like arthritis down the road. Unfortunately, many people aren't aware of these benefits until their backs start acting up after years upon years of poor posture. Along with better mobility comes improved flexibility, and those who suffer from bad posture tend to spend far less time working out. In fact, studies show that just 15 minutes per week of yoga can affect your posture by improving your flexibility, mood, and overall physical fitness. Here is advice on what you can do now to improve your posture before you become vulnerable to diseases or injuries associated with bad posture.

In this paper, we proposed T-Net containing a small encoder-decoder inside the encoder-decoder structure (EDiED). T-Net overcomes the limitation that U-Net can only have a single set of the concatenate layer between encoder and decoder block. To be more precise, the U-Net symmetrically forms the concatenate layers, so the low-level feature of the encoder is connected to the latter part of the decoder, and the high-level feature is connected to the beginning of the decoder. T-Net arranges the pooling and up-sampling appropriately during the encoder process, and likewise during the decoding process so that feature-maps of various sizes are obtained in a single block. As a result, all features from the low-level to the high-level extracted from the encoder are delivered from the beginning of the decoder to predict a more accurate mask. We evaluated T-Net for the problem of segmenting three main vessels in coronary angiography images. The experiment consisted of a comparison of U-Net and T-Nets under the same conditions, and an optimized T-Net for the main vessel segmentation. As a result, T-Net recorded a Dice Similarity Coefficient score (DSC) of 0.815, 0.095 higher than that of U-Net, and the optimized T-Net recorded a DSC of 0.890 which was 0.170 higher than that of U-Net. In addition, we visualized the weight activation of the convolutional layer of T-Net and U-Net to show that T-Net actually predicts the mask from earlier decoders. Therefore, we expect that T-Net can be effectively applied to other similar medical image segmentation problems.

Lets Start with some basics of American Utilities companies and procedures. Television Television is broken up into several subcategories. You have Broadcast Networks and Cable Television Networks. Note: These are not analogous to Antenna vs. Cable Television. Broadcast Networks, are your standard American Broadcast Company (ABC), Columbia Broadcasting Service (CBS), FOX, and the National Broadcasting Company (NBC). These are your network television providers, or are most often associated with the local news networks. These 4 (sometimes more) are by law established as free to access networks that utilize primarily Antenna based transmissions. As these networks grow, or gain competition, they are required to remain free-to-broadcast, meaning you don't have to pay any monthly subscription fees or access fees to get things like local news. However, these are still public entities, and rely on advertising, viewership and other sales in order to continue operations, and have become very wealthy as a result. Cable networks, are not analogous with "Cable TV," though their roots do stem from the invention of Community Access Television, CATV. Cable networks first started appearing in local networks where CATV systems were designed with local content and programming. After the first CATV system was built, local municipalities and other organizations had lots of free space, not dependent on radio waves through the air, and so began to produce their own local content. These eventually started being shared and rebroadcasted as producers and things grew. Stations like CNN, FXX, USA, TNT, TBS etc. all started as local or regional stations, and did not fall under government jurisdiction like the Broadcast Networks above. CATV networks began charging for the services that the Community Antenna networks began providing, and also sharing information back and forth. As they got larger, small, regional companies like Alert Cable, Adelphia and Carolina Cable were bought up by multi-state conglomerates to become the likes of Comcast, Time Warner, Charter, Brighthouse and the other Major Service Providers (MSOs). Cable companies quickly stopped and diverged from producing content, and the two became separate. So, Cable Networks started to divide the space between Broadcasters and Cable networks, as you can only recieve Cable Channels by using a Cable Network. CATV eventually morphed into being known as a "Cable Provider" because of the transmission medium, similar to Satellite or Fiber Optics. Essentially though, Satellite and Fiber are still just CATV systems, just using different transmission means than before. Broadcasters on the other hand, are still able to be recieved with just an antenna with no subscription, and are limited to only a few local providers and your major 4-5 networks. Currently as of 2017, you have still ABC, CBS, FOX, NBC and The CW (formerly UPN and The WB before the merger). And before anyone says it no, PBS is not a broadcast network, they are more a local station that has many affiliates but is the only large scale non-profit and goverment funded educational television source. They are a public broadcaster, and considered Public Televison, but are not included in the Major Networks of most cities. CATV networks you do have to pay a subscription service for, and monthly base rates for just your local stations are around 15-40monthly depending on your location. That only covers your subscription fee and taxes for local stations, and doesn't include any of the aformentioned "cable networks." Currently the list includes in most areas some variation of the following: ABC, CBS, FOX, NBC, The CW PBS (3-5 stations depending on where you are) El-Ray C-Span other local government and local broadcast stations Your "Cable" channels start after that, and depending on the provider, can be cut up in a multitude of ways. This is where negotiations with the Production Companies come into play. Discovery Networks, Viacom and the like, the companis like mentioned before that split off and started producing content, well now they sell it to various cable and satellite companies for redistrobution instead of making and producing locally for one service provider. Your baseline cable packages vary in price, between 12-80month on top of the broadcast rate. Then you have your "Cable Premiums." These are going to be HBO (gotta have your thrones), Showtime (gotta have your Longmire), Cinemax (gotta have your.... skin-e-max), Epix, Starz, Encore and TMCSundance. These "Premiums" are basically your Adult Programming, and do not have to be purchased in addition with the Cable channels, but again you MUST subscibe to at least your broadcasters to have access. In recent years, HBO and Showtime have begun offering their own streaming services like HBO Go, and bypass the Provider level and become an Internet based provider like Netflix and Hulu, where now an Internet connection is required. If you get Antenna only stations, you will normally only get around 5-15 channels, depending on your local area. Some have more, and some have less, but the Majors will normally always be present, though quality is an issue. This quality issue was the direct reason leading to the development in CATV in the first place, to bring antennas down into the areas where radio was having difficulty reaching. Thus the name, Community Antenna Television, and not "CAble TeleVision" like it is colloquially known. Internet Internet, is of course a more modern phenomenon, spanning only the past 40 or so years. Originally what we now consider "Internet" was actually a government project for Universities and Government entities to communicate and share information privately using Dial-up modems and analog telephone networks. Up until around 1997, you only had one choice in service. Dial-upDSLT-1 through the local telephone company. Internet networks were completely dependent and intertwined with public telephone. Since by law, every house had to have access to 911 service, it made for a convenient way to distribute internet by means of additional, already accessible, twisted-pair copper wires. In 1997, CableLabs, in conjunction with around 30 other corporations, developed DOCSIS, the Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification. With this new development, CATV networks superseded their original intended function of being a television service, and were able to add Internet to their arsenal as well. Cable networks were able to provide services without using additional coax lines to the house unlike dialup, which required you use either phone or internet, or have separate numbers dedicated to each service. Cable Internet was able to utilize technology in the network to do TV and Internet at the same time without interference. Satellite providers like Hughes-net or Gen5, Fiber-optic Providers like Google or Verizon FiOS and even Mobile Data providers like Verizon or T-Mobile began their own versions of offerings, however still cannot compete to the scale and size of CATV or Telephone networks due to many years of both saturation and technological investment. Satellite has great download capability, but lacks in upload capability and is for very obvious reasons prohibitively expensive. Fiber-optic is amazing bi-directional capability but is prohibitively expensive and is running into alot of roadblocks due to federal regulation and local government push back to increasing construction costs and size. Finally Mobile data is extremely portable and scale-able, however is beginning to feel MASSIVE strains from over-utilization and restrictive bandwidth requirements that make it prohibitively expensive as well, although has been fairly well adapted in comparison to the Fiber and Satellite. Internet Services generally range between 10-500month or more, depending on your requirement, limitations of provider, service tier choice and any overages you may see based on usage. The most expensive of these, tend to be Mobile Data and Satallite, due to restrictive and often used "overage fees" can easily be in the 200mo range. CATV and Fiber options tend to be less expensive, often operating between 15-100mo depending on what bandwidth size you request. Dialup is fairly obselete in urban areas but is still widely used in rural areas, and often now is 100mo or more due to it's aging obselecence but required nature. Streaming Services Ahh.... the raging bastard-child between Television and Internet services. Services like Netflix and Hulu are popping up left and right, trying to craft out a new market for themselves and stay relevant currently. All kidding and jokes aside, Internet based streaming is a relatively new phenomenon of course, and is still evolving and disrupting the landscape in which we consume service. With service tiers between 5mo and as high as an insane 50mo, each provider is crafting it's own library of unique original content, as well as historical content. None of these services is considered a "public option" as they do not rebroadcast local news affiliates and cannot be held to any standards but they are convienent for those who are looking for a more a-la-carte option for their viewing pleasure.
