Consider the problem of sampling sequentially from a finite number of N 2 populations, specified by random variables X I k, I 1, ..., N, and k 1, 2, ...; where n is some integer. The functions f1 0...,fN are continuous, i.e., they do not have an expiration time either stored in their form or as a real-valued function on n, but rather behave like discrete functions (see point 5). Furthermore, to compute the values for each population we must also know how many samples we can use per sample: if it is zero then we start with the first one, otherwise we begin with the last one. For example, if two samples are taken at different times, we always choose a sample at least twice equal in size to the number of samples taken together. In this case we only need to count the true samples in each population when making a choice about which sample fits best into our model. But what happens if a single sample cannot be chosen? We could consider stopping all calculations after one sample was selected since there will be no more samples available until that sample gets picked up. The same procedure would apply here except that instead of waiting for all samples to get collected before moving forward, then using them to select among multiple choices, we continue picking out samples based upon their uniqueness (the probability density function) and their "luckiness" (their power). If this method of selecting randomly works well for small numbers of cases, we may want to expand its scope so that we specify how many samples are needed per case. However, this strategy becomes very complex when the number of cases increases rapidly. It turns out that once we achieve the maximum size of our population, we should stop counting samples altogether unless one were to pick out those species that are larger than the others. This holds true even though we might want to proceed onward via other selection methods. The way we solve this dilemma is to perform a search or clustering algorithm involving a statistical technique such as nonparametric statistics [34]. A first step involves identifying the most logical clusters to group, as shown in Fig. 3. Next, we ask the user to assign probabilities to each cluster according to a set of predefined criteria, hopefully under constraints sufficient to ensure that we select the closest possible cluster to whatever design objective we intend to reach. It should be apparent that the inference will tend towards being biased toward the nearest cluster, because it is easier to determine whether something belongs to a given cluster compared to its neighbors. We typically add additional parameters, usually latent variables, to position models closer to some desired state; these parameters provide information about the causal relationships between factors and allow us to make better predictions about future states. As discussed earlier in this paper, these latent variables include latent prognostic traits such as likelihood that animals in the same population will exhibit certain characteristics during life: for example, individual cats having an identical disposition will likely live in the same area, breed, and not mate together. Various approaches employing latent variables andor cluster analysis techniques can be used to obtain meaningful conclusions regarding natural systems. One common approach requires that a user define a set of attributes associated with a variable that represent its characteristic trait and ask him or her to rate that attribute's significance relative to another such value (for instance, "strongly agree" means that the characteristic has a relatively high effect on the outcome while "disagree" means that the characteristic has a relatively low influence on the outcome). This approach allows users to estimate the strength of the association between a factor and a feature in a given data set using exactly the same set of parameters as was employed in finding the original relationship between the factor and the feature. However, another alternative based on latent variables is to base recurrent decision trees [35] on aggregate estimates of predicted outcomes obtained from a sample of data as described above. Using this technique, the user defines a new set of predefined attributes called "features," assigns probabilities to each of these features independently, and asks for further attribute values assigned to each of these features. These feature weights are structured around a set of predictors defined by the attributes themselves; the general idea is to weight some attributes higher more significant than others. Experiments show that statistically robust regression results, including strong correlations, are achieved through such classification algorithms. Moreover, modeling behavior of any animal inevitably introduces error depending solely on the representation taken. To overcome this drawback, a more sophisticated type of approach is proposed in [36], termed "model predictive control." That is, instead of asking the user to give his own preferences for the number of traits he wishes to account for, the system itself decides the values that the user should assign to each element of the model by incorporating various prediction algorithms designed to monitor the current state of affairs using currently available data sets. While this approach offers statistical stability due to its use of reinforcement learning, we note that there still remains a risk that the system may fail to properly handle uncertainty or drift in the environment, especially with respect to unknown situations. Assumptions are necessary for denoising techniques concerning the signal and the disturbance. Most denoising techniques presuppose awareness of the noise intensity, yet this information might be unavailable in real-world scenarios. Here, we postulate that the signal's representation in a specific dictionary has a heavier tail distribution compared to the noise. We demonstrate how this assumption generates an independent-of-noise-level stopping criterion for greedy pursuit algorithms. Motivated by the effectiveness of ensemble methods in machine learning, we suggest a methodology to minimize the variance of greedy estimates through averaging pursuits derived from randomly selected dictionaries. Your query is essentially about the distinction between Einstein's mass-energy equivalence formula (E=mc²) and the energy content of food, represented in calories. Although both involve energy, they serve unique purposes. The former calculates the energy contained in a mass as it approaches the speed of light, while the latter quantifies the energy obtainable from food through metabolic processes.

The energy content of food, such as pasta or lettuce, varies significantly due to differences in their compositions. For instance, pasta contains high levels of carbohydrates, which our bodies can efficiently convert into energy. On the other hand, lettuce has fewer calories since our bodies find it harder to break down its cellular structure.

It is essential to recognize that not all consumed food is transformed into usable energy. Instead, some parts remain undigested and exit the body as waste. The energy that does enter our system comes from the breakdown of chemical bonds within food molecules. Thus, the energy derived from food depends on the specific composition of the food being consumed.

In essence, E=mc² is an equation describing the relationship between mass and energy, whereas food calories represent the energy our bodies can extract from food through metabolism.

Intelligent gadgets, storage, and dispersed technologies hold significant promise for enhancing network infrastructure's efficiency and integrating renewable energy sources. Decentralized management of these technologies addresses numerous scalability and privacy issues, yet typically necessitates a convex problem foundation to ensure attainment of an overall optimal solution. Given the non-convex characteristics of AC power flows and the often discrete choices required for handling household appliances, there has been skepticism about employing distributed approaches in practical contexts. This research builds upon previous studies applying the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to address the complex dynamic optimal power flow (D-OPF) problem. By incorporating more authentic line and load simulations and implementing a two-staged strategy for addressing discrete choices and uncertainties, our findings from a suburban microgrid reveal near-optimal outcomes with acceptable computational speed for recursive control. This study moves us closer to making distributed control of smart-grid innovations a viable reality.

" Yes, I can hear you, " came a soft voice much like my own. I looked around but found no one there. I brushed it off as hearing things. But as I took a few more steps I heard it again. nbsp; " I said I can hear you. " Came the voice, louder this time, but still retaining it's gentle nature. I looked around once more. There was no one near me. The house was empty. I spoke into my own head, feeling slightly silly as I did. nbsp; " Hi? " I thought. I wondered what could be causing this? Had I finally gone off the deep end or was I about to find out I had an new allergy I never even knew about. nbsp; " Hi, " replied the voice a few moments later. I couldn't deny it, it was coming from my head. I shook a little at the thought. nbsp; " Who are you? " I asked, before instantly feeling silly. Why I am asking myself who I am? nbsp; " I don't know, " the voice responded. I paused for a few moments, unsure of my next move. How do you react when you are talking to yourself but don't seem to know the answers to the questions you are posing? nbsp; " Well this has never happened before, " I thought to myself, only to be interrupted by the voice once more. nbsp; " Well I haven't been around before. I just started. " It replied. I was confused, to talk to yourself is one thing, but to interrupt yourself during the conversation is a whole new level of madness. After a few moments of silence, the voice spoke up again. nbsp; " I'm a part! " It exclaimed. It's voice showing a solid emotion for the first time since it started talking. nbsp; " A part? " I asked, slightly confused by what it meant and slightly distracted by trying to remember the number of my doctor. nbsp; " Remember? We learned about it in psychology class, " continued the voice, talking over my attempts to find the number. I thought about it for a moment and suddenly it flooded back into my head, like it was almost fresh. The boring classes on Richard Schwartz and his idea that people were made up of little bits. My train of thought was cut off by the voice speaking once more. nbsp; " But if I am a part, what part am I? " It mused, leaving me unsure if it was asking a rhetorical question or not. " Could I be an exile? Running away from something we didn't like? " It rambled. I found myself trying not to think so as not to interrupt. nbsp; " No, I don't feel like an exile, anyhow exiles don't just walk back in. That never happens in any story, apart from that game we played that time. But that is because Alice forgot she was playing an exile. " It finished. It was weird hearing this new voice talking about memories from years ago. But as it did, I felt the memory come to the forefront of my mind, like I was remembering it myself. I smiled at the memory, I had forgotten those silly games we used to play. I had forgotten Alice, work had gotten on top of me since I moved and I never found the time to call her. nbsp; " Well, I doubt I can be a firefighter. I never really had the looks for it, " the voice started again. " I mean being a firefighter suggests I am good in a crisis. But, I would think a part that was good in a crisis wouldn't pop up and scare you half to death. " nbsp; " You didn't. Don't worry. " I thought, trying to reassure whatever this voice was. nbsp; " I can hear your thoughts you know. I heard you mentally rehearsing the call to the doctor. " The voice replied. I shuffled awkwardly, realizing my thoughts about it had not been dramatically positive. " It's okay, I would do the same if I was in your position. Because I am you, so I can't pretend like I would think differently. " It said, a slight touch of humour coming into it's voice. I smiled and nodded. nbsp; " Well I can't think what part you are, " I thought. nbsp; " Maybe we don't need to know yet? Maybe I just popped out at random? " The part replied. I nodded to myself and the self inside myself. It had a point, I mean psychology was never exact. I smiled, I remembered my professor saying that. I smiled some more as I remembered another friend dropping psych the second they could, they couldn't handle the non-exact sciences. nbsp; " Yeah. That could be it. " nbsp; " Well then. I guess I should follow the model right? " It said. And I quickly remembered the model. I hadn't thought about it for years, but it felt like yesterday. I could almost smell the classroom, the memory was that fresh. nbsp; " Become part of the whole again, " I recited, " Until reality and your role clash once more. " I sat down and smiled as I remembered a few more of my school buddies. nbsp; " That is exactly it. " replied the voice. " So I guess I'll be seeing you? Or hearing you at least. " It said. I laughed a little and nodded. nbsp; " See you around, " I thought. I sat there in silence for a little bit. My head quiet once more. I got up from the chair and smiled, still basking in the glow of the memories that had resurfaced. I moved to my computer, I had a few people I needed to catch up with.

The ongoing commercial deployment of millimeter wave systems brings into focus a number of practical issues in form factor user equipment (UE) design. With wavelengths becoming smaller, antenna gain patterns becoming directional, and link budgets critically dependent on beamforming, it becomes imperative to use a number of antenna modules at different locations of the UE for good performance. While more antennasmodules can enhance beamforming array gains, it comes with the tradeoff of higher component cost, power consumption of the associated radio frequency circuitry, and a beam management overhead in learning the appropriate beam weights. Thus, the goal of a good UE design is to provide robust spherical coverage corresponding to good array gains over the entire sphere around the UE with a low beam management overhead, complexity, and cost. The scope of this paper is to study the implications of two popular commercial millimeter wave UE designs (a face and an edge design) on spherical coverage. We show that analog beam codebooks can result in good performance for both the designs, and the edge design provides a better tradeoff in terms of robust performance (with hand blockage), beam management overhead, implementation complexity from an antenna placement standpoint and cost.

Video Object Segmentation (VOS) is an active research area of the visual domain. One of its fundamental sub-tasks is semi-supervised one-shot learning: given only the segmentation mask for the first image and the remaining parts of the video, a VOS mode is used to make it possible to identify the segments that are missing from the original scene. Using this technique, students can see which part of the body has been copied in the previous scene. However, while some aspects of learning are still being studied, there are several methods available to overcome the problems associated with such a high level immersion experience. One method involves the use of techniques known as "virtual objects"; these are virtual images of previously-missing or expanded portions of the image. This technology relies on the fact that if all of the portions of the scene have been referenced by camera movement, then the video will be rendered by using a captured portion of the computer animation. However, these techniques require expert decision making to accomplish their task. Thus, there exists a need for a system that allows for a student to re-enact the scene and the scene itself in real time without having to select footage from the previous scene.

The deluge of date rate in today's networks imposes a cost burden on the backhaul network design. Developing cost efficient backhaul solutions becomes an exciting, yet challenging, problem. Traditional technologies for backhaul networks include either radio-frequency backhauls (RF) or optical fibers (OF). While RF is a cost-effective solution as compared to OF, it supports lower data rate requirements. Another promising backhaul solution is the free-space optics (FSO) as it offers both a high data rate and a relatively low cost. FSO, however, is sensitive to nature conditions, e.g., rain, fog, line-of-sight. This paper combines both RF and FSO advantages and proposes a hybrid RFFSO backhaul solution. It considers the problem of minimizing the cost of the backhaul network by choosing either OF or hybrid RFFSO backhaul links between the base-stations (BS) so as to satisfy data rate, connectivity, and reliability constraints. It shows that under a specified realistic assumption about the cost of OF and hybrid RFFSO links, the problem is equivalent to a maximum weight clique problem, which can be solved with moderate complexity. Simulation results show that the proposed solution shows a close-to-optimal performance, especially for practical prices of the hybrid RFFSO links.

More recently, women's football soared in popularity after the nation's female team won the World Cup in 2011 and Olympic Games silver in 2012. Now rugby union is looking for a similar breakthrough into the national consciousness, when its World Cup is hosted by Japan in 2019. With the Olympic Games being held in Tokyo a year afterwards, the end of the decade is shaping up to be a major sporting time for Japan. "These two events coming together means the Japanese citizens' interest in sport has already gone up, and should increase rapidly nearer the events," Koji Tokumasu, general manager of the Japan 2019 Rugby World Cup Organising Committee, tells BBC News. He was recently in the UK for his nation's friendlies against Scotland and Gloucester, where Japan played with tenacity but lost both matches. Japan - known as the Cherry Blossoms or Brave Blossoms - are traditionally the strongest rugby union power in Asia. But Mr Tokumasu says in Japan, where baseball is the most popular sport and football second, rugby union lags behind in about 10th spot. "This is something we have to work on over the next six years," he says. "We want to approach our existing fans - we do already have some rugby fans in Japan, and activate them to spread the World Cup message." He says this hardcore fan-base can use digital media to publicise the rugby experience and the excitement surrounding the sport, including the thrill of match day. They will also be able to explain the intricacies of the sport, including the scoring system. "We want to raise interest and passion in the sport by bringing quality teams like New Zealand to our fans, who can then pass on the message to their family, friends and colleagues," says Mr Tokumasu. When Japan hosted world champions the All Blacks earlier in November, the 25,000 tickets were sold out after half an hour. The host nation, not surprisingly, lost that encounter, but there has been playing success this year. Japan won this year's HSBC Asian Five Nations tournament, and also beat a Wales second string team in the summer. That victory was their first win over a major rugby nation in eight decades of trying. To show it was no fluke, they have also beaten the US and Canada this year. In addition, this month Japan beat Russia, thrashed Spain, and also won the 2013 HSBC Asian Rugby Sevens. The first stage of 2019 preparation is already under way, with the release of the criteria for would-be World Cup host cities and stadiums. Organisers want to select between 10 and 12 match venues before March 2015, for the 48-game tournament. "The reason we have chosen that date is because we want the successful host venues to then be able to attend that year's World Cup in England to see and experience how the event is staged," says Mr Tokumasu. "At present we are visiting cities and telling them how exciting hosting the 2019 World Cup can be for them." In Tokyo, a showpiece 80,000-capacity Olympic Stadium is being built in time for the 2019 rugby event, and in other match venue centres local government will pay for stadiums. In many cities stadiums have remained underused since the 2002 World Cup. Mr Tokumasu says: "We would like it if we could use some of the those stadiums, but we cannot force those cities to take part - they have to express an interest." As well as increasing awareness, another major pre-2019 aim is to increase playing participation. "This is a major aim, and our government supports this, they think that sport is good for health," he says. "We are going to take rugby into primary schools, first going into 5,000 schools, and by 2019 hoping to have spread the word in all 22,000 primary schools. "Boys and girls can learn together and we will be introducing tag [touch] rugby, so that teachers won't be worried about children getting hurt. So by 2019 a lot of young people will know all about rugby." That work among the young should widen the base of the next generation of rugby players in a country where 95 of participants are university graduates. Rugby playing is also very intertwined at present with the top end of the corporate workplace, In the premier domestic competition, the Top League, the clubs are owned by large Japanese corporations such as Toshiba or Panasonic, and when a player's career comes to an end, they then usually take up a management role with the parent company. The government also wants to see people taking part as event volunteers, following a successful programme at the 2002 global football event, and ahead of Tokyo 2020. But he stresses again that the 2019 organisers want to bring rugby to a wider audience. "In Japan people tend to stay at home to watch the very best of global or national sports on TV or the internet, rather than actually attending live events - we want to overcome this and attract people to rugby games," he says. "We are going to produce more opportunities for people to attend a match - we really want to make the best use of the next six years "

There is experimental evidence that supports the concept that mitosis-specific phosphorylation of amyloid precursor protein (APP) at threonine 668 (T668) influences its processing and association with centrosomes. Studies have shown that phosphorylation of APP at T668 occurs during mitosis and is highly restricted to dividing cells. This phosphorylation event seems to play a role in the observed altered processing of APP and generation of amyloid-beta (A) peptides, which are involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease. Phosphorylated APP at T668 (pT668-APP) has been found to accumulate in centrosomes during mitosis. Centrosomes play a key role in cell division, as they are involved in the formation of mitotic spindles that ensure proper chromosome segregation. The localization of pT668-APP at centrosomes suggests that it may participate in the regulation of cell division. Moreover, it has been reported that the altered processing of APP, associated with the generation of A peptides, is regulated by cell cycle-dependent kinases that control the phosphorylation of APP at T668. Inhibition of these kinases affects the generation of A, highlighting the importance of this phosphorylation event in APP processing. Overall, APP phosphorylation at T668 during mitosis may affect its processing and lead to its association with centrosomes. Further research is needed to fully understand the relevance of this phosphorylation event, its role in cell cycle regulation, and implications for neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's.

ABC's flagship show, The Mary Tyler Moore Show (which is unique for having been created by an African American woman on a major broadcast network), ran from , and helped establish the network's image as a vital voice for social justice issues during the 1960s. It also drew hundreds of thousands of fans who took to the streets in protest when it ended. In 1972, ABC aired its first half hour drama series The New Adventures of Old Christine starring Jane Fonda, which lasted three seasons and won two Emmys - a record at the time for a primetime scripted series. When the career of Mary Richards finally ended, she would be succeeded by another black actress: Edie Falco. In 1966, ABC signed actor Don Knotts as host of ABC's game show, Life Goes On; he hosted the program for five years before being replaced by Jack Paar beginning in 1968. In 1967, ABC acquired the rights to the popular children's book series Will Rogers' America featuring the adventures of Kipling's Golden Compass hero Tom Sawyer and his sidekick Buckaroo Banzai. This led to numerous new shows based on books written by Kipling or Williams. During the 1960s, ABC produced several successful sitcoms including The Jeffersons, The Brady Bunch, Saturday Night Live and Cheers, each of them drawing huge audiences and earning critical acclaim on their respective premieres, but ultimately failed to sufficiently compete against the success of NBC and CBS' prime time lineup. ABC owned the rights to The Walt Disney Company's animated series Sideways and other product lines, but these were mostly produced by Hanna-Barbera Productions, who had already established themselves as a powerhouse company producing cartoon productions for syndication. Some of ABC's most notable animation programs include Rowan Martin's Laugh-In, The Vikings, Rugrats, The Jetsons, Space Ghost Coast To Coast, Hee Haw!, Beakman's World, Entourage, McHale's Navy, The New Adventures of Old Christine, and Barney Miller. Twin pregnancies yielding a single tetra-zygotic individual occur when a woman carrying two fertilized eggs (ova) by two different partners' sperm fusionally merge into one embryo prior to or during the blastocyst stage. This merging results in an individual possessing genetic material from all four gametes - one sperm from each partner and one egg from each woman. While this phenomenon is extremely rare in humans, undetected instances might exist if an individual undergoes genetic testing. In such cases, only some cells may display DNA from one twin while others carry the DNA of the second twin.

A milder form of chimerism is microchimerism, characterized by the presence of cells containing foreign DNA from another individual. For instance, children often inherit cells from their mothers due to placental transfer during fetal development. Similarly, marmosets, which give birth as fraternal twins, typically exhibit cellular exchange through shared blood supplies during development, leading to organ tissue, blood cells, or even gametes bearing the DNA of their co-twins.

Identifying cases of chimera involving fused identical twins poses significant challenges, making extensive research on this subject limited primarily to fraternal twins due to their distinguishable genetic makeup.

As we walked in, three or four people were waiting around a table - but which one, I wondered, was the father of Bitcoin? Then I realised that one man was staring intensely at a very chunky laptop - this was Dr Craig Wright. He carried on working, apparently unaware that we had entered the room. Once we had been introduced he gradually warmed up - especially when it came to performing the demonstration that showed that he did have access to the cryptographic keys used by Satoshi when he made the first Bitcoin transaction in 2009. We had arrived wondering just how convincing a case would be made that the almost mythical creator of Bitcoin was at last stepping out of the shadows. What we saw seemed impressive - though it would need a far higher level of expertise than we possess to be certain. But Jon Matonis, a senior figure in the Bitcoin world, was in the room watching, having had his own demonstration some time before. And the news that Gavin Andresen, chief scientist at the Bitcoin Foundation, was also convinced provided more reassurance. Now Craig Wright has published his evidence on his blog, it will be examined in minute detail for any chink in his case. But put aside the question of whether you believe him or not - and he told me he didn't care either way - there were still plenty of questions we wanted to put to the fascinating, if somewhat prickly Dr Wright. Why keep his secret so long? Why come out now? What about that run-in with the Australian tax authorities? And is he fabulously rich, with a huge stock of Bitcoin? At our first meeting - without a television camera - we roamed freely over all sorts of territory. We learned that he ran a substantial business in London, employing quite a few people here in what seemed to be some kind of Bitcoin trading and consultancy operation. We challenged him about that tax investigation - he conceded that there was what he called an "audit" underway in Australia but insisted that this was mainly due to the tax authorities there not really understanding Bitcoin. We asked where the pseudonym had come from - he mentioned a 17th century libertarian philosopher called Nakamoto but said he'd keep the Satoshi bit to himself. He talked of the French writer and philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre, whose statement refusing the Nobel Prize is used in the Satoshi-signed file given as evidence in the blog published today. His politics were very far from the "lefty" Sartre, he explained, but like him he did not want his identity to be defined by one thing - he refused to be Craig "Satoshi" just as Sartre did not want to be Jean-Paul Nobel. What he wouldn't say is how many Bitcoins he has - "that would be telling" - though he indicated that he would not be spending any of them in a hurry. He told us that he had a "nice big house and a nice fast car" in London, went on holidays to Paris, and didn't feel the need to acquire vast riches. The second time we met, to film a television interview, the mood changed. It was immediately clear that he hated the whole process, refusing to move from behind his laptop to a more spacious room where the shot would have been much better. At first, he insisted that he would give an answer to just one question - why he had decided to go public after all these years. Once we started filming he opened up a little, but mainly because he wanted to express his anger at, as he sees it, being forced into the public eye. "I don't want money, I don't want fame, I don't want adoration, I just want to be left alone," he said with some venom. He accused journalists of threatening to make up stories about him if he did not cooperate and said lies had been told that would affect his family and his staff. It seems his main grievance surrounds the stories that spread last December when he was first identified as a potential Satoshi, then dismissed by some as a hoaxer. At that time, questions were asked about his academic and business career, and there were some who said he just did not have the intellectual capacity to be the man behind Bitcoin. Throughout the demonstrations he showed us he kept on stressing the complexity of the process - "obviously everyone said I have no idea about this stuff so I'm going to do it in the most convoluted way possible." We were then supplied with a series of documents providing evidence that Dr Craig Stephen Wright was a Master of Statistics, IT Management, and Law, and a long list of peer-reviewed articles. Now he says he intends to continue his research into improving the technology behind Bitcoin, and plans to publish several papers over the coming months. With the community around the currency in some turmoil right now over how it develops, you might think that Craig Wright could provide some leadership. After all, he could be said to be to Bitcoin what Tim Berners-Lee is to the web. But he bridled at my suggestion that he could be a figurehead for the currency, making clear that this was the first and last television interview he would do. Having emerged from the shadows, Craig Satoshi Wright now wants to return to them as quickly as possible.

The German privacy regulator, the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information, has ordered Facebook to stop collecting and storing data from German users of its messaging app WhatsApp. Facebook acquired the popular messaging app in 2014 and has since been using the service to collect and store user data for advertising purposes. However, the German regulator has now ruled that this practice is a breach of EU data protection laws. The ruling was announced after a lengthy investigation by the regulator into whether Facebook was violating data protection laws with its collection of user data. The regulator concluded that Facebook was not adequately informing users about how their data was being collected and used, nor did they provide them with sufficient means to give their consent. The regulator has now ordered Facebook to delete all existing user data and to stop collecting any further data from German users. They have also demanded that Facebook provide more transparency on how it collects, stores and uses user data. Facebook has said it will comply with the ruling and has stated it will take steps to ensure it adheres to data protection laws across Europe. This ruling comes as a further blow to Facebook following multiple scandals over the past year concerning the misuse of user data. It remains to be seen if other European regulators will follow Germany's lead and impose similar restrictions on Facebook's data collection practices.

Question-answering (QA) is certainly the best known and probably also one of the most complex problem within Natural Language Processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence (AI). Since the complete solution to QA is an unreachable goal, many researchers have investigated different approaches for its subtasks. In particular, supervised learning methods such as statistical machine translation [Durrani et al., 2006], neural network architectures [Lee et al., 2005b] or case-based reasoning [Klementiev and Roth, 2012; Simoes et al., 2015a] are widely used in order to produce a system that can be trained from available annotated data. In this work we propose an informative approach for Question Answering based on two main ideas: 1) using knowledge about possible answers provided by users for querying purposes when training systems, 2) combining multiple sources of information including user feedback for improving performance. We apply our model to three well-known datasets. The experimental results show improved accuracy compared with state-of-the-art algorithms without relying on external resources like web search engines. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 overviews related works. Sections 3, 4 and 5 describe the proposed framework, dataset preparation and experiments performed, respectively. Finally, conclusions are drawn in Section 6 along with future research directions. Related Works Traditional models for text classification divide the set of documents into disjoint categories according to predefined rules. Over time, however, better performing techniques emerged since they were able to learn the features defining each category through large amounts of labeled examples [Shenker et al., 2008]. This paradigm has been applied successfully to various areas such as Spotlight Search [Agarwal et al., 2007 ], sentiment analysis [Baroni and Lenci, 2002], authorship identification [Cui et al., 2011] and question answering [Liu and Barzilay, 2015]. Supervised Learning Methods These methodologies use classifiers whose parameters are optimized by minimizing the error between predicted label values and ground-truth labels [Geman and Geman, 1984]. They usually assume some form of distributional hypothesis and exploit linguistic properties to define features [Rosenfeld et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2003]. Among these last ones, named entity recognition (NER), which aims at identifying words denoting persons, locations, organizations etc., is particularly relevant for QA tasks in languages where proper names occur frequently. As shown by Liu [2015], NER is one of the major factors affecting answer quality in automatic QA systems. Unsupervised Methods Non-supervised clustering methods aim at grouping similar instances together while allowing them to belong to distinct clusters. Many distinct unsupervised learning paradigms exist but agglomerative hierarchical clustering seems promising for task-specific applications [Vlachos et al., 1991; Jain and Dubey, 2004; Chen and Lin, 2007; Blitzer et al., 2008; Karypis et al., 1997; Haghighi and Kleinberg, 2004]. However, cluster discovery remains challenging due to noise inherent to free-text document representation, mostly caused by homonyms, synonymy, spelling mistakes, repetitions etc. To overcome this issue, several heuristics have been devised to filter out noisy units following diverse criteria e.g. edit distance [Manning et al., 2003a [Manning et al.,,b, 2009 Widdows et al., 2005; Coecke and Manning, 2009; Suardari et al., 2010]. These methods are easily integrated into existing frameworks for unsupervised learning such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). Recently, deep learning became quite popular in computer vision, speech processing and natural language understanding because it allows designing more expressive models than traditional methods [Lin et al., 2014; LeCun et al., 1998 ]. For example, convolutional networks allow capturing local patterns rather than global characteristics, leading to higher generalization capacity [Lin et al., 2014]. On another hand, recurrent attention mechanisms provide end-to-end trainability thanks to multi-layered structures that capture sequential dependencies among elements [Huang et al., 2016; Luong et al., 2015; Vaswani et al., 2017]. Combining Multiple Sources of Information Several studies showed how incorporating additional knowledge sources improves performances in linguistic tasks both in monolingual [Mehmood and Dagan, 2011; Snir and Schiele, 2010; Caffarel et al., 2009; Maezawa et al., 2002; Blei and Lafferty, 2006; Ng et al., 2003; McCallum et al., 2000] and cross-lingual scenarios [Klein et al., 2011; Zoph and Knight, 2001; Fung et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012; Headden and Callan, 2013]. Although allance approaches are not suitable for every application domain, they seem particularly well suited for combination problems in QA settings, given their flexibility and ability to leverage complementary forms of information. For example, Zhang et al. [2012] combine word embeddings derived from Wikipedia corpora and lexical similarity calculated from WordNet to improve query expansion for fast retrieval methods. Some berries have adaptations that select for preferential eaters. For instance, many of the fruits we consider'hot peppers' or chili peppers, are primarily dispersed by birds. Where a large mammal may eat the fruit, it will often eat it from a standing position, often at a higher level than the other animals. A bird, on the other hand, will fly to the fruit and eat it while airborne, or drop it from a high perch. This requires that the bird have strong talons and can fly, and also that the fruit be large enough to sustain this activity. Most berries are therefore dispersed by birds. Other species of fruit are dispersed by rodents, which may also have a preference for certain species of berries. The fruits of many plant species have specialized or modified structures to aid in dispersal. One example is the orange-red fruit of the passionfruit. The fruit is large and has numerous seeds. It is also very fleshy and somewhat succulent. Birds that eat the fruit are often severely dehydrated. As a result, they are unable to transport the fruit to the nest, and it usually perishes in the bird's crop. In addition, the bird must eat the fruit from a standing position, which is unlikely for most birds. In this case, the fruit has evolved a structure that prevents the bird from being able to eat it while standing, and is so fleshy and succulent that the bird cannot transport it to the nest. It has evolved a structure that is nearly inedible by birds. Large volumes of daily-produced digital videos generate extensive media repositories. To make these data readily searchable, efficient methods are required. This paper introduces a new approach for identifying media genres and programs through acoustic features, textual features, or their combination, in conjunction with existing metadata. The integration of metadata, including broadcast times, significantly enhances performance. By employing Latent Dirichlet Allocation, we model both acoustics and text, producing consistent media recording representations suitable for Support Vector Machines classification. Results from experiments on over 1200 hours of BBC TV broadcasts demonstrate genre and show identification accuracies of 98.6% and 85.7%, respectively, when utilizing a blend of acoustic, textual features, and metadata.

Acid-base reactions are ubiquitous in nature. Understanding their mechanisms is crucial in many fields, from biochemistry to industrial catalysis. Unfortunately, experiments only give limited information without much insight into the molecular behaviour. Atomistic simulations could complement experiments and shed precious light on microscopic mechanisms. The large free energy barriers connected to proton dissociation however make the use of enhanced sampling methods mandatory. Here we perform an ab initio molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and enhance sampling with the help of methadynamics. This has been made possible by the introduction of novel descriptors or collective variables (CVs) that are based on a conceptually new outlook on acid-base equilibria. We test successfully our approach on three different aqueous solutions of acetic acid, ammonia, and bicarbonate. These are representative of acid, basic, and amphoteric behaviour.

The main response of the immune system to tumors is to destroy the abnormal cells using killer T cells, sometimes with the assistance of helper T cells. Tumor antigens are presented by cells such as macrophages, which are phagocytic cells that engulf and digest cellular debris and pathogens. When activated, T cells recognize a processed form of the tumor antigen, which is presented to them by an antigen-presenting cell (APC). This causes the T cells to proliferate and produce cytokines such as IFN- and TNF, as well as cell surface molecules that enable them to kill tumor cells. For example, CD8 T cells will produce perforin and granzymes, which are used to kill tumor cells. In addition to T cells, Natural Killer (NK) cells are also involved in the destruction of tumor cells. NK cells are innate immune cells that are stimulated to kill tumor cells in a manner that is similar to CD8 T cells. However, in most cases, the tumor is not destroyed by the immune system. There are several possible explanations for this: Antigen presentation: The tumor may not be recognised as foreign. Evasion: The tumor may evade the immune system by a variety of mechanisms including suppression of immune cells, antigen loss and the ability to avoid the immune system. Immunosuppression: The immune system may be suppressed, for example, by the tumor. Defective immune system: The immune system may be defective. Failure of immune response: The immune system may fail to respond. The normal immune response to tumors is discussed in more detail in the immune system, cancer and immunotherapy notes. A generation skipping tax may apply if grandparents bequeath funds to their grandchildren. If the inherited funds were previously housed in a tax-deferred account like an IRA, neither the parents nor the heir were initially taxed on it. Taxes and penalties would be due when the deceased IRA is distributed, with the beneficiary making mandatory withdrawals at age 70, based on their life expectancy. This allows the remaining balance to keep growing tax-free, potentially surpassing the annual withdrawal amount. Alternatively, the account could be liquidated immediately, resulting in significant tax liabilities. Generally, opting for gradual distributions is more advantageous; however, seeking advice from a financial consultant is advisable.

The mountain range running the length of the east coast (the Great Dividing Range) causes moist air that's coming off the ocean to rise (called orographic uplift), when it rises it cools, condenses, and comes down as rain, allowing forests to exist. At least to the seaward side of that range. The west of the range, even tho it's still in the east of Australia, is in a rain shadow, and get very little rain also. The west coast has no such mountain range, the air coming in from the ocean to the west doesn't have that lift so misses out on the rain. There's also associated temperature, geology and soil differences that prevent forests from occuring in the west, but that's it in a nutshell.,Essentially, because there is a mountain range (well..."mountain" by Australian standards) running along the entire length of the east coast. This causes rain to fall on the coastal side of the mountain range, and this provides enough to support a forest-type environment in places. In the west, there's virtually no mountain range. There IS the Darling Scarp that promotes rainfall in the south-western 'corner' of Australia, which is where the city of Perth and the vast majority of Western Australia's population lives. There are in fact some small areas of forest in this small south-western corner that are well-watered. Parts of western and north-western Australia DO get some heavy rainfall, but it's the seasonal monsoon. So it's extremely heavy rain for a couple of months and then parched dry for the rest of the year, not really conducive to the sustainable growth of forests.

It was..... painful. But that wasn't my job or my concern. I wanted to tell the story of soldiers, and race didn't matter. "No. None of that horseshit. You as people. I'll be gentle too. Fair enough?" They nodded in agreement. "So," flipping the camera back on, "can you tell me why you joined up with the volunteers to start with?" The woman actually smiled a bit, pushing the worst of the mud off her body armor. "That's easy. They said'the bad guys are coming for your world, we need help.' Went straight to a recruiting station and signed up. This world's my home, figure I owe it at least that much." Nodding, I turned toward the man, who shrugged and tried to look sheepish. "She says it better than me. I was military before, though, so I knew they needed bodies. Signed up that day, haven't been home since." "I see - so how did you end up with the legendary Red Vipers, a special forces regiment." Scratching his chin and ignoring the blood, he shrugged again. "Honestly, I don't know. I told them, I'm military, I want to be near the front lines, where can I do the most help? They looked up my records and said'we want you to help with the Vipers.' I used to fight the Vipers, so I knew who he meant." "I just said put me up front," the woman offered, "put me up front and let me protect my neighbors. I won't complain about anything, just give me a shot. Next thing I know, I'm meeting this tall drink of water who tells me I better ask for help when I need it, and I better get it when I ask." Nodding, I flipped the camera to face me. "The Red Vipers have been at the front of many battles, despite being on the flanks and behind enemy lines. They were the first to respond to this new incursion just last month, even though they've been fighting for 7 years straight. Tell me, how do the Vipers you work with look?" "Scary," the woman offered calmly, "they see a target, they go for it, they make it dead, and they get everyone out. Sure, we get a few wounds, but we live." "Yeah," the man agreed, "best of the best of the best, definitely. They're tired as hell, you can see it, but they're still fighting top form. We haven't lost anyone since I got here." Inadvertently answering the question as to why he'd been embedded here. Of course, my thoughts get interrupted as a MAC90D set opens up full rate on an enemy something. Even in the trench, I can feel the wind from the launching shells and reloads. That's when it occurs to me; they said social interest. I turned toward one of the Bovi - looks like a Major. "Sir, can I ask you a few quick questions?" He grunted and nodded, using a soaked handkerchief to try and clear some of the mud from his muzzle. "You've had the volunteers here a few days now. How would you describe the relationship?" That actually made him pause, thinking about it, not necessarily in diplomatic terms. "A week ago, would've refused. Sat'em down as aides. But frankly, having seen them fight? Maybe they can't haul an AMR, maybe they can't carry a hundred kilos at a go, but damned if they don't have it where it counts." Rising to his hooves, he turned and actually saluted the two humans. "I'd take these two into hell with me - done themselves more than proud." Predictably, they both saluted back, clearly stunned. That setup always worked for the propaganda stuff. Besides, folks like that never shirked their duties. They'd fight twice as hard just to prove they were every bit as good as the other species. "Then can I ask you all.... how do you think the battle is going here?" Looks were quickly exchanged, and the Major took over again. "Official canned answer, we expect to rout the enemy any hour and completely destroy their assets. Unofficially, we've taking a pounding but they're getting it worse. Soon as we get some air support, it's mopping up time. We're in a good position, we have the best people, we'll be home for breakfast at least." "So we're winning?" "Yep. We're winning," he agreed, "just as soon as the air support gets here." There was a scream of engines approaching, and he looked up while also pointing. There was no mistaking that it was a Hog II ground attack aircraft. There was an unusual whirring as the main gun fired, the camera tracking as it moved off into the distance. And didn't turn around. "Well shit. Bingo ammo. So we wait a little longer." All I could do was turn toward the humans, who looked elated and dejected at the same time. "So what are you thinking?" The woman shrugged helplessly, but the man shook his head confidently. "Bad call, should have sent fresh planes. Gotten some of ours out of mothballs faster, maybe. But, if the Major says we can take them out? I wouldn't doubt it for a minute. We'll win. Then we'll go find another fight and win that too. Biggest mistake these idiots ever made was invading our homes. Every inch they want to take, we'll make them fight and bleed for." I couldn't have asked for a more perfect close. Flipping the camera to face me again, I put on my best smile. "And there you have it. This is Larry Sun for DFIC, signing off."

Let's begin with some fundamental concepts of American Utilities companies and processes. The realm of television can be divided into various categories. There are Broadcast Networks and Cable Television Networks. Contrary to popular belief, these aren't equivalent to Antenna versus Cable Television. Broadcast Networks encompass entities such as ABC, CBS, FOX, and NBC - your typical American Broadcast Companies. They are commonly linked to local news networks and operate under a legal mandate to broadcast freely, which means viewers don't pay monthly or access fees to enjoy local news. Although they generate revenue via advertising and other sales, these entities remain public entities.

On the other hand, Cable networks differ from traditional Cable TV but share roots with Community Access Television (CATV). Initially, CATV systems emerged in areas where local content and programming thrived. Following the creation of the first CATV system, there was an abundance of unused space in local networks, independent of radio waves, leading to the production of local content. Over time, these productions were shared and retransmitted as things expanded. Stations like CNN, FXX, USA, TNT, and TBS originated as local or regional stations and didn't come under the same regulatory oversight as Broadcast Networks.

As CATV networks expanded, smaller, regional companies such as Alert Cable, Adelphia, and Carolina Cable were acquired by multinational corporations. CATV networks began billing for the services that the Community Antenna networks initially provided and established communication channels between each other. With growth came consolidation within the industry.

As you go deeper into the Earth, both pressure and temperature increase greatly. They increase so much, that it makes it incredibly difficult to get too far past the crust into hotter depths. The reason why this is true in general, but also especially for hot magma from deep within the earths interior (which can reach temperatures of several thousand degrees C when erupted), comes down to two different things: 1) The more energy dissipation there is along a system's lengthline, 2) the higher heat capacity of materials closer to their melting point. To oversimplify things, as we drill through rock deeper into the Earth, it gets harder each time because at some depth, all of the energy can be absorbed and not redistributed or converted back into something else. This means that after a certain depth, extracting energy is like hitting brick walls with your hands instead of removing them via kinetic action. It's important to note here that while we're talking about the existence of 'hot rocks' on the surface of our planet, these are actually cold by comparison - they don't have enough thermal mass to maintain very high internal heats without being eroded away fairly quickly. If I had an analogy relating to my favorite sport, swimming, imagine trying to swim laps underwater without goggles...it'd be nearly impossible! But if one was wearing large sunglasses over said goggles, then yes; the ability would dramatically improve! So what happens? Some of that hard-hitting heat transfers up to the surface of the oceans, where it melts icecaps and snowpack for example.

Humans' large brains may be due to a single "typo" in their genetic code, according to new research. In a study recently published in the journal Nature Ecology and Evolution, researchers from the University of Edinburgh analyzed the DNA of humans and Neanderthals. They found that humans have a unique variation in a gene called NOTCH2NL, which is known to affect brain size. The researchers believe that this variation may have occurred as a result of a random error in the genetic code when our ancestors first split from Neanderthals, around 600,000 years ago. This "typo" then became part of the human genetic code, contributing to the larger brains we see today. This study adds to the evidence that small changes in our genetics can have a huge impact on our evolution. It also provides further insight into why humans have such large brains compared to our closest evolutionary relatives. Lead researcher Dr. Gunchin Zhang said: "Our findings suggest that a single letter change in the genetic code was enough to give rise to an important difference between humans and Neanderthals. We don't know yet what precise role this gene plays in brain development, but our research opens up new avenues for future studies." The team now plans to investigate further how this variation affects the development of the human brain, and how it has impacted our evolution.

In the world of international football, there is much debate over which team can claim to be the greatest of all time. Many nations have had teams that have achieved unprecedented success on the biggest stages and have gone down in history as some of the most iconic sides ever seen. The Brazil national side of is often hailed as one of the best international teams of all time. Led by the likes of Pele, Jairzinho and Garrincha, Brazil won three World Cups during this period and were the first nation to win consecutive titles. They also boasted an impressive record in friendly matches, winning 79 out of 103 games, with 39 wins coming in a row. Another team considered to be among the greatest is the Hungarian side of the 1950s. Their run at the 1954 World Cup was particularly remarkable, where they beat West Germany 3-2 in the final. Hungary went unbeaten in 31 games leading up to the tournament, which remains a record unbeaten streak for any international team. In terms of individual honours, the Spanish national team of 2008-2012 is arguably the greatest ever. Under the guidance of Vicente Del Bosque, Spain won two European Championships and their first ever World Cup. During this period, they also reached the top of the FIFA rankings, becoming the first country to hold the distinction of being number one in the world for two consecutive years. The German national team of 2014-2018 is also deserving of recognition. They won the 2014 World Cup, becoming the first European team to win the title in South America. They then successfully defended their crown four years later in Russia, becoming the first nation to win back-to-back World Cups since Brazil in 1962. So who can claim to be the greatest international side of all time? It is difficult to definitively answer such a subjective question. However, the four aforementioned teams are certainly worthy contenders for the title.

For the first several decades of disc record manufacturing, sound was recorded directly on to the "master disc" at the recording studio. From about 1950 on (earlier for some large record companies, later for some small ones) it became usual to have the performance first recorded on audio tape, which could then be processed andor edited, and then dubbed on to the master disc. A record cutter would engrave the grooves into the master disc. Early versions of these master discs were soft wax, and later a harder lacquer was used. The mastering process was originally something of an art as the operator had to manually allow for the changes in sound which affected how wide the space for the groove needed to be on each rotation.

When the neurons that contain certain information die, that's it. Dead. Saying that though, your memory on'cats' for example isn't confined to 1 neuron. You have around 70 Billion neurons, each one connected to others in a certain way. So let's say that you learned german in second grade and don't use it for 10 years. Now let's say you and a stranger who has never learned any german both try and learn german. Some of the neurons that surrounded the once strong neurons will help you tremendously. TL;DR - Use your language to remember it.

Where every component state of a federation possesses the same powers, we are said to find 'symmetric federalism'. Asymmetric federalism exists where states are granted different powers, or some possess greater autonomy than others do. This is often done in recognition of the existence of a distinct culture in a particular region or regions. In Spain, the Basques and Catalans, as well as the Galicians, spearheaded a historic movement to have their national specificity recognized, crystallizing in the "historical communities" such as Navarre, Galicia, Catalonia, and the Basque Country. They have more powers than the later expanded arrangement for other Spanish regions, or the Spain of the autonomous communities (called also the "coffee for everyone" arrangement), partly to deal with their separate identity and to appease peripheral nationalist leanings, partly out of respect to specific rights they had held earlier in history. However, strictly speaking Spain is not a federalism, but a decentralized administrative organization of the state.

Installing software can result in more alterations than merely transferring files to your hard drive. Deleting the files alone won't revert those modifications. For instance, the installer might generate desktop shortcuts and numerous system registry entries, assigning the application as a default handler for specific file extensions, among other things. The uninstaller is responsible for eliminating such entries along with the files. Merely erasing the files won't accomplish this task. Consequently, if the installer carried out the aforementioned registry registrations, Windows will persistently attempt (and fail) to initiate the application upon double-clicking an .mp3 file. Furthermore, you'll possess a defunct shortcut on your desktop. Any additional modifications the installer made, which you opted against reversing, will also remain. Essentially, your computer could become somewhat disorganized, with certain functions becoming faulty.

Programs frequently introduce new registry keys during installation, which aren't eliminated through file deletion. Typically, an installer handles their removal. Additionally, some applications keep cache and other files scattered across various locations on your computer. Without extensive knowledge of these locations, you likely can't guarantee locating and removing every last one. It's crucial to remember that installers and uninstallers stem from the same developer. Should the uninstaller not be engineered to eliminate items thoroughly, it won't. There's no regulatory body enforcing the uninstaller to carry out its duties correctly. Therefore, even with uninstallers, you'll generally retain leftover files, settings, and registry keys from your programs.

Immigrants arrived from all over the world to search for gold, especially from Ireland and China. Many Chinese miners worked in Victoria, and their legacy is particularly strong in Bendigo today where there are many restaurants with a distinctly Asian flavour thanks to them. However, most people came here looking for work - Australian agriculture was booming around this time due to increasing demand by European countries such as Britain and France following World War I, so jobs were plentiful at first. This made life much easier for those coming across the seas into Australia; they could find employment almost immediately without having to pay recruitment agents or travel huge distances to reach these destinations (about 40 of immigrants travelled on ships that would take between 6-8 weeks). A lot of Irish emigrated during this period because of famine conditions back home, it's often said that more than 100,000 left after 1847 alone! There had been a gradual decline in job opportunities though throughout the 1880s which eventually saw large numbers of unemployed men who couldn't get off the boats. The solution? Ship out thousands of women instead. In fact, some female passengers even refused to go until male relatives joined up too - but in reality, families acted together like one unit when leaving a country under threat anyway, whether husbandsfathers went away or not. And while it's now common knowledge about the number of girls sent overseas to be married against their will (even if this practice has mostly ended), less well known is how desperate the situation was for young single working age men once their wives were gone: widowers outnumbered children aged 5 years old and below fivefold...and yet still no room aboard ship. It took longer before any white man found himself compelled to leave his family behind simply because he lacked money. Most times they became labourers themselves rather than become homeless wanderers roaming through western Europe. When immigration quotas began being introduced in 1901 by our government, an estimated 200 million migrants passed through ports worldwide trying to make it to new lives elsewhere. Of course, only half actually managed to arrive safely!

Virtually all staple foods come either directly from primary production by plants, or indirectly from animals that eat them. Plants and other photosynthetic organisms are at the base of most food chains because they use the energy from the sun and nutrients from the soil and atmosphere, converting them into a form that can be used by animals. This is what ecologists call the first trophic level. The modern forms of the major staple foods, such as maize, rice, wheat and other cereal grasses, pulses, bananas and plantains, as well as flax and cotton grown for their fibres, are the outcome of prehistoric selection over thousands of years from among wild ancestral plants with the most desirable characteristics. Botanists study how plants produce food and how to increase yields, for example through plant breeding, making their work important to mankind's ability to feed the world and provide food security for future generations. Botanists also study weeds, which are a considerable problem in agriculture, and the biology and control of plant pathogens in agriculture and natural ecosystems. Ethnobotany is the study of the relationships between plants and people. When applied to the investigation of historical plant-people relationships ethnobotany may be referred to as archaeobotany or palaeoethnobotany.

When your videogame creates the video, each frame is generated separately, and is a completely static image - you can take a screenshot and it'll look like it was taken from a film or a painting. For example, a monitor running at 60Hz can display 60 unique images per second. If you force it to display 120 images per second, each image will be shown twice - it won't be displayed twice as fast. It'll be shown twice, and then the next image will be shown twice. It's not a big deal, but the video will look weird, because now every frame will be displayed twice. The problem is, you're displaying a static image. Most monitors, and most video cards, are designed to work with static images. And that's where G-SYNC comes in. G-SYNC is a new technology, invented by NVIDIA, and available only on NVIDIA video cards. It's designed to make video output look much better, in terms of motion. The idea is simple: it changes the refresh rate of your monitor dynamically. To understand how it works, let's take a look at a normal monitor. Your monitor, when it runs at 60Hz, displays 60 unique images per second. It refreshes the whole screen 60 times per second. And it refreshes the screen at the same rate, no matter what. So if your video card generates 60 frames per second, the monitor will display each frame once. If it generates 120 frames per second, it will display each frame twice. Now, let's see what happens if we turn on G-SYNC. You can see that now, your monitor is refreshing at different rates. In fact, the rate at which it refreshes the screen is completely determined by the video card, and is dynamic - the refresh rate changes as the video card generates new frames. So if your video card generates 60 frames per second, the monitor will refresh at 60Hz, and each frame will be displayed once. If your video card generates 120 frames per second, the monitor will refresh at 120Hz, and each frame will be displayed once. And if your video card generates 150 frames per second, the monitor will refresh at 150Hz. As you can see, if you have a G-SYNC monitor, you don't need to worry about VSYNC. John Dalton's original atomic hypothesis assumed that all elements were monatomic and that the atoms in compounds would normally have the simplest atomic ratios with respect to one another. For example, Dalton assumed that water's formula was HO, giving the atomic mass of oxygen as 8 times that of hydrogen, instead of the modern value of about 16. In 1805, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Alexander von Humboldt showed that water is formed of two volumes of hydrogen and one volume of oxygen; and by 1811 Amedeo Avogadro had arrived at the correct interpretation of water's composition, based on what is now called Avogadro's law and the assumption of diatomic elemental molecules.[a]

An upward trend has emerged in employing robust control schemes founded on the graph theoretic characteristics of r- and (r, s)-resilience. Such algorithms ensure agreement among healthy agents despite a restricted number of errant agents when r and s integers hold adequate sizes. However, assessing an arbitrary graph's resilience is a complex task. In this study, we propose a new technique for evaluating r- and (r, s)-resilience in directed graphs using mixed integer linear programming. To our knowledge, this marks the initial application of mixed integer programming techniques to the robustness assessment problem. With merely the graph Laplacian matrix information, this strategy can be framed in terms of binary integer variables. We leverage mixed integer programming algorithms like branch-and-bound to progressively optimize the lower and upper limits of r and s through iterative processes. Performance comparisons versus previous robustness determination algorithms are provided via simulations.

Members of the genus Dinophysis have a phycobilin-containing chloroplast taken from a cryptophyte. However, the cryptophyte is not an endosymbiont - only the chloroplast seems to have been taken, and the endosymbiont's nucleus has been lost. Dinophysis also contain a protein complex (a phycobilisome) that is composed of phycobiliproteins, but they lack the typical phycobilin pigments. Thus, it is believed that they were once free-living, photosynthetic organisms, but acquired a phycobilisome via endosymbiosis. Other species of the genus have lost the phycobilisome and now contain a single membrane-bound chlorophyll-containing plastid. Like most cyanobacteria, dinophysids are rod-shaped, but their plastids are flattened and form a small disk. This structure, called a prostoclum, is located at the distal end of the cell, near the base of the rod. They are usually transparent, but they sometimes stain green or blue. The two-celled dinoflagellates have been studied in a variety of detail because of their importance as model organisms for the study of cell biology and biochemistry. They are known to be able to accumulate large amounts of copper in their cytoplasm, which is then stored in the mitochondria. The copper is then taken up by bacteria in the surrounding water, and they use it to fix carbon dioxide. Some species of dinoflagellates can also oxidize manganese. One of the most common species of dinoflagellate is Karenia brevis. The genome of this organism was sequenced in 2012. Dinoflagellates are unusual in that they contain more than one nucleus, located at different sites in the cell. The nucleus located in the prostoclum has been shown to have the ability to proliferate in vitro. The mitochondrial nucleus is a vestigial remnant of the endosymbiotic event, and is found at the base of the cell near the end of the rod-shaped body. The mitochondrial genome is also double-stranded, but the nuclear genome is single-stranded.

Missile Defense Systems, contrary to their title, serve offensive rather than protective functions. Their primary role is to thwart a reprisal attack, contingent upon a preliminary assault decimating a significant portion of an adversary's existing nuclear arsenal. Thus, the defensive mechanism wouldn't be overpowered during the actual retaliation. Be it Iran or Russia, every nation has the legitimate prerogative to erect such systems. The notion of MAD, or mutual assured destruction, hinges on the idea that war serves no benefit to either party, with each side facing annihilation equivalent to that inflicted upon the other. With a more robust defensive system, this equilibrium is disrupted, granting an upper hand. Consequently, one could potentially eliminate their adversary while enduring lesser damage. The apprehension lies in the ensuing arms race. As the weaker party, your adversary would endeavor to bolster their defenses and weaponry. In response, you would follow suit, creating a vicious cycle. This could shift the landscape of conflict into a potentially "winnable" scenario, leading to increased instability.

Autism represents a range of developmental disorders, marked chiefly by complications in social relations and language comprehension. Symptoms encompass challenges in interpreting body language, maintaining friendships, and grasping abstract ideas. These issues emerge during childhood. Asperger syndrome is a type of autism, featuring notable struggles in social interaction and verbal and nonverbal communication, accompanied by rigid routines and fixated interests. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), formerly recognized as Attention Deficit Disorder (ADD), denotes a persistent condition distinguished by attention lapses, excessive activity, and occasional impulsiveness. Clarifying these distinctions? Autism signifies a collection of developmental conditions that predominantly revolve around difficulties with socializing. Manifestations fluctuate significantly, including trouble deciphering body language, reticence, and failure to comprehend sarcasm. Individuals with autism may appear "uncomfortable" to others. The autism spectrum spans from those with minimal symptoms to those entirely incapacitated. Asperger's is a distinct autistic subtype. ADHD, a prevalent affliction, principally presents as a limited capacity to maintain concentration, diminished motivation, and deficiency in focusing. ADHD stems from an unusually low default level of neural activity, compelling the brain to persistently seek fresh stimuli to elevate the baseline to standard levels. Consequently, individuals with ADHD effortlessly lose interest. The ADHD mind functions much like an individual perpetually famished, consistently yearning for sustenance due to insufficient satiety. Hence, ADHD is frequently managed with stimulants like Adderall, which augment the baseline level of cerebral activity and facilitate better application of energy. Intriguingly, individuals with autism or ADHD frequently exhibit exceptional aptitude in unrelated domains. While not all, some autistic individuals are labeled as "savants," exhibiting remarkable abilities in diverse fields such as art, music, or memory recall.

Over time, this designation became synonymous with medical professionals. However, contemporary academic regulations necessitate completing a doctoral degree for the official title. In the past, surgeons were considered a lower discipline due to limited educational opportunities, resulting in their being addressed as "Mr./Mrs." Instead. Notably, at Cambridge and Oxford universities, doctors hold Ph.D. and D.Phil., respectively. The term "doctor" derives from the Latin root "docere," which means "to teach." While physicians pursue the Doctor of Medicine degree, other disciplines such as law (Juris Doctor) and pharmacy (Doctor of Pharmacy) possess unique doctorate-level degrees. For the next three hundred years, Scotland was directly governed by the Parliament of Great Britain and the subsequent Parliament of the United Kingdom, both seated at Westminster, and the lack of a Parliament of Scotland remained an important element in Scottish national identity. Suggestions for a'devolved' Parliament were made before 1914, but were shelved due to the outbreak of the First World War. A sharp rise in nationalism in Scotland during the late 1960s fuelled demands for some form of home rule or complete independence, and in 1969 prompted the incumbent Labour government of Harold Wilson to set up the Kilbrandon Commission to consider the British constitution. One of the principal objectives of the commission was to examine ways of enabling more self-government for Scotland, within the unitary state of the United Kingdom. Kilbrandon published his report in 1973 recommending the establishment of a directly elected Scottish Assembly to legislate for the majority of domestic Scottish affairs.

Software items seldom originate solely from scratch, and weaknesses in these items may lie in components derived from open source software or external entities. Consequently, a product's comprehensive cybersecurity relies on collaboration, either overt or covert, among various organizations. Our research investigates the approaches and tendencies of corporations within software ecosystems concerning the dissemination of vulnerability data. Additionally, we assess these practices against current cybersecurity standards. This examination ensues through a questionnaire-driven qualitative study. The questionnaire comprises two sections: providers' viewpoint and purchasers' viewpoint. Our findings reveal that businesses are prepared to exchange vulnerability details with one another. Such disclosures are deemed advantageous neither for security nor business purposes, although most respondents regard vulnerability data as confidential. Nevertheless, companies are reluctant to initiate the distribution of vulnerability information. Moreover, suppliers do not believe that their clients exhibit substantial curiosity toward vulnerability data. Therefore, the corporate mindset towards disseminating vulnerability information is predominantly passive yet open. In contrast, modern cybersecurity suggestions advocate active exposure and information exchange among ecosystem participants.

Instead of fees rising to PS9,250 per year in the autumn, Jeremy Corbyn is proposing a complete handbrake turn in saying that university tuition should not cost students anything. But what about when you're trying to get on the housing ladder? Do we still go against market logic and offer free museums or parks? No, it just doesn't work like that. We study the problem of joint information and energy transfer in a two-hop channel with a Radio frequency (RF) energy harvesting relay. We consider a finite battery size at the relay and aim to maximize the system throughput subject to the energy causality constraint and the battery capacity constraint. The channel includes a source node, an energy harvesting relay, and a destination node. The source node has information to transmit to the destination node, and the relay harvests energy from the RF signal transmitted by the source and then uses it to forward the information to the destination node. The energy harvested by the relay is used to power both the relay's circuits and the retransmission of the source's signal. To solve this problem, we propose a joint power allocation and relay selection algorithm that maximizes the system throughput while satisfying the energy causality constraint and the battery capacity constraint. The algorithm considers the trade-off between maximizing the harvested energy and minimizing the transmit power at the source node. It also selects the best relay to forward the information to the destination node based on the channel state. Simulation results show the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in maximizing the system throughput while ensuring energy efficiency.
